### Variable Definitions and Mathematical Notation {#sec-beta-variables}

The dataset contains the final-grade response together with ten recorded student characteristics. Nevertheless, for the regression equation modelling, a categorical variable with more than two levels cannot generally be represented by a single numerical regressor when treatment coding is used. Instead, as shown in @tbl-dummy-variables, a variable with $u$ levels contributes $u-1$ indicator regressors after one level is chosen as the reference category.

Accordingly, we use $x_{i,j}$ to denote the **numerical regressors that can appear as columns of a design matrix**, rather than using one $x$-symbol for each raw data column. Moreover, let $\mathbb{1}{\cdot}$ denote the indicator function, which equals $1$ when the condition inside braces is true and $0$ otherwise. Indicator functions let us convert category membership into numerical regressors that can enter the design matrix. For example, $\mathbb{1}{\text{Study Time is 1-3 hours}}=1$ for a student in the 1–3 hours category and equals $0$ for a student in any of the other study time categories. Using one such indicator for each non-reference category allows a categorical regressor to be represented numerically without imposing an artificial numerical spacing among its levels.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-etherpad-group-work-3683373/).](img/interval.png){width="500"}

Now, for student $i$, define the full candidate regressor vector

$$
\mathbf{x}_i
=
\left(
x_{i,1},
x_{i,2},
\ldots,
x_{i,21}
\right)^\top,
$$

where $i=1,\ldots,n$. The 21 entries correspond to the treatment-coded categorical regressors and the numerical regressors listed in @tbl-beta-variable-dictionary. This indexing is fixed for the remainder of the chapter.

The first three entries, $x_{i,1}$, $x_{i,2}$, and $x_{i,3}$, encode **study time** because study time is the primary inferential and predictive regressor. With `<1 hour` as the reference category,

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{i,1} = \mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 1-3 hours}\} \\
x_{i,2} = \mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 3-5 hours}\} \\
x_{i,3} = \mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 5+ hours}\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, a student in the `<1 hour` reference category has $x_{i,1}=x_{i,2}=x_{i,3}=0$. This treatment coding respects the ordering of the study time categories without imposing equally spaced numerical scores.

The remaining categorical variables are encoded using the same **reference-category (treatment) coding** principle. When a categorical variable has no scientifically chosen baseline, we select one fixed level. Hence, every non-reference indicator shares a common comparison category, and the resulting coefficients have a consistent interpretation.


::: {.Tip}
::::{.Tip-header}
Tip on why we use a common reference category!
::::
::::{.Tip-container}
Categorical regressors can be represented in several mathematically equivalent full-rank ways, but the resulting coefficients answer different comparison questions. In this chapter, we use **reference-category (treatment) coding** because each non-reference coefficient compares one category with the same baseline. This makes the coefficient interpretation transparent and aligns directly with the category-versus-reference comparisons used in the inferential workflow [@fox2019].

This choice is especially useful for **ordinal regressors** such as **study time**. An ordering of categories does not, by itself, imply that the distances between adjacent levels are equal. The study time categories `<1 hour`, `1–3 hours`, `3–5 hours`, and `5+ hours` are not equally spaced numerical measurements, and the final category is open-ended. We therefore do not encode study time using a numerical score or an orthogonal-polynomial trend.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-emotion-fear-expression-6230192/).](img/curious.png){width="250"}

Other coding systems can be appropriate when the scientific question is different. For example, Helmert, sum-to-zero, successive-difference, or polynomial coding can target comparisons with averages, adjacent levels, or structured trends. In fact, treatment coding is itself one type of **contrast coding** in the general statistical sense. Here, the important distinction is that we deliberately use a **common baseline** rather than polynomial or other structured contrasts. The official `R` documentation for [`contr.treatment()` and `contr.poly()`](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/contrast.html) summarizes these different constructions.
::::
:::

With the reference-category coding fixed, we also need to distinguish the 21 non-intercept regressor columns from the intercept that will appear in the fitted design matrix.

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on regressor columns and the intercept!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
The vector $\mathbf{x}_i$ contains the **21 numerical, non-intercept regressor columns** defined for student $i$. Therefore, a multi-level categorical variable contributes several entries to $\mathbf{x}_i$, not one.

The intercept is still kept separate. When we later write a model in matrix form, the design matrix will prepend a **column of $1$s** to the selected columns of $\mathbf{x}_i$, so the intercept coefficient $\beta_0$ is represented explicitly. For example, the **core study time mean model** will use an intercept together with $x_{i,1}$, $x_{i,2}$, and $x_{i,3}$, whereas a larger candidate mean model can use additional columns from the same fixed 21-regressor design basis.

Keeping this distinction explicit ensures that the $x_{i,j}$ notation introduced here remains consistent with the design matrix used later for estimation.
::::
:::

@tbl-beta-variable-dictionary records the raw variables, their roles, and the exact design-matrix columns they generate.

::: {.table-scroll}

| **Code variable** | **Role** | **Data type** | **Mathematical notation** | **Units** | **Description** | **Category/reference coding** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| `Final Grade (%)` | Response | Continuous numeric | $Y_i$ / $y_i$ after response preparation | Percentage in the raw data; proportion on the modelling scale | Final course grade for student $i$. | Not applicable. | 
| `Study Time` | Primary inferential and predictive regressor | Ordered categorical | $x_{i,1}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ studies 1-3 hours per week}\}}$ <br> $x_{i,2}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ studies 3-5 hours per week}\}}$ <br> $x_{i,3}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ studies 5+ hours per week}\}}$ | Weekly study-time category | Recorded amount of time spent studying. | `<1 hour` is the reference category. | 
| `Café Location` | Candidate regressor | Nominal categorical | $x_{i,4}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ uses Bean Around the World}\}}$ <br> $x_{i,5}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ uses Ike's Café}\}}$ <br> $x_{i,6}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ uses Koerner's Pub}\}}$ <br> $x_{i,7}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ uses The Loop Café}\}}$ | Category | Primary café or study location recorded for the student. | `AMS Nest` is the reference category. |
| `Year in School` | Candidate regressor | Ordered categorical | $x_{i,8}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ is in 2nd Year}\}}$ <br> $x_{i,9}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ is in 3rd Year}\}}$ <br> $x_{i,10}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ is in 4th Year}\}}$ | Academic-year category | Recorded academic year of the student. | `1st Year` is the reference category. | 
| `Hobbies` | Candidate regressor | Nominal categorical | $x_{i,11}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ reports Music}\}}$ <br> $x_{i,12}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ reports Reading}\}}$ <br> $x_{i,13}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ reports Sports}\}}$ | Category | Primary hobby recorded for the student. | `Gaming` is the reference category. | 
| `Primary Sport` | Candidate regressor | Nominal categorical | $x_{i,14}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ reports Basketball}\}}$ <br> $x_{i,15}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ reports Soccer}\}}$ | Category | Main sport recorded for the student, if any. | `None` is the reference category after the working-data recoding below. | 
| `Living Arrangement` | Candidate regressor | Nominal categorical | $x_{i,16}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ lives At Home}\}}$ <br> $x_{i,17}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ lives With Friends}\}}$ | Category | Recorded living situation of the student. | `Alone` is the reference category. | 
| `Part-time Work Hours` | Candidate regressor | Numeric integer | $x_{i,18}$ | Hours per week | Number of hours worked per week in a part-time job. | Numerical regressor; no reference category. | 
| `Study Group Participation` | Candidate regressor | Binary categorical | $x_{i,19}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ participates in a study group}\}}$ | Indicator | Whether the student participates in a study group. | `No` is the reference category. |
| `Hours of Sleep per Night` | Candidate regressor | Continuous numeric | $x_{i,20}$ | Hours per night | Average number of hours of sleep per night. | Numerical regressor; no reference category. | 
| `Has a Tutor` | Candidate regressor | Binary categorical | $x_{i,21}=\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ has a tutor}\}}$ | Indicator | Whether the student receives tutoring support. | `No` is the reference category. | 

: Variable dictionary and fixed design-matrix notation for the student final-grade Beta regression case study (scroll from left to right). {#tbl-beta-variable-dictionary .striped .hover}

:::

For the multi-level categorical variables in @tbl-beta-variable-dictionary, each listed $x_{i,j}$ is an indicator for membership in the corresponding non-reference category. Consequently, the complete candidate design basis contains 21 non-intercept columns, **but the core running model does not use all 21**. Its mean structure is intentionally based on study time and therefore uses only $x_{i,1}$, $x_{i,2}$, and $x_{i,3}$ together with an intercept. The larger set of columns is available only for explicitly motivated training-stage model-complexity checks.

### Initial Data-integrity Checks {#sec-beta-data-integrity}

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/children-teacher-rectangular-figures-7464615/).](img/round.png){width="600"}

Before transforming the response or creating the training/testing split, we check the dimensions of the imported object, exact duplicate rows, missing or blank entries, the raw response range, the occurrence of boundary grades, and the categorical levels needed for the design coding in @tbl-beta-variable-dictionary. We also verify whether `Primary Sport` contains any blank or missing entries that would need to be represented explicitly as `None`. No response transformation or model-specific filtering is performed at this stage.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-integrity-r
#| tbl-cap: "Initial data-integrity summary for the full academic performance dataset."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

count_missing_or_blank <- function(data) {
  missing <- sum(is.na(data))
  blanks <- sum(vapply(data, function(column) {
    if (!(is.character(column) || is.factor(column))) return(0L)
    sum(trimws(as.character(column)) == "", na.rm = TRUE)
  }, integer(1)))
  missing + blanks
}

primary_sport_values <- trimws(as.character(academic_raw$`Primary Sport`))
primary_sport_none <- is.na(academic_raw$`Primary Sport`) | primary_sport_values == ""

academic_raw_missing_or_blank <- count_missing_or_blank(academic_raw)
primary_sport_none_n <- sum(primary_sport_none, na.rm = TRUE)

academic_data <- academic_raw |>
  mutate(`Primary Sport` = if_else(primary_sport_none, "None", primary_sport_values))

academic_missing_or_blank <- count_missing_or_blank(academic_data)

expected_levels <- list(
  `Study Time` = c("<1 hour", "1–3 hours", "3–5 hours", "5+ hours"),
  `Café Location` = c("AMS Nest", "Bean Around the World", "Ike's Café",
    "Koerner's Pub", "The Loop Café"),
  `Year in School` = c("1st Year", "2nd Year", "3rd Year", "4th Year"),
  Hobbies = c("Gaming", "Music", "Reading", "Sports"),
  `Primary Sport` = c("None", "Basketball", "Soccer"),
  `Living Arrangement` = c("Alone", "At Home", "With Friends"),
  `Study Group Participation` = c("No", "Yes"),
  `Has a Tutor` = c("No", "Yes")
)

categorical_levels_ok <- all(vapply(names(expected_levels), function(variable) {
  setequal(unique(as.character(academic_data[[variable]])), expected_levels[[variable]])
}, logical(1)))

academic_integrity <- tibble(
  Check = c("Number of observations", "Number of variables", "Exact duplicate rows",
    "Raw missing/blank entries", "Entries recoded as no primary sport",
    "Remaining missing/blank entries", "Categorical level check",
    "Minimum final grade (%)", "Maximum final grade (%)", "Exact 100% grades",
    "Exact 0% grades"),
  Value = c(format(nrow(academic_data), big.mark = ","), ncol(academic_data),
    sum(duplicated(academic_raw)), academic_raw_missing_or_blank, primary_sport_none_n,
    academic_missing_or_blank, if_else(categorical_levels_ok, "Passed", "Failed"),
    sprintf("%.4f", min(academic_data$`Final Grade (%)`)),
    sprintf("%.4f", max(academic_data$`Final Grade (%)`)),
    sum(academic_data$`Final Grade (%)` == 100),
    sum(academic_data$`Final Grade (%)` == 0))
)

stopifnot(
  academic_raw_missing_or_blank == primary_sport_none_n,
  academic_missing_or_blank == 0,
  categorical_levels_ok
)

academic_integrity |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

import pandas as pd

def count_missing_or_blank(data):
    missing = int(data.isna().sum().sum())
    text_data = data.select_dtypes(include=["object", "string", "category"])
    blanks = sum(int(text_data[column].astype("string").str.strip().eq("")
                     .fillna(False).sum()) for column in text_data.columns)
    return missing + blanks


primary_sport_values = academic_raw["Primary Sport"].astype("string").str.strip()
primary_sport_none = primary_sport_values.isna() | primary_sport_values.eq("")

academic_raw_missing_or_blank = count_missing_or_blank(academic_raw)
primary_sport_none_n = int(primary_sport_none.sum())

academic_data = academic_raw.copy()
academic_data["Primary Sport"] = primary_sport_values.mask(primary_sport_none, "None")
academic_missing_or_blank = count_missing_or_blank(academic_data)

expected_levels = {
    "Study Time": ["<1 hour", "1–3 hours", "3–5 hours", "5+ hours"],
    "Café Location": ["AMS Nest", "Bean Around the World", "Ike's Café",
                      "Koerner's Pub", "The Loop Café"],
    "Year in School": ["1st Year", "2nd Year", "3rd Year", "4th Year"],
    "Hobbies": ["Gaming", "Music", "Reading", "Sports"],
    "Primary Sport": ["None", "Basketball", "Soccer"],
    "Living Arrangement": ["Alone", "At Home", "With Friends"],
    "Study Group Participation": ["No", "Yes"],
    "Has a Tutor": ["No", "Yes"],
}

categorical_levels_ok = all(
    set(academic_data[variable].dropna().astype(str)) == set(levels)
    for variable, levels in expected_levels.items()
)

response = academic_data["Final Grade (%)"]

academic_integrity = pd.DataFrame([
    ["Number of observations", f"{academic_data.shape[0]:,}"],
    ["Number of variables", academic_data.shape[1]],
    ["Exact duplicate rows", int(academic_raw.duplicated().sum())],
    ["Raw missing/blank entries", academic_raw_missing_or_blank],
    ["Entries recoded as no primary sport", primary_sport_none_n],
    ["Remaining missing/blank entries", academic_missing_or_blank],
    ["Categorical level check", "Passed" if categorical_levels_ok else "Failed"],
    ["Minimum final grade (%)", f"{response.min():.4f}"],
    ["Maximum final grade (%)", f"{response.max():.4f}"],
    ["Exact 100% grades", int(response.eq(100).sum())],
    ["Exact 0% grades", int(response.eq(0).sum())],
], columns=["Check", "Value"])

assert academic_raw_missing_or_blank == primary_sport_none_n
assert academic_missing_or_blank == 0
assert categorical_levels_ok

academic_integrity_html = scrollable_table_html(academic_integrity)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-integrity-py
#| tbl-cap: "Initial data-integrity summary for the full academic performance dataset."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", reticulate::py$academic_integrity_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

As shown in @tbl-beta-integrity-r, the dataset contains **`r format(nrow(academic_data), big.mark = ",")` students measured on `r ncol(academic_data)` variables**, with **`r sum(duplicated(academic_raw))` exact duplicate rows**. The package object is also complete: it contains **`r academic_raw_missing_or_blank` missing or blank entries**, and **`r primary_sport_none_n` observations require recoding** to the explicit `None` level for `Primary Sport`. Consequently, no observations need to be removed or imputed before modelling. The categorical-level check also passes, confirming that the levels used to define the reference categories and the 21 design-matrix regressors in @tbl-beta-variable-dictionary are all represented as expected in the imported data.

The final-grade response requires more attention. Its observed values range from **`r sprintf("%.4f", min(academic_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]))`%** to **`r sprintf("%.4f", max(academic_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]))`%**, so all students have positive grades and the upper boundary of the grading scale is actually attained. Specifically, **`r sum(academic_data[["Final Grade (%)"]] == 100)` students received exactly 100%**, while **`r sum(academic_data[["Final Grade (%)"]] == 0)` students received exactly 0%**. This distinction is critical because simply dividing the percentages by $100$ would place the six perfect grades exactly at $y_i=1$, whereas a standard Beta distribution has support only on $0<y_i<1$. Therefore, rescaling alone is not sufficient for this dataset. In @sec-beta-response-preparation, we will distinguish the percentage-to-proportion rescaling from the additional boundary-handling step required before fitting the Beta regression model.

Finally, we verify the representation of the **study time categories** that generate $x_{i,1}$, $x_{i,2}$, and $x_{i,3}$.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-study-time-counts-r
#| tbl-cap: "Number and percentage of students in each study time category."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

study_time_order <- c("<1 hour", "1–3 hours", "3–5 hours", "5+ hours")

study_time_counts <- academic_data |>
  count(`Study Time`, name = "Students") |>
  mutate(`Study Time` = factor(`Study Time`, levels = study_time_order)) |>
  arrange(`Study Time`) |>
  mutate(`Sample percentage` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * Students / nrow(academic_data)))

study_time_counts |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

study_time_order = ["<1 hour", "1–3 hours", "3–5 hours", "5+ hours"]

study_time_counts = (
    academic_data["Study Time"].value_counts().reindex(study_time_order)
    .rename_axis("Study Time").reset_index(name="Students")
)
study_time_counts["Sample percentage"] = (
    100 * study_time_counts["Students"] / len(academic_data)
).map(lambda value: f"{value:.1f}%")

study_time_counts_html = scrollable_table_html(study_time_counts)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-study-time-counts-py
#| tbl-cap: "Number and percentage of students in each study time category."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", reticulate::py$study_time_counts_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

As @tbl-beta-study-time-counts-r shows, the four **study time categories** are quite evenly represented. The `<1 hour` reference category contains `r study_time_counts$Students[1]` students, followed by `r study_time_counts$Students[2]` in `1–3 hours`, `r study_time_counts$Students[3]` in `3–5 hours`, and `r study_time_counts$Students[4]` in `5+ hours`. These correspond to approximately `r study_time_counts[["Sample percentage"]][1]`, `r study_time_counts[["Sample percentage"]][2]`, `r study_time_counts[["Sample percentage"]][3]`, and `r study_time_counts[["Sample percentage"]][4]` of the full dataset, respectively. The **largest and smallest categories** differ by only `r max(study_time_counts$Students) - min(study_time_counts$Students)` students, so none of the study time indicators is being defined from a sparsely represented category. In particular, the `<1 hour` baseline itself has ample representation for the category-versus-reference comparisons encoded by $x_{i,1}$, $x_{i,2}$, and $x_{i,3}$.

Checking these counts before the training/testing split does not use the response $Y_i$ and therefore does not constitute outcome-based EDA. Instead, it verifies that the categorical structure we intend to preserve is present in the full dataset. This is particularly useful because the split in @sec-beta-data-splitting will be stratified by study time: maintaining these four categories in similar proportions across the training and testing sets will ensure that each part of the analysis contains observations from every study time level.

At this stage, the integrity checks do not indicate a need to remove observations, collapse study time categories, or alter the fixed 21-column design basis. The feature that **does require additional preparation** is the response itself: six students have an exact grade of 100%, which would become $y_i=1$ after simple division by 100 and would fall outside the open support of the standard Beta distribution. We address precisely that issue next in @sec-beta-response-preparation.

## Preparing the Response for Standard Beta Regression {#sec-beta-response-preparation}

The integrity checks in @sec-beta-data-integrity identified one feature that must be resolved before a **standard Beta likelihood** can be fitted: although the final grade is naturally bounded, six observations occur exactly at the upper boundary of the grading scale. Hence, response preparation requires two distinct operations:

- First, we rescale the original percentage to the unit interval. 
- Second, we apply one fixed boundary-handling rule that moves the modelling response strictly inside $(0,1)$.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-social-network-3704066/).](img/privacy.png){width="500"}

These operations are **deterministic preprocessing steps**. They are defined before the training/testing split and then kept unchanged throughout model development, inference, and prediction. The original percentage variable is also retained so that fitted means, contrasts, and point-prediction errors can later be communicated on the familiar grade-percentage scale.

### Rescaling to the Unit Interval {#sec-beta-rescaling}

Let $g_i$ denote the observed final-grade percentage for student $i$. The first step converts this percentage to a proportion:

$$
y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}
=
\frac{g_i}{100}.
$${#eq-beta-rescaling}

This transformation changes only the scale: a grade of $75\%$ becomes $0.75$, a grade of $100\%$ becomes $1$, and the ordering and relative positions of the observations are preserved. We use the superscript $\mathrm{raw}$ here because this simple rescaling does **not yet** produce the final response used in the standard Beta likelihood.

In the code, we retain the original percentage column and create a separate proportion column.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-rescaling-r
#| lst-cap: "Rescaling the final-grade percentage to a proportion."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

academic_prepared <- academic_data |>
  mutate(grade_proportion_raw = `Final Grade (%)` / 100)
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-rescaling-py
#| lst-cap: "Rescaling the final-grade percentage to a proportion."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

academic_prepared = academic_data.copy()
academic_prepared["grade_proportion_raw"] = academic_prepared["Final Grade (%)"] / 100
```

:::

After this rescaling, the **observed proportions range** from `r sprintf("%.6f", min(academic_prepared[["grade_proportion_raw"]]))` to `r sprintf("%.6f", max(academic_prepared[["grade_proportion_raw"]]))`. In particular, **`r sum(academic_prepared[["grade_proportion_raw"]] == 1)` observations equal exactly $1$**, so the rescaled response still does not satisfy the open-support requirement of standard Beta regression.

### The Boundary Problem {#sec-beta-boundary-problem}

The standard Beta distribution is defined for a continuous response whose possible values lie strictly inside the open unit interval. Thus, the modelling response must satisfy

$$
0<Y_i<1.
$$

The endpoints are excluded. Thus, a value of $Y_i=0$ or $Y_i=1$ cannot contribute an ordinary Beta density value under the standard likelihood developed in this chapter [@ferrari2004; @smithson2006].

For the student dataset, simple division by $100$ leaves **`r sum(academic_prepared[["grade_proportion_raw"]] == 1)` perfect grades at $y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}=1$** and **`r sum(academic_prepared[["grade_proportion_raw"]] == 0)` observations at $y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}=0$**. The issue is consequently concentrated at the upper boundary, but even one exact endpoint would be enough to prevent us from fitting the standard Beta likelihood directly to the rescaled response.

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on why rescaling is not the same as handling the boundaries!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
Dividing a percentage by $100$ maps the interval from $[0,100]$ to $[0,1]$; it does not change whether an observation lies on a boundary. Therefore, $100\%$ becomes exactly $1$, not a value just below $1$.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-download-data-transfer-3947910/).](img/pulling.png){width="600"}

This distinction is crucial because the standard Beta model requires an **interior response**. Hence, boundary handling is a separate modelling decision from ordinary percentage-to-proportion rescaling.
::::
:::

A different model would be appropriate if exact boundary values represented a scientifically distinct outcome-generating mechanism that we wanted to model directly (as discussed in @sec-beta-limitations). Nevertheless, in this synthetic teaching case, we use a fixed literature-supported transformation so that the standard Beta-regression workflow can be developed consistently.

### Boundary-handling Strategy {#sec-beta-boundary-strategy}

For this case study, we adopt the transformation proposed by @smithson2006 for bounded responses containing endpoint observations. Let $n$ denote the size of the **full dataset before splitting**, and let $y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}$ denote the simply rescaled proportion as in @eq-beta-rescaling. We define the modelling-scale observation as

$$
y_i
=
\frac{
y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}(n-1)+0.5
}{
n
}.
$${#eq-beta-smithson-verkuilen}

This transformation sends every observation to the open unit interval. In particular,

$$
y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y_i=\frac{0.5}{n}>0,
$$

and

$$
y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y_i=1-\frac{0.5}{n}<1.
$$

It is important that @eq-beta-smithson-verkuilen is applied to **every observation**, not only to the observations at $0$ or $1$. The same transformation can be written as

$$
y_i
=
y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}
+
\frac{0.5-y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}}{n},
$$

which shows that each rescaled proportion is moved slightly toward $0.5$. For a large sample size $n$, this movement is small for interior observations while still moving exact endpoints away from $0$ and $1$.

For this chapter, we calculate $n$ once from the full imported dataset and then **freeze that value for the entire workflow**. We do not recompute the transformation separately within the training and testing sets. Consequently, a testing observation and a training observation with the same original grade receive exactly the same modelling-scale value.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-boundary-transform-r
#| lst-cap: "Applying the fixed Smithson--Verkuilen boundary transformation."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

full_sample_n <- nrow(academic_prepared)

academic_prepared <- academic_prepared |>
  mutate(
    grade_beta = (grade_proportion_raw * (full_sample_n - 1) + 0.5) / full_sample_n
  )

stopifnot(all(academic_prepared$grade_beta > 0 & academic_prepared$grade_beta < 1))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-boundary-transform-py
#| lst-cap: "Applying the fixed Smithson--Verkuilen boundary transformation."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

full_sample_n = len(academic_prepared)
academic_prepared["grade_beta"] = (
    academic_prepared["grade_proportion_raw"] * (full_sample_n - 1) + 0.5
) / full_sample_n

assert ((academic_prepared["grade_beta"] > 0) &
        (academic_prepared["grade_beta"] < 1)).all()
```

:::

With `r full_sample_n` observations as the overall sample size $n$, an **exact rescaled value of $1$** is mapped to `r sprintf("%.6f", (full_sample_n - 0.5) / full_sample_n)`. The **transformed response** therefore ranges from `r sprintf("%.6f", min(academic_prepared[["grade_beta"]]))` to `r sprintf("%.6f", max(academic_prepared[["grade_beta"]]))`, with no observations remaining at either endpoint.

::: {.Tip}
::::{.Tip-header}
Tip on what we should consider before moving boundary values!
::::
::::{.Tip-container}
The Smithson--Verkuilen adjustment should not be interpreted merely as a mechanical trick for replacing $0$s and $1$s. Smithson and Verkuilen first distinguish the **theoretical bounds of the response scale** from the smallest and largest values that happen to appear in a particular sample. For a response defined on a bounded interval $[a,b]$, they recommend rescaling using those known theoretical bounds and then modifying the rescaled values slightly when necessary to avoid exact $0$s and $1$s [@smithson2006]. This distinction is straightforward for the student-grade response. Its grading scale has known theoretical bounds of $0\%$ and $100\%$, regardless of whether both endpoints appear in the observed dataset. Hence, dividing by $100$ uses the bounds of the measurement scale itself rather than the observed sample minimum and maximum.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-college-3702064/).](img/plug.png){width="500"}

The authors also emphasize that the **meaning of the boundaries is important when choosing a model**. A standard Beta distribution is defined on the open interval $(0,1)$. By contrast, if a response genuinely lives on the closed interval $[0,1]$ and observations at $0$ or $1$ represent genuine probability masses, Smithson and Verkuilen argue that the response may be better viewed as a mixed discrete--continuous process. They discuss Tobit regression as one possible alternative when boundary observations arise through censoring and note that such models treat boundary cases as qualitatively distinct from interior observations [@smithson2006]. Therefore, their broader recommendation is to consider **how the response is generated, whether its bounds are fixed or censoring limits, whether its domain is naturally open or closed, and whether boundary observations have a distinct substantive meaning** before deciding that standard Beta regression is appropriate.

For this synthetic teaching case, we adopt the Smithson--Verkuilen transformation as a fixed preprocessing rule so that all observations can be represented on the open interval required by the standard Beta model. This is a decision for the workflow developed in this chapter. Once chosen, we keep the transformation unchanged throughout the subsequent training/testing analysis and retain the original grade percentage separately for later interpretation on the familiar grading scale.
::::
:::

### Categorical Coding and Reference Levels {#sec-beta-categorical-coding}

Response preparation also gives us an appropriate place to lock the categorical coding that will be used by software implementations. The mathematical design basis was defined in @sec-beta-variables; here we ensure that the software uses the same category order and common reference levels. That said, for the primary study time regressor, `<1 hour` remains the reference category. Using the indicator-function convention introduced in @sec-beta-variables,

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{i,1}
&=
\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ studies 1-3 hours per week}\}}, \\
x_{i,2}
&=
\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ studies 3-5 hours per week}\}}, \\
x_{i,3}
&=
\mathbb{1}{\{i\text{ studies 5+ hours per week}\}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, a student in the `<1 hour` category has

$$
x_{i,1}=x_{i,2}=x_{i,3}=0.
$$

Although study time and year in school have a natural ordering, we do not ask the software to treat either variable as a numerical score or as an ordered factor with **polynomial contrasts**. Their ordering is substantive, but it does not establish equally spaced levels. Hence, we store them as ordinary categorical factors with an explicitly chosen level order and use reference-category treatment coding, consistent with the discussion in @sec-beta-variables.

As shown in @lst-beta-categorical-coding-r (or @lst-beta-categorical-coding-py), the first level listed for each categorical variable below is its common reference category. These are the same reference levels used to define the 21-column candidate design basis in @tbl-beta-variable-dictionary.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-categorical-coding-r
#| lst-cap: "Fixing categorical levels and treatment coding in."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

category_levels <- list(
  `Study Time` = c("<1 hour", "1–3 hours", "3–5 hours", "5+ hours"),
  `Café Location` = c("AMS Nest", "Bean Around the World", "Ike's Café",
    "Koerner's Pub", "The Loop Café"),
  `Year in School` = c("1st Year", "2nd Year", "3rd Year", "4th Year"),
  Hobbies = c("Gaming", "Music", "Reading", "Sports"),
  `Primary Sport` = c("None", "Basketball", "Soccer"),
  `Living Arrangement` = c("Alone", "At Home", "With Friends"),
  `Study Group Participation` = c("No", "Yes"),
  `Has a Tutor` = c("No", "Yes")
)

options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))

for (variable in names(category_levels)) {
  academic_prepared[[variable]] <- factor(
    academic_prepared[[variable]], levels = category_levels[[variable]]
  )
}

stopifnot(
  identical(levels(academic_prepared[["Study Time"]]), category_levels[["Study Time"]]),
  !is.ordered(academic_prepared[["Study Time"]]),
  !is.ordered(academic_prepared[["Year in School"]])
)
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-categorical-coding-py
#| lst-cap: "Fixing categorical levels for treatment coding in."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

category_levels = {
    "Study Time": ["<1 hour", "1–3 hours", "3–5 hours", "5+ hours"],
    "Café Location": ["AMS Nest", "Bean Around the World", "Ike's Café",
                      "Koerner's Pub", "The Loop Café"],
    "Year in School": ["1st Year", "2nd Year", "3rd Year", "4th Year"],
    "Hobbies": ["Gaming", "Music", "Reading", "Sports"],
    "Primary Sport": ["None", "Basketball", "Soccer"],
    "Living Arrangement": ["Alone", "At Home", "With Friends"],
    "Study Group Participation": ["No", "Yes"],
    "Has a Tutor": ["No", "Yes"],
}

for variable, levels in category_levels.items():
    academic_prepared[variable] = pd.Categorical(
        academic_prepared[variable], categories=levels, ordered=False
    )

assert list(academic_prepared["Study Time"].cat.categories) == category_levels["Study Time"]
assert not academic_prepared["Study Time"].cat.ordered
assert not academic_prepared["Year in School"].cat.ordered
```

:::

The two implementations, in `R` and `Python`, now use the same category order and the same common baselines. In particular, the three study time indicators represented mathematically by $x_{i,1}$, $x_{i,2}$, and $x_{i,3}$ have the same meaning. Later model-fitting formulas will preserve these reference choices rather than allowing software defaults to redefine the coefficient comparisons.

At the end of response preparation, `academic_prepared` therefore contains three versions of the grade information with distinct roles: the untouched percentage for interpretation, the simply rescaled proportion for documenting the original support, and the boundary-adjusted interior response used by the standard Beta likelihood. The categorical levels are also frozen. Now, we can create the training/testing split without changing either the response transformation or the design coding.

## Training and Testing Sets {#sec-beta-data-splitting}

The response transformation and categorical coding are now fixed, so we can divide `academic_prepared` into the subsets that will support the remaining workflow. As established in @sec-ds-workflow-eda, the purpose of a split depends on the inquiry. In this chapter, one shared split supports both **inferential** and **predictive** goals, but the two branches will use the testing data differently.

### Why Split the Data? {#sec-beta-why-split}

The student dataset contains `r format(nrow(academic_prepared), big.mark = ",")` observations, which is large enough to reserve a meaningful testing set while retaining substantial data for model development. Hence, we allocate **70% of the observations to training** and **30% to testing**. Note that the split is **stratified by the variable study time**. Stratification does not force the grade distributions to be the same in the two subsets. Instead, it protects the representation of the four study time categories so that each subset contains approximately the same category proportions as the full dataset. This is especially useful here because study time is the primary regressor in both the inferential and predictive inquiries.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-to-learn-3674106/).](img/pieces.png){width="250"}

The **training data** will be used for:

- exploratory data analysis (EDA);
- fitting the initial constant-precision Beta regression model;
- model-adequacy and diagnostic checks;
- the pre-specified precision-model refinement;
- any pre-specified candidate mean-model comparison;
- fitting the intercept-only predictive baseline; and
- freezing the final model specification before testing outcomes are examined.

The **testing data** are then reserved for the **results stage**. Apart from structural sanity checks, such as the number of rows and the study time allocation created by the stratified split, we do not inspect the testing response values during model development. Furthermore, we do not create a separate validation set for this running case. The chapter is not conducting broad predictive tuning across many competing algorithms or hyperparameter choices. Instead, the limited model refinements are motivated and assessed within the training data, after which the final specification is frozen.

### Canonical `R`/`Python` Split {#sec-beta-split-parity}

For the side-by-side workflow to be genuinely comparable, `R` and `Python` must ultimately use the **same students** in their training and testing sets. Using the same nominal split proportion and the same seed in two different software ecosystems does not guarantee the same sampled observations. Thus, we create the **canonical split in `R`** and later import those exact subsets into `Python`.

Because the four study time strata do not all divide into exact 70/30 integer counts, the `R` code first determines an **exact proportional allocation** for the `r round(0.70 * nrow(academic_prepared))` training places. Within each study time category, it begins with the integer part of 70% of that category count, then assigns any remaining training places to the categories with the largest fractional remainders. This preserves the study time distribution as closely as possible while ensuring that the overall split contains exactly 70% training observations and 30% testing observations.

@lst-beta-data-splitting-r implements that allocation, randomly samples the required number of students within each study time category using seed `123`, and stores the resulting indices in an [{rsample}](https://rsample.tidymodels.org/) split object.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-data-splitting-r
#| lst-cap: "Creating the canonical 70/30 stratified training/testing split."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(rsample)

split_prop <- 0.70
split_seed <- 123
target_train_n <- round(split_prop * nrow(academic_prepared))

study_time_allocation <- academic_prepared |>
  count(`Study Time`, name = "n_total") |>
  mutate(
    exact_train = split_prop * n_total,
    n_train = floor(exact_train),
    remainder = exact_train - n_train
  )

n_extra <- target_train_n - sum(study_time_allocation$n_train)
extra_rows <- order(study_time_allocation$remainder, decreasing = TRUE)[seq_len(n_extra)]
study_time_allocation$n_train[extra_rows] <-
  study_time_allocation$n_train[extra_rows] + 1L

set.seed(split_seed)
training_ids <- unlist(lapply(seq_len(nrow(study_time_allocation)), function(j) {
  group_ids <- which(
    academic_prepared[["Study Time"]] == study_time_allocation[["Study Time"]][j]
  )
  sample(group_ids, size = study_time_allocation$n_train[j], replace = FALSE)
}), use.names = FALSE)

testing_ids <- setdiff(seq_len(nrow(academic_prepared)), training_ids)

beta_split <- make_splits(
  list(analysis = sort(training_ids), assessment = sort(testing_ids)),
  data = academic_prepared
)

training_data <- training(beta_split)
testing_data <- testing(beta_split)

stopifnot(
  nrow(training_data) == target_train_n,
  nrow(testing_data) == nrow(academic_prepared) - target_train_n,
  length(intersect(training_ids, testing_ids)) == 0L,
  setequal(c(training_ids, testing_ids), seq_len(nrow(academic_prepared)))
)
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-data-splitting-py
#| lst-cap: "Demonstrating an analogous independent 70/30 stratified split."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

split_prop = 0.70
split_seed = 123

training_data_py_independent, testing_data_py_independent = train_test_split(
    academic_prepared,
    train_size=split_prop,
    random_state=split_seed,
    stratify=academic_prepared["Study Time"],
)

assert len(training_data_py_independent) == round(split_prop * len(academic_prepared))
assert len(training_data_py_independent) + len(testing_data_py_independent) == len(academic_prepared)
```

:::

The `Python` split, in @lst-beta-data-splitting-py, is **conceptually equivalent**, but it is only a demonstration of how stratified splitting is carried out with `train_test_split()` from [{scikit-learn}](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/). It is not the split used for the downstream `Python` analysis.

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on using the same seed in `R` and `Python`!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
A seed makes a random procedure reproducible **within a software implementation**. It does not create a universal sequence of sampled observations across different random-number generators and splitting algorithms. Therefore, seed `123` in `R` and `random_state=123` in `Python` can both be perfectly reproducible while still selecting different students.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-to-learn-safari-3699332/).](img/safari.png){width="530"}

For the remainder of this chapter, the `R`-generated split is the canonical one. This prevents apparently equivalent `R` and `Python` analyses from disagreeing merely because they were fitted to different observations.
::::
:::

We now transfer the exact `R` training and testing subsets into `Python` through [{reticulate}](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/). After transfer, the categorical levels are restored explicitly so that study time and the other categorical variables retain the same category ordering and reference levels fixed in @sec-beta-categorical-coding.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-import-r-split-py
#| lst-cap: "Importing the canonical `R`-generated training and testing sets into `Python`."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

training_data = r.training_data.copy()
testing_data = r.testing_data.copy()

for variable, levels in category_levels.items():
    training_data[variable] = pd.Categorical(
        training_data[variable], categories=levels, ordered=False
    )
    testing_data[variable] = pd.Categorical(
        testing_data[variable], categories=levels, ordered=False
    )

assert len(training_data) == round(split_prop * len(academic_prepared))
assert len(training_data) + len(testing_data) == len(academic_prepared)
assert list(training_data["Study Time"].cat.categories) == category_levels["Study Time"]
assert list(testing_data["Study Time"].cat.categories) == category_levels["Study Time"]
```

:::

The canonical split contains `r nrow(training_data)` training observations and `r nrow(testing_data)` testing observations. @tbl-beta-split-summary-r and @tbl-beta-split-summary-py verify that every study time category remains well represented in both subsets.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-split-summary-r
#| tbl-cap: "Study-time allocation in the full dataset and the canonical training/testing split."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

study_time_levels <- levels(academic_prepared[["Study Time"]])

full_counts <- academic_prepared |>
  count(`Study Time`, name = "Full") |>
  arrange(match(`Study Time`, study_time_levels))

training_counts <- training_data |>
  count(`Study Time`, name = "Training") |>
  arrange(match(`Study Time`, study_time_levels))

testing_counts <- testing_data |>
  count(`Study Time`, name = "Testing") |>
  arrange(match(`Study Time`, study_time_levels))

split_summary <- full_counts |>
  left_join(training_counts, by = "Study Time") |>
  left_join(testing_counts, by = "Study Time") |>
  mutate(
    `Training (%)` = 100 * Training / Full,
    `Testing (%)` = 100 * Testing / Full
  )

split_summary |>
  kable(
    digits = 1,
    align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c")
  )
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

study_time_levels = category_levels["Study Time"]

full_counts = (
    academic_prepared["Study Time"]
    .value_counts(sort=False)
    .reindex(study_time_levels)
    .rename("Full")
    .rename_axis("Study Time")
    .reset_index()
)

training_counts = (
    training_data["Study Time"]
    .value_counts(sort=False)
    .reindex(study_time_levels)
    .rename("Training")
    .rename_axis("Study Time")
    .reset_index()
)

testing_counts = (
    testing_data["Study Time"]
    .value_counts(sort=False)
    .reindex(study_time_levels)
    .rename("Testing")
    .rename_axis("Study Time")
    .reset_index()
)

split_summary = (
    full_counts
    .merge(training_counts, on="Study Time", how="left")
    .merge(testing_counts, on="Study Time", how="left")
)

split_summary["Training (%)"] = (
    100 * split_summary["Training"] / split_summary["Full"]
)

split_summary["Testing (%)"] = (
    100 * split_summary["Testing"] / split_summary["Full"]
)

split_summary["Training (%)"] = split_summary["Training (%)"].round(1)
split_summary["Testing (%)"] = split_summary["Testing (%)"].round(1)

split_summary_html = scrollable_table_html(split_summary)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-split-summary-py
#| tbl-cap: "Study-time allocation in the full dataset and the canonical training/testing split."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat(
  "\n",
  reticulate::py$split_summary_html,
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)
```

:::

@tbl-beta-split-summary-r and @tbl-beta-split-summary-py are **split-integrity checks**, not analyses of the testing outcomes. Specifically, they verify that the canonical split contains `r nrow(training_data)` **training observations** and `r nrow(testing_data)` **testing observations**, and show how those observations are distributed across the `r nlevels(academic_prepared[["Study Time"]])` **study time categories**. The within-category training/testing counts and percentages confirm that the stratified procedure has preserved the study time composition of the full dataset as closely as possible. Note that the table does not summarize, plot, compare, or otherwise use the **final grade** response (or either of its rescaled modelling versions) in the testing set. Thus, inspecting these allocation summaries does not expose the testing outcomes or influence subsequent model development. The testing grade responses remain uninspected until the **results stage**.

### Protecting Against Double Dipping {#sec-beta-double-dipping}

The split also protects the inferential workflow from **double dipping**. As discussed in @sec-ds-workflow-eda, double dipping can arise when the same observations are used to discover or refine a statistical claim and then to provide the formal inferential evidence for that claim. If hypotheses or model specifications are shaped by exploratory patterns in the same data used for the final test, nominal error rates can become misleading.

Data splitting is **not a universal requirement for valid statistical inference**. Here, it is an intentional workflow choice because the training data will be used for EDA, model fitting, diagnostics, and a planned check of whether the precision structure should be extended. Those activities can affect the final model specification. Accordingly, the chapter uses the two subsets as follows:

- **Training stage:** explore the data, fit the candidate Beta models, diagnose the mean and precision structures, carry out the pre-specified training-stage model comparisons, fit the predictive baseline, and freeze the final specification.
- **Testing stage:** only after that specification is frozen, use the testing data for the final coefficient-level inferential analysis and for the held-out predictive evaluation described in @sec-beta-testing-roles.

The term **frozen specification** is crucial. Before the testing outcomes are examined, we commit to the response definition and boundary transformation, mean and precision regressors, links, category/reference coding, and the model-refinement decisions supported by the training analysis. A surprising testing result does not send us back to modify those choices and then reuse the same testing observations as if the revised analysis had been pre-specified.

### Different Testing-set Roles for Inference and Prediction {#sec-beta-testing-roles}

The same testing set supports both guiding inquiries in this chapter, but **inference and prediction ask different questions**. Consequently, they do not use the testing observations in the same way. Simply saying that the testing data are "*used at the end*" is not precise enough: we must distinguish whether the model is being **estimated using those observations** or whether an already fitted model is being **evaluated against them**.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/tablet-games-tetris-building-blocks-7426706/).](img/tablet.png){width="300"}

For the **inferential inquiry**, our goal is to obtain final evidence about how the conditional mean final-grade proportion differs across study time categories. The training data are used to explore this relationship, assess the Beta regression model, diagnose the precision structure, carry out the planned model comparisons, and determine the final model specification. Once that specification has been **frozen**, we fit that same model structure to the testing data. The resulting testing-set fit will provide the joint study time test, coefficient estimates, model-based SEs, CIs, and original-scale conditional-mean contrasts used for the chapter's final inferential conclusions. Importantly, this testing-set refit is **not another model-development stage**. The testing results cannot be used to add or remove regressors, change the precision structure, alter the mean or precision links, redefine the study time coding, reconsider the boundary transformation, or otherwise modify the specification selected from the training analysis.

For the **predictive inquiry**, the goal is different: we want to assess how well the model developed from the training sample predicts grades for students whose response values were not used to fit that model. Therefore, the final training-fitted Beta regression model is **not refitted on the testing responses**. Instead, the testing regressors are supplied to the frozen training model to obtain held-out conditional-mean predictions, fitted precision values, predictive Beta distributions, and predictive intervals. Only after these predictive quantities have been generated are the observed testing grades brought into the analysis to evaluate predictive performance using the pre-specified point and probabilistic metrics.

The distinction between these two uses of the testing set is summarized in @tbl-beta-testing-roles.

| **Inquiry** | **Model Used at the Results Stage** | **Role of the Testing Response** | **Main Purpose** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Inference** | Frozen specification refitted on the testing data | Used to estimate the fixed model and obtain the final inferential quantities | Provide protected coefficient-level and original-scale inferential evidence |
| **Prediction** | Frozen model already fitted on the training data | Used only after predictions have been generated to evaluate held-out performance | Assess out-of-sample predictive performance |

: Different roles of the testing data for the inferential and predictive inquiries. {#tbl-beta-testing-roles .striped .hover}

The **intercept-only Beta regression model** used as the predictive baseline follows the same predictive principle. It is estimated using the **training data** and then applied unchanged to the testing observations. Therefore, both the study time model and its baseline are evaluated against the same genuinely held-out responses without allowing those responses to influence model fitting.

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on the two roles of the testing set!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
"*Using the testing set*" does not mean the same operation in the two branches of the workflow:

- **Inference:** refit the already frozen specification on the testing data and use that fit for final inferential evidence.
- **Prediction:** keep the training-fitted model fixed and use the testing responses only for final out-of-sample evaluation.

The critical rule is that **both branches begin only after the model specification has been frozen**. Results obtained from the testing data must not be used to revise the mean model, precision model, links, category coding, boundary treatment, or predictive evaluation plan and then be presented as though those revised choices had been made beforehand.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-coffee-3702057/).](img/coffee.png){width="610"}

Likewise, results from one testing-set branch must not be used to modify the other. For example, an unexpectedly weak held-out prediction metric does not justify changing the model and then repeating the inferential analysis on the same testing data, just as a testing-set coefficient or $p$-value does not justify revising the model before reporting its predictive performance.
::::
:::

With the split and its two roles established, the next stage is **EDA using the training data only**. From this point until the **results stage**, the testing grade responses remain outside the model-development workflow. We will first use the training data to understand the response and its relationship with study time, and later to fit, diagnose, and refine the Beta regression model before its final specification is frozen.

## Exploratory Data Analysis {#sec-beta-eda}

The EDA now uses **only the training data**. This restriction is critical for both guiding inquiries: the training observations can inform our understanding of the response, the initial mean structure, and the aspects of model adequacy that will later need attention, whereas the testing grade outcomes remain protected until the **results stage**. This EDA has three specific goals: 

- First, we examine the distribution and support of the final-grade response on both the familiar percentage scale and the interior Beta-modelling scale. 
- Second, we study the relationship between **study time** and final grade because study time is the primary regressor for both inference and prediction. 
- Third, we conduct a deliberately concise screen of the remaining variables to determine whether any of them show descriptive mean-grade structure comparable with study time. These are **exploratory summaries**, not fitted Beta regression results, formal tests, or causal evidence.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-outlook-success-3704053/).](img/explore.png){width="400"}

### Exploring the Response {#sec-beta-eda-response}

We begin with the response itself. Two versions of the grade are relevant:

- `Final Grade (%)` preserves the original percentage scale and is the most natural scale for describing the students' grades.
- `grade_beta` is the boundary-adjusted response from @sec-beta-boundary-strategy and is the version that will enter the standard Beta likelihood.

The two scales contain essentially the same ordering and distributional information, but they serve different purposes. The original percentage scale is easier to interpret, while the transformed scale verifies that every modelling observation lies strictly inside $(0,1)$.

@tbl-beta-response-summary-r and @tbl-beta-response-summary-py summarize the centre, spread, and observed range of both response versions in the training data.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-response-summary-r
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive summary of the original and boundary-adjusted final-grade responses in the training data."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

response_quantities <- c(
  min(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]),
  quantile(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]], 0.25),
  median(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]),
  mean(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]),
  sd(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]),
  quantile(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]], 0.75),
  max(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]])
)

response_beta_quantities <- c(
  min(training_data[["grade_beta"]]),
  quantile(training_data[["grade_beta"]], 0.25),
  median(training_data[["grade_beta"]]),
  mean(training_data[["grade_beta"]]),
  sd(training_data[["grade_beta"]]),
  quantile(training_data[["grade_beta"]], 0.75),
  max(training_data[["grade_beta"]])
)

beta_response_summary <- tibble(
  Quantity = c(
    "Minimum", "First quartile", "Median", "Mean",
    "Standard deviation", "Third quartile", "Maximum"
  ),
  `Original grade (%)` = sprintf("%.2f", response_quantities),
  `Transformed Beta response` = sprintf("%.4f", response_beta_quantities)
)

beta_response_summary |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

response_quantities = [
    training_data["Final Grade (%)"].min(),
    training_data["Final Grade (%)"].quantile(0.25),
    training_data["Final Grade (%)"].median(),
    training_data["Final Grade (%)"].mean(),
    training_data["Final Grade (%)"].std(ddof=1),
    training_data["Final Grade (%)"].quantile(0.75),
    training_data["Final Grade (%)"].max(),
]

response_beta_quantities = [
    training_data["grade_beta"].min(),
    training_data["grade_beta"].quantile(0.25),
    training_data["grade_beta"].median(),
    training_data["grade_beta"].mean(),
    training_data["grade_beta"].std(ddof=1),
    training_data["grade_beta"].quantile(0.75),
    training_data["grade_beta"].max(),
]

beta_response_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Quantity": [
            "Minimum", "First quartile", "Median", "Mean",
            "Standard deviation", "Third quartile", "Maximum",
        ],
        "Original grade (%)": [
            f"{value:.2f}" for value in response_quantities
        ],
        "Transformed Beta response": [
            f"{value:.4f}" for value in response_beta_quantities
        ],
    }
)

beta_response_summary_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_response_summary
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-response-summary-py
#| tbl-cap: "Descriptive summary of the original and boundary-adjusted final-grade responses in the training data."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat(
  "\n",
  reticulate::py$beta_response_summary_html,
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)
```

:::

The training grades range from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]))`% to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]))`%, a span of `r sprintf("%.2f", diff(range(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]])))` percentage points. Their **mean** is `r sprintf("%.2f", mean(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]))`%, compared with a **median** of `r sprintf("%.2f", median(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]))`%, while the **training-set standard deviation (SD)** is `r sprintf("%.2f", sd(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]))` percentage points.

The **upper end of the scale** deserves particular attention. In the training set, `r sum(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]] == 100)` students have a grade of **exactly 100%**, and `r sum(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]] >= 95)` students have grades of **at least 95%**, corresponding to `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]] >= 95))`% of the training observations. These counts quantify how much of the upper-boundary and near-boundary behaviour documented in the full dataset is actually present in the training sample that will drive model development.

The boundary transformation changes the **support** much more than it changes the substantive grade information. On the **transformed scale**, the training response ranges from `r sprintf("%.4f", min(training_data[["grade_beta"]]))` to `r sprintf("%.4f", max(training_data[["grade_beta"]]))`, and the **largest absolute movement induced by the transformation** is only `r sprintf("%.3f", max(abs(100 * training_data[["grade_beta"]] - training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]])))` percentage point when expressed back on the original grading scale. Hence, the transformed observations remain extremely close to their original grades while satisfying the open-support requirement of standard Beta regression.

@fig-beta-response-distribution-r (or @fig-beta-response-distribution-py) shows the training grades on their original percentage scale. The orange vertical line marks the training-set mean.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| label: fig-beta-response-distribution-r
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of final-grade percentages in the training data. The orange vertical line marks the training-set mean."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| echo: true
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

grade_breaks <- seq(0, 105, by = 5)
grade_y_max <- 20 * ceiling(max(hist(
  training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]], breaks = grade_breaks, plot = FALSE
)$counts) / 20)

beta_response_distribution_plot <- ggplot(
  training_data, aes(x = `Final Grade (%)`)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = grade_breaks, fill = "#0072B2",
    colour = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]),
    colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 10)) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, grade_y_max, by = 20)) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = c(0, grade_y_max),
    expand = FALSE) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 15.5),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 20),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 20, vjust = 0.5,
      margin = margin(r = 12)),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "\n Final grade (%)", y = "Number of students")

beta_response_distribution_plot
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| label: fig-beta-response-distribution-py
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of final-grade percentages in the training data. The orange vertical line marks the training-set mean."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| echo: true
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

grade_breaks = np.arange(0, 106, 5)
grade_y_max = int(20 * np.ceil(
    np.histogram(training_data["Final Grade (%)"], bins=grade_breaks)[0].max()
    / 20))

beta_response_distribution_plot, beta_response_distribution_axis = (
    plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 8)))

_ = beta_response_distribution_axis.hist(
    training_data["Final Grade (%)"], bins=grade_breaks,
    color="#0072B2", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.3)

_ = beta_response_distribution_axis.axvline(
    training_data["Final Grade (%)"].mean(),
    color="#D55E00", linewidth=1.2)

_ = beta_response_distribution_axis.set_xlim(0, 100)
_ = beta_response_distribution_axis.set_xticks(np.arange(0, 101, 10))
_ = beta_response_distribution_axis.set_ylim(0, grade_y_max)
_ = beta_response_distribution_axis.set_yticks(
    np.arange(0, grade_y_max + 1, 20))
_ = beta_response_distribution_axis.set_xlabel(
    "\n Final grade (%)", fontsize=20)
_ = beta_response_distribution_axis.set_ylabel(
    "Number of students", fontsize=20, labelpad=12)

beta_response_distribution_axis.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=15.5)
beta_response_distribution_axis.grid(
    True, which="major", axis="both", alpha=0.3)
beta_response_distribution_axis.grid(False, which="minor")

beta_response_distribution_plot.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

The histogram in @fig-beta-response-distribution-r is a **marginal description of final grades in the training data**, not a diagnostic for a fitted Beta regression model. Most training-set grades lie roughly between 60% and 95%, with the overall mean near 80%. However, this plot pools students from all four `Study Time` categories—`<1 hour`, `1–3 hours`, `3–5 hours`, and `5+ hours`. Thus, it does not show whether the **conditional grade distributions differ across study-time groups**. For example, differences in group-specific centres or spreads could be obscured when all observations are combined into a single histogram.

This distinction is critical for the modelling workflow. The bounded percentage scale, together with the absence of observations at 0% after the boundary adjustment described earlier, motivates modelling the transformed response with a Beta distribution. However, the marginal histogram does not tell us whether `Study Time` is associated with the conditional mean of final grades, nor whether the conditional spread is similar across its four categories. Those are features of the **conditional distribution** that must be investigated using the explanatory variables and, later, assessed through the fitted Beta regression model. Hence, we examine the relationship between final grades and `Study Time` next.

### Response and Study Time {#sec-beta-eda-primary}

Study time is the primary regressor in both guiding inquiries, so this is the central relationship in the EDA. We want to determine whether the **location of the grade distribution** changes across study time categories, whether all four categories remain sufficiently represented in the training sample, how much their grade distributions overlap, and whether their within-category spread appears broadly similar or markedly different on the original percentage scale.

@tbl-beta-study-time-summary-r reports the category sizes together with several summaries of the training-grade distribution.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-study-time-summary-r
#| tbl-cap: "Final-grade summaries by study time category in the training data."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

study_time_summary <- training_data |>
  group_by(`Study Time`) |>
  summarise(
    students = n(), mean_grade = mean(`Final Grade (%)`),
    median_grade = median(`Final Grade (%)`), sd_grade = sd(`Final Grade (%)`),
    q1_grade = quantile(`Final Grade (%)`, 0.25),
    q3_grade = quantile(`Final Grade (%)`, 0.75),
    min_grade = min(`Final Grade (%)`), max_grade = max(`Final Grade (%)`),
    .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(iqr_grade = q3_grade - q1_grade)

study_time_mean_span <- diff(range(study_time_summary$mean_grade))
study_time_sd_min <- min(study_time_summary$sd_grade)
study_time_sd_max <- max(study_time_summary$sd_grade)

study_time_summary_display <- study_time_summary |>
  transmute(
    `Study Time` = `Study Time`, Students = students,
    `Mean grade (%)` = round(mean_grade, 2),
    `Median grade (%)` = round(median_grade, 2),
    `SD (percentage points)` = round(sd_grade, 2),
    `IQR (percentage points)` = round(iqr_grade, 2),
    `Minimum grade (%)` = round(min_grade, 2),
    `Maximum grade (%)` = round(max_grade, 2))

study_time_summary_display |>
  kable(align = c(rep("c", 8)))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

study_time_summary = (
    training_data.groupby("Study Time", observed=True)
    .agg(
        students=("Final Grade (%)", "size"),
        mean_grade=("Final Grade (%)", "mean"),
        median_grade=("Final Grade (%)", "median"),
        sd_grade=("Final Grade (%)", "std"),
        q1_grade=("Final Grade (%)", lambda x: x.quantile(0.25)),
        q3_grade=("Final Grade (%)", lambda x: x.quantile(0.75)),
        min_grade=("Final Grade (%)", "min"),
        max_grade=("Final Grade (%)", "max"))
    .reset_index()
)

study_time_summary["iqr_grade"] = (
    study_time_summary["q3_grade"] - study_time_summary["q1_grade"])

study_time_mean_span = (
    study_time_summary["mean_grade"].max()
    - study_time_summary["mean_grade"].min())
study_time_sd_min = study_time_summary["sd_grade"].min()
study_time_sd_max = study_time_summary["sd_grade"].max()

study_time_summary_display = study_time_summary[
    ["Study Time", "students", "mean_grade", "median_grade",
     "sd_grade", "iqr_grade", "min_grade", "max_grade"]].rename(columns={
        "students": "Students",
        "mean_grade": "Mean grade (%)",
        "median_grade": "Median grade (%)",
        "sd_grade": "SD (percentage points)",
        "iqr_grade": "IQR (percentage points)",
        "min_grade": "Minimum grade (%)",
        "max_grade": "Maximum grade (%)"})

summary_numeric_columns = [
    "Mean grade (%)", "Median grade (%)", "SD (percentage points)",
    "IQR (percentage points)", "Minimum grade (%)", "Maximum grade (%)"]

study_time_summary_display[summary_numeric_columns] = (
    study_time_summary_display[summary_numeric_columns].round(2))

study_time_summary_html = scrollable_table_html(study_time_summary_display)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-study-time-summary-py
#| tbl-cap: "Final-grade summaries by study time category in the training data."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat(
  "\n",
  reticulate::py$study_time_summary_html,
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)
```

:::

The category summaries in @tbl-beta-study-time-summary-r show a clear **ordered shift in final grades across the four study-time groups**. The **mean final grade** rises from `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_summary$mean_grade[1])`% in the `<1 hour` reference category to `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_summary$mean_grade[2])`% for `1–3 hours`, `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_summary$mean_grade[3])`% for `3–5 hours`, and `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_summary$mean_grade[4])`% for `5+ hours`. These correspond to successive increases of `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_summary$mean_grade[2] - study_time_summary$mean_grade[1])`, `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_summary$mean_grade[3] - study_time_summary$mean_grade[2])`, and `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_summary$mean_grade[4] - study_time_summary$mean_grade[3])` percentage points. Overall, the **mean** differs by `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_mean_span)` percentage points between the lowest and highest study-time categories. The **medians** follow essentially the same ordering, ranging from `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_summary$median_grade[1])`% to `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_summary$median_grade[4])`%, so the pattern is not being created solely by a few unusually high or low grades. Descriptively, this strong separation in group location provides a direct reason for including `Study Time` in the initial conditional-mean submodel.

The **within-category spread is much more stable than the group centres**. The **four standard deviations** lie between `r sprintf("%.2f", study_time_sd_min)` and `r sprintf("%.2f", study_time_sd_max)` percentage points, a **range** of only `r sprintf("%.2f", study_time_sd_max - study_time_sd_min)` percentage points, compared with the `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_mean_span)`-percentage-point span in the category means. The **interquartile ranges (IQRs)** tell the same story: they range from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(study_time_summary$iqr_grade))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(study_time_summary$iqr_grade))` percentage points. Thus, on the original grade scale, increasing study time is associated descriptively with a pronounced upward shift in the centre of the distribution, while the amount of within-group variation changes comparatively little. This distinction between **location and spread** will be especially relevant when we later assess whether the Beta regression requires only a study-time-dependent mean or also a study-time-dependent precision parameter.

Finally, the ordered pattern is not being driven by a sparsely represented category. The `<1 hour`, `1–3 hours`, `3–5 hours`, and `5+ hours` groups contain **`r paste(study_time_summary$students, collapse = ", ")` students**, respectively. All four categories therefore contribute substantial numbers of training observations to the comparisons above.

The distributional comparison is easier to inspect in @fig-beta-study-time-grade-r and @fig-beta-study-time-grade-py. The boxplots summarize the centre and middle spread, the blue points retain the individual training observations, and the orange diamonds mark the category means.

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on the jittered grade points!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
The individual observations in @fig-beta-study-time-grade-r (or @fig-beta-study-time-grade-py) are jittered **only in the horizontal direction**. Their vertical positions remain the students' actual final-grade percentages. Hence, the display separates overlapping points without altering the response values.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-emotion-fear-expression-6230192/).](img/curious.png){width="250"}

The horizontal jitter is only a visualization device. Neither the jittered positions nor the boxplots are components of the Beta regression model fitted later.
::::
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{r}
#| label: fig-beta-study-time-grade-r

jitter_seed <- 123

beta_study_time_grade_plot <- ggplot(
  training_data,
  aes(x = `Study Time`, y = `Final Grade (%)`)
) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.48, outlier.shape = NA, linewidth = 0.8) +

  scale_x_discrete(expand = expansion(add = 0.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), breaks = seq(0, 100, 10),
    expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +

  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 15.5),
    axis.text.x = element_text(hjust = 1),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 20),
    axis.title.y = element_text(margin = margin(r = 12)),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

beta_study_time_grade_plot
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-beta-study-time-grade-py

jitter_seed = 123
study_time_positions = np.arange(1, len(study_time_levels) + 1)
```

:::

The individual observations add two important details beyond the group means. First, the four distributions still **overlap substantially**: students in different study time categories can achieve similar final grades, so study time alone does not determine individual performance. Second, the within-group spread is fairly similar across categories, even as the centres shift upward with greater study time. The main EDA pattern is therefore a clear increase in the **conditional mean** of final grade across study time categories, with broadly comparable variability around those means.

These are still **unadjusted descriptive differences**. They do not account for other student characteristics, are not Beta regression effects, and should not be interpreted causally. Their purpose is to identify the dominant training-data pattern that the initial conditional-mean submodel should be able to capture.

### Response and the Remaining Variables {#sec-beta-eda-secondary}

The remaining variables should be examined without allowing the EDA to become a long catalogue of plots. The question relevant to the running analysis is narrower: 

> **Does any other recorded variable show mean-grade structure comparable with the study time pattern?**

There are nine remaining candidate variables: seven categorical variables and two numerical variables. To compare their exploratory relationships with final grade on a common practical scale, we summarize **mean-grade contrasts in percentage points**:

- For a **categorical variable**, the raw contrast is the difference between the largest and smallest category-specific mean grades.
- For a **numerical variable**, the raw contrast is the absolute difference between the mean grade among observations in the upper quartile of that regressor and the mean grade among observations in its lower quartile.

These definitions are deliberately simple because they do not pretend that categorical and numerical regressors have identical mathematical structures; instead, they provide a common percentage-point scale for judging whether another descriptive pattern is remotely comparable to the study time mean span.

We also compute a second, more targeted descriptive quantity. For each training observation, define its **study-time-centred grade** as the observed final grade minus the mean grade of its own study time category. Then, we repeat the same secondary-variable comparisons using these centred grades. This centring removes the four study time group means before asking whether a secondary variable still shows a sizeable location shift.

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on study-time-centred grades!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
