A study-time-centred grade is not a Beta regression residual, an adjusted coefficient, or a formal conditional effect. It is only an exploratory quantity:

$$
\text{centred grade}
=
\substack{
\text{observed}\\
\text{grade}
}
-
\substack{
\text{training mean for the student's}\\
\text{study time category}
}.
$$

Therefore, the centred contrasts below help us assess whether noticeable mean-grade differences remain after removing the dominant four-group study time pattern. They do not replace the later regression model, a likelihood-ratio test, or any formal adjustment for the other regressors.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-download-data-transfer-3947910/).](img/pulling.png){width="600"}
::::
:::

@tbl-beta-secondary-screen-r reports this compact screen. The variables are ordered by the study-time-centred contrast so that the largest remaining descriptive differences appear first.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-secondary-screen-r
#| tbl-cap: "Exploratory mean-grade contrasts for the remaining candidate regressors in the training data."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

secondary_categorical_variables <- c(
  "Café Location", "Year in School", "Hobbies", "Primary Sport",
  "Living Arrangement", "Study Group Participation", "Has a Tutor"
)

secondary_numeric_variables <- c(
  "Part-time Work Hours", "Hours of Sleep per Night"
)

training_secondary <- training_data |>
  group_by(`Study Time`) |>
  mutate(
    study_time_centered_grade =
      `Final Grade (%)` - mean(`Final Grade (%)`)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

categorical_secondary_screen <- bind_rows(lapply(
  secondary_categorical_variables,
  function(variable) {
    group_summary <- training_secondary |>
      group_by(category = .data[[variable]]) |>
      summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_grade = mean(`Final Grade (%)`),
        mean_centered_grade = mean(study_time_centered_grade),
        .groups = "drop"
      )

    tibble(
      Variable = variable,
      Comparison = "Largest minus smallest category mean",
      raw_contrast = diff(range(group_summary$mean_grade)),
      centered_contrast = diff(range(group_summary$mean_centered_grade)),
      smallest_group_n = min(group_summary$n)
    )
  }
))

numeric_secondary_screen <- bind_rows(lapply(
  secondary_numeric_variables,
  function(variable) {
    q <- quantile(training_secondary[[variable]], c(0.25, 0.75))
    lower <- training_secondary |> filter(.data[[variable]] <= q[1])
    upper <- training_secondary |> filter(.data[[variable]] >= q[2])

    tibble(
      Variable = variable,
      Comparison = "Upper versus lower regressor quartile",
      raw_contrast = abs(
        mean(upper[["Final Grade (%)"]]) -
          mean(lower[["Final Grade (%)"]])
      ),
      centered_contrast = abs(
        mean(upper$study_time_centered_grade) -
          mean(lower$study_time_centered_grade)
      ),
      smallest_group_n = min(nrow(lower), nrow(upper))
    )
  }
))

secondary_screen <- bind_rows(
  categorical_secondary_screen,
  numeric_secondary_screen
) |>
  arrange(desc(centered_contrast), Variable)

secondary_raw_max <- secondary_screen |>
  slice_max(raw_contrast, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

secondary_centered_max <- secondary_screen |>
  slice_max(centered_contrast, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

secondary_centered_share <-
  100 * secondary_centered_max$centered_contrast / study_time_mean_span

secondary_screen |>
  transmute(
    Variable,
    `Descriptive comparison` = Comparison,
    `Raw mean-grade contrast (percentage points)` = round(raw_contrast, 2),
    `Study-time-centred contrast (percentage points)` =
      round(centered_contrast, 2),
    `Smallest comparison group` = smallest_group_n
  ) |>
  kable(align = rep("c", 5))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

secondary_categorical_variables = [
    "Café Location", "Year in School", "Hobbies", "Primary Sport",
    "Living Arrangement", "Study Group Participation", "Has a Tutor",
]

secondary_numeric_variables = [
    "Part-time Work Hours", "Hours of Sleep per Night",
]

training_secondary = training_data.copy()
training_secondary["study_time_centered_grade"] = (
    training_secondary["Final Grade (%)"]
    - training_secondary.groupby("Study Time", observed=True)[
        "Final Grade (%)"
    ].transform("mean")
)

def categorical_contrast(variable):
    summary = training_secondary.groupby(variable, observed=True).agg(
        n=("Final Grade (%)", "size"),
        mean_grade=("Final Grade (%)", "mean"),
        mean_centered_grade=("study_time_centered_grade", "mean"),
    )
    return {
        "Variable": variable,
        "Comparison": "Largest minus smallest category mean",
        "raw_contrast": summary["mean_grade"].max() - summary["mean_grade"].min(),
        "centered_contrast": (
            summary["mean_centered_grade"].max()
            - summary["mean_centered_grade"].min()
        ),
        "smallest_group_n": summary["n"].min(),
    }

def numeric_contrast(variable):
    q1, q3 = training_secondary[variable].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
    lower = training_secondary.loc[training_secondary[variable] <= q1]
    upper = training_secondary.loc[training_secondary[variable] >= q3]

    return {
        "Variable": variable,
        "Comparison": "Upper versus lower regressor quartile",
        "raw_contrast": abs(
            upper["Final Grade (%)"].mean()
            - lower["Final Grade (%)"].mean()
        ),
        "centered_contrast": abs(
            upper["study_time_centered_grade"].mean()
            - lower["study_time_centered_grade"].mean()
        ),
        "smallest_group_n": min(len(lower), len(upper)),
    }

secondary_screen = pd.DataFrame(
    [categorical_contrast(v) for v in secondary_categorical_variables]
    + [numeric_contrast(v) for v in secondary_numeric_variables]
).sort_values(
    ["centered_contrast", "Variable"],
    ascending=[False, True],
).reset_index(drop=True)

secondary_raw_max = secondary_screen.loc[
    secondary_screen["raw_contrast"].idxmax()
]
secondary_centered_max = secondary_screen.loc[
    secondary_screen["centered_contrast"].idxmax()
]

secondary_centered_share = (
    100
    * secondary_centered_max["centered_contrast"]
    / study_time_mean_span
)

secondary_screen_display = secondary_screen.rename(columns={
    "Comparison": "Descriptive comparison",
    "raw_contrast": "Raw mean-grade contrast (percentage points)",
    "centered_contrast": "Study-time-centred contrast (percentage points)",
    "smallest_group_n": "Smallest comparison group",
})[
    [
        "Variable",
        "Descriptive comparison",
        "Raw mean-grade contrast (percentage points)",
        "Study-time-centred contrast (percentage points)",
        "Smallest comparison group",
    ]
]

contrast_columns = [
    "Raw mean-grade contrast (percentage points)",
    "Study-time-centred contrast (percentage points)",
]
secondary_screen_display[contrast_columns] = (
    secondary_screen_display[contrast_columns].round(2)
)

secondary_screen_html = scrollable_table_html(secondary_screen_display)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-secondary-screen-py
#| tbl-cap: "Exploratory mean-grade contrasts for the remaining candidate regressors in the training data."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat(
  "\n",
  reticulate::py$secondary_screen_html,
  "\n",
  sep = ""
)
```

:::

The raw screen reinforces **why study time remains the focal relationship in the EDA**. Using the pre-specified descriptive comparisons in @tbl-beta-secondary-screen-r, the largest unadjusted mean-grade contrast across the nine secondary variables is **`r sprintf("%.2f", secondary_raw_max$raw_contrast)` percentage points** for **`r secondary_raw_max$Variable`**. The remaining contrasts are similarly modest. By comparison, the four study time category means span **`r sprintf("%.2f", study_time_mean_span)` percentage points**. Thus, before accounting for any overlap with study time, none of the secondary variables exhibits a mean-grade separation approaching the magnitude of the study time pattern identified earlier.

Nevertheless, the raw contrasts are not the most informative comparison for deciding whether the running mean model should immediately become more complex. A secondary variable may appear associated with final grade partly because its categories also differ in their composition across the four study time groups. The **study-time-centred contrasts** provide a more targeted exploratory check. For each observation, we first subtract the training mean for that student's study time category and then repeat the same categorical or quartile-based comparisons. In effect, we ask whether a noticeable location shift remains after removing the dominant between-group study time pattern from the grades.

Under this centred comparison, the **largest remaining contrast** is only **`r sprintf("%.2f", secondary_centered_max$centered_contrast)` percentage points**, occurring for **`r secondary_centered_max$Variable`**. For scale, this is approximately **`r sprintf("%.1f", secondary_centered_share)`% of the raw study time mean span** observed earlier. The table also shows that this is not an isolated consequence of one unusual secondary variable: the centred contrasts are small across the full set of candidate regressors. Descriptively, once the broad study time structure has been removed, there is relatively little remaining separation in mean final grade under these simple comparisons.

Note that this screening exercise has an intentionally limited role. It does not imply that every coefficient associated with the secondary variables would equal zero in a Beta regression, nor does it account simultaneously for all regressors, interactions, nonlinear effects, or other possible model structures. It is also **not a formal variable-selection procedure** and should not be interpreted as one. Its narrower conclusion is that the training-stage EDA does not reveal another mean-grade pattern comparable in magnitude with the study time relationship.

That conclusion supports keeping the initial conditional-mean submodel focused and interpretable rather than adding regressors simply because they are available in the dataset. The study time structure is the dominant descriptive feature that the running Beta regression model should first be able to reproduce. Later, a **pre-specified training-stage comparison of nested mean models** can provide the formal likelihood-based assessment of whether adding secondary mean terms produces enough improvement in fit to justify the additional model complexity.

### Exploratory Data Analysis Summary {#sec-beta-eda-summary}

<br>

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-blended-learning-6230153/).](img/blender.png){width="400"}

The training-stage EDA has now established a focused set of empirical features that the subsequent Beta regression should address. @tbl-beta-eda-summary separates **what the training data show descriptively** from **what those observations motivate for modelling**. None of these summaries is itself a fitted-model result.

::: {.table-scroll}

| **Feature** | **Descriptive Evidence from the Training Data** | **Modelling Implication** | **Caution** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Response support and upper boundary** | Final grades range from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]))`% to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]]))`%. There are **`r sum(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]] == 100)` observations at exactly 100%** and **`r sum(training_data[["Final Grade (%)"]] >= 95)` at or above 95%**. After the fixed boundary transformation, `grade_beta` ranges from `r sprintf("%.4f", min(training_data[["grade_beta"]]))` to `r sprintf("%.4f", max(training_data[["grade_beta"]]))`, while remaining very close to the original percentage values. | The boundary-adjusted response satisfies the open-support requirement for a standard Beta likelihood, while substantive interpretation can remain on the familiar percentage scale. | Making the response admissible for a Beta likelihood does not establish that a particular Beta regression mean or precision specification will fit the data adequately. |
| **Study time and grade location** | The four study-time groups show a clear ordered shift in location. **Mean grades** increase from `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_summary$mean_grade[1])`% for `<1 hour` to `r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_summary$mean_grade[4])`% for `5+ hours`, a span of **`r sprintf("%.1f", study_time_mean_span)` percentage points**. The **medians** follow essentially the same ordering, and the four groups contain `r paste(study_time_summary$students, collapse = ", ")` training observations, respectively. | `Study Time` provides the clearest descriptive structure for the initial conditional-mean submodel and should be the focal regressor in the running analysis. | These are **unadjusted training summaries**. They are not Beta regression coefficients and do not establish that greater study time causes higher grades. |
| **Overlap and within-study-time spread** | Despite the strong upward shift in group centres, the four grade distributions still **overlap substantially**. Their **SDs** range only from `r sprintf("%.2f", study_time_sd_min)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", study_time_sd_max)` percentage points, while their **IQRs** range from `r sprintf("%.2f", min(study_time_summary$iqr_grade))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(study_time_summary$iqr_grade))` percentage points. | The fitted model should reproduce both the pronounced change in mean grade across study-time categories and the substantial within-group variation around those means. The comparatively stable raw spread provides a specific feature to revisit when the Beta precision structure is introduced. | Similar SDs on the original percentage scale do not by themselves imply constant or varying Beta precision. That question depends on the Beta mean–variance relationship and must be assessed with the fitted model. |
| **Remaining candidate regressors** | Across the nine secondary variables, the **largest raw descriptive contrast** is `r sprintf("%.2f", secondary_raw_max$raw_contrast)` percentage points for **`r secondary_raw_max$Variable`**. After removing the four study-time group means descriptively, the **largest remaining contrast** is `r sprintf("%.2f", secondary_centered_max$centered_contrast)` percentage points for `r secondary_centered_max$Variable`, only about `r sprintf("%.1f", secondary_centered_share)`% of the **raw study-time mean span**. | The initial mean structure can remain focused on study time rather than becoming complex simply because additional variables are available. A larger mean model can instead be evaluated later through a **pre-specified training-stage comparison**. | The study-time-centred screen is exploratory. It is not a regression adjustment, hypothesis test, likelihood-based comparison, or automated variable-selection procedure. |

: Synthesis of the training-stage exploratory data analysis for student final grades (scroll from left to right). {#tbl-beta-eda-summary .striped .hover}

:::

All together, the EDA identifies a clear **location–variation structure** for the running analysis. Study time is associated with a pronounced and ordered shift in the centre of the final-grade distribution, while students from different study-time categories still achieve overlapping grades and exhibit broadly comparable amounts of variation on the original percentage scale. The remaining recorded variables show much smaller descriptive mean-grade differences, particularly after the dominant study-time group means are removed.

This evidence motivates a deliberately focused starting model. The initial **conditional-mean submodel** should first capture the four-category study-time structure rather than incorporating every available regressor. At the same time, the similarity of the observed within-group spreads gives us a second feature that the fitted distribution will eventually need to reproduce. Importantly, the EDA alone cannot tell us what precision structure is required: raw percentage-scale SDs cannot be translated directly into conclusions about the Beta precision parameter.

Thus, we turn next to the **Beta distribution and its mean–precision parameterization**. Once we establish how the conditional mean and precision jointly determine the variance of a Beta response, we can ask a more precise modelling question: 

> **Can a common precision parameter reproduce the amount of variation observed across study-time groups whose mean grades differ substantially, or will the precision structure need to change as well?**

## The Beta Distribution {#sec-main-beta-distribution}

The EDA left us with a specific modelling question. The centre of the final-grade distribution changes substantially across study time categories, while the within-category spread changes much less on the original percentage scale (see @tbl-beta-study-time-summary-r). Before deciding what mean and precision structure a Beta regression requires, we need to understand **what the Beta distribution can represent and how its mean and variance are controlled**.

After the response preparation in @sec-beta-response-preparation, the modelling response lies strictly inside $(0,1)$. A Beta distribution is a natural probability model for a continuous response on this open unit interval. Unlike a Normal distribution (see @sec-normal-distribution), whose support extends over the entire real line, a Beta distribution assigns probability only to values between $0$ and $1$.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-presentation-3704067/).](img/label.png){width="330"}

Just as importantly, the Beta distribution is not one fixed shape. It is a **family of distributions** capable of representing symmetric, asymmetric, centrally concentrated, nearly uniform, and boundary-concentrated responses. We begin with the traditional shape-parameter form and then re-express the same family using a mean–precision parameterization that is much more useful for regression.

### Shape-parameter Form {#sec-beta-shape-parameters}

Let

$$
Y \sim \operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),
$$

where

$$
\alpha>0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\beta>0.
$$

The probability density function (PDF) is

$$
f(y;\alpha,\beta)
=
\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1},
\quad
0<y<1,
$${#eq-beta-pdf}

where $B(\alpha,\beta)$ is the **Beta function**,

$$
B(\alpha,\beta)
=
\int_0^1
t^{\alpha-1}(1-t)^{\beta-1}\,dt.
$${#eq-beta-function}

The Beta function can also be written using the Gamma function:

$$
B(\alpha,\beta)
=
\frac{
\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
}{
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
=
\frac{
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
}{
\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
},
$$

and the probability density function (PDF) can equivalently be written as

$$
f(y;\alpha,\beta)
=
\frac{
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
}{
\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
}
y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1},
\qquad
0<y<1.
$$

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on the Gamma function!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
The Gamma function is a mathematical generalization of the **factorial function**, but applied to non-integer numbers. In many different probability distributions, this function appears as a **normalizing constant**. Moreover, it also appears as part of the expressions of expected values and variances.

That said, for a variable $z$ in general, we can represent the Gamma function via the following integral:

$$
\Gamma(z) = \int_{t = 0}^{t = \infty} t^{z - 1} \exp{\left( -t \right)} \mathrm{d}t.
$$

@weisstein2 provides further insights on this Gamma function along with some useful properties.
::::
:::

The role of the normalizing constant is worth making explicit. Starting from the kernel 

$$
y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1},
$$

we have (via @eq-beta-function with $t = y$)

$$
\int_0^1
y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy
=
B(\alpha,\beta).
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1 f(y;\alpha,\beta)\,dy
&=
\int_0^1
\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy
\\
&=
\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\int_0^1
y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy
\\
&=
\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
B(\alpha,\beta)
\\
&=
1.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, dividing by $B(\alpha,\beta)$ turns the positive kernel into a valid probability density on $(0,1)$.

::: {.Tip}
::::{.Tip-header}
Tip on a short history of the Beta distribution!
::::
::::{.Tip-container}
![Portrait of Leonhard Euler [@holl].](img/leonhard-euler.jpg){width="300"}

The mathematics behind the Beta distribution predates its modern statistical use. Integrals of the form

$$
\int_0^1
x^{p-1}(1-x)^{q-1}\,dx
$$

were studied well before modern probability theory. Pietro Mengoli evaluated related integrals in the seventeenth century, and Leonhard Euler studied such integrals for non-integer exponents in 1730 while working on extensions of the factorial. This mathematical history is documented in detail by @massa2009.

The distribution also has an early connection to statistical inference. Thomas Bayes' posthumously published 1763 essay contains a density with the mathematical form now recognized as a Beta distribution when reasoning about an unknown probability of success from repeated Bernoulli-type outcomes [@bayes1763].

![The unique known portrait of Reverend Thomas Bayes according to @odonnell1936, even though @bellhouse2004 argues it might not be a Bayes' portrait.](img/thomas-bayes.jpg){width="300"}

More than a century later, Karl Pearson developed a systematic family of flexible frequency curves for modelling non-Normal variation [@pearson1895]. The modern Beta family on $(0,1)$ is the standardized unit-interval form associated with **Pearson's Type I distribution**. Pearson's broader statistical programme and the historical setting in which these flexible distribution families emerged are discussed by @magnello1996.

Thus, the Beta distribution connects several strands in the history of mathematics and statistics: the study of special integrals, early inverse-probability reasoning, and the development of flexible probability models beyond the Normal distribution.
::::
:::

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on Karl Pearson and Eugenics!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
Karl Pearson made foundational contributions to modern statistics, including the development of flexible families of frequency distributions such as the **Pearson Type I distribution** discussed here. However, his scientific legacy cannot be separated from his substantial involvement in the **eugenics movement**.

Pearson was an enthusiastic supporter of Francis Galton's eugenic ideas. He directed the **Francis Galton Laboratory for National Eugenics at University College London (UCL)** and, in 1911, became the first **Galton Professor of Eugenics**. His eugenic work included attempts to use quantitative methods to support claims about heredity, social class, disability, and supposed racial and national differences. Historical scholarship has also emphasized that Pearson's development of biometry and statistics was closely connected to his broader programme of establishing eugenics as a scientific discipline [@norton1978; @cain2021].

These views and the eugenic programme they supported are now recognized as **scientifically discredited and ethically unacceptable**. UCL itself has undertaken a formal examination of this history, describing Pearson as one of the institution's most influential eugenicists. In 2020, UCL removed Pearson's name from buildings and spaces, and in 2021 the university formally apologized for its historical role in the development and promotion of eugenics [@cain].

Acknowledging this history does not change the mathematical properties of the statistical methods discussed in this chapter. It does, however, place their development in its proper historical context and reminds us that statistical methods have always been developed and applied within broader scientific and social settings. 
::::
:::

Now, the two shape parameters determine how the density is distributed across $(0,1)$. @fig-beta-shape-parameters preserves the useful visual comparison of several Beta distributions while making an important point explicit: **the relationship between $\alpha$ and $\beta$ is important, but so do their magnitudes**.


```{r}
#| label: fig-beta-shape-parameters
#| fig-cap: "Selected Beta densities under different shape-parameter settings. Equal shape parameters can produce a U-shaped, Uniform, or centrally peaked distribution depending on their common magnitude, while unequal parameters produce asymmetric distributions."
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.height: 8.5
#| fig.width: 12

beta_shape_parameters <- tibble(
  shape1 = c(0.5, 1, 2, 5, 2, 5),
  shape2 = c(0.5, 1, 2, 5, 5, 2),
  curve = factor(
    c("a05_b05", "a1_b1", "a2_b2", "a5_b5", "a2_b5", "a5_b2"),
    levels = c(
      "a05_b05", "a1_b1", "a2_b2",
      "a5_b5", "a2_b5", "a5_b2"
    )
  )
)

beta_shape_plot_data <- tidyr::crossing(
  y = seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 800),
  curve = beta_shape_parameters$curve
) |>
  left_join(beta_shape_parameters, by = "curve") |>
  mutate(
    density = dbeta(
      y,
      shape1 = shape1,
      shape2 = shape2
    )
  )

beta_shape_colours <- c(
  "a05_b05" = "#0072B2",
  "a1_b1"   = "#D55E00",
  "a2_b2"   = "#009E73",
  "a5_b5"   = "#CC79A7",
  "a2_b5"   = "#56B4E9",
  "a5_b2"   = "#E69F00"
)

beta_shape_labels <- expression(
  alpha == 0.5 * "," ~ beta == 0.5,
  alpha == 1   * "," ~ beta == 1,
  alpha == 2   * "," ~ beta == 2,
  alpha == 5   * "," ~ beta == 5,
  alpha == 2   * "," ~ beta == 5,
  alpha == 5   * "," ~ beta == 2
)

beta_shape_parameter_plot <- ggplot(
  beta_shape_plot_data,
  aes(x = y, y = density, colour = curve)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = beta_shape_colours,
    labels = beta_shape_labels
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.2)
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "\nResponse value, y",
    y = "Density",
    colour = "Shape parameters"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 15),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 17.5),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.title = element_text(size = 15, hjust = 0.5),
    legend.title.position = "top",
    legend.text = element_text(
      size = 14,
      margin = margin(r = 18)
    ),
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.8, "cm"),
    legend.key.height = grid::unit(0.7, "cm"),
    legend.key.spacing.x = grid::unit(0.8, "cm"),
    legend.key.spacing.y = grid::unit(0.25, "cm"),
    legend.box.margin = margin(t = 10),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  guides(
    colour = guide_legend(
      nrow = 2,
      byrow = TRUE,
      override.aes = list(linewidth = 1.8)
    )
  )

beta_shape_parameter_plot
```

@fig-beta-shape-parameters shows several qualitatively different members of the same Beta family:

- $\alpha=\beta=0.5$ produces a **symmetric U-shaped density**, with greater density near the two boundaries than near the middle.
- $\alpha=\beta=1$ produces the **Uniform distribution** on $(0,1)$.
- $\alpha=\beta=2$ produces a **symmetric unimodal density** centred at $0.5$.
- $\alpha=\beta=5$ remains symmetric around $0.5$ but is **more concentrated near the centre** than $\operatorname{Beta}(2,2)$.
- $\alpha=2,\ \beta=5$ produces an **asymmetric density with more probability concentrated toward smaller values**.
- $\alpha=5,\ \beta=2$ gives the reflected pattern, with **more probability concentrated toward larger values**.

More generally, when both shape parameters exceed $1$, the density has an interior mode. To see where it occurs, consider the log-density (see @eq-beta-pdf) up to an additive constant:

$$
\log f(y;\alpha,\beta)
=
C
+
(\alpha-1)\log(y)
+
(\beta-1)\log(1-y),
$$

where $C$ does not depend on $y$. Differentiate with respect to $y$:

$$
\frac{d}{dy}\log f(y;\alpha,\beta)
=
\frac{\alpha-1}{y}
-
\frac{\beta-1}{1-y}.
$$

At an interior mode, this derivative equals zero:

$$
\frac{\alpha-1}{y}
-
\frac{\beta-1}{1-y}
=
0.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\alpha-1}{y}
=
\frac{\beta-1}{1-y}.
$$

Cross-multiplying gives

$$
(\alpha-1)(1-y)
=
(\beta-1)y.
$$

Expanding the left-hand side,

$$
(\alpha-1)
-
(\alpha-1)y
=
(\beta-1)y.
$$

Move the two terms involving $y$ to the right:

$$
\alpha-1
=
(\alpha-1)y
+
(\beta-1)y.
$$

Factor out $y$:

$$
\alpha-1
=
y(\alpha+\beta-2).
$$

Hence, for $\alpha>1$ and $\beta>1$,

$$
\operatorname{mode}(Y)
=
\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha+\beta-2}
$$

This expression helps explain why increasing $\alpha$ relative to $\beta$ shifts the interior peak toward $1$, while increasing $\beta$ relative to $\alpha$ shifts it toward $0$.

A useful qualitative summary is shown in @tbl-beta-shape-patterns.

| **Shape-Parameter Pattern** | **Resulting Behaviour** |
|:---:|:---:|
| $\alpha=\beta=1$ | Uniform on $(0,1)$ |
| $\alpha=\beta>1$ | Symmetric and unimodal around $0.5$ |
| $0<\alpha=\beta<1$ | Symmetric and U-shaped |
| $\alpha>1,\ \beta>1,\ \alpha>\beta$ | Interior mode shifted toward $1$ |
| $\alpha>1,\ \beta>1,\ \beta>\alpha$ | Interior mode shifted toward $0$ |
| $\alpha>1,\ 0<\beta\leq1$ | Density increases toward $1$ |
| $0<\alpha\leq1,\ \beta>1$ | Density decreases toward $0$ |
| $0<\alpha<1,\ 0<\beta<1$ | U-shaped, with greater density near both boundaries |

: Qualitative behaviour of the Beta density under different shape-parameter regimes. {#tbl-beta-shape-patterns .striped .hover}

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on equal shape parameters!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
The condition

$$
\alpha=\beta
$$

implies that the Beta density is **symmetric around $0.5$**, but it does not imply that observations are concentrated around $0.5$.

To see why, compare three cases:

$$
\begin{array}{rcl}
0<\alpha=\beta<1
&\Longrightarrow&
\text{symmetric and U-shaped},\\[4pt]
\alpha=\beta=1
&\Longrightarrow&
\text{Uniform on }(0,1),\\[4pt]
\alpha=\beta>1
&\Longrightarrow&
\text{symmetric and centrally peaked}.
\end{array}
$$

Therefore, **symmetry and concentration are different properties**. Equality of the two shape parameters determines symmetry; their common magnitude determines whether that symmetric density is boundary-concentrated, Uniform, or centrally concentrated.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-star-star-hour-reward-3974182/).](img/stars.png){width="550"}
::::
:::

The $(\alpha,\beta)$ representation is excellent for describing the shape of the Beta family, but it is less convenient for regression. In regression, we want one parameter to have a direct interpretation as the **conditional mean** and another to describe how concentrated the response distribution is around that mean. This motivates a reparameterization.

### Mean-precision Parameterization {#sec-beta-mean-precision}

For Beta regression, we re-express the same distribution using a **mean parameter** $\mu$ and a **precision parameter** $\phi$ [@ferrari2004; @cribari2010].

Start by defining

$$
\mu
=
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
$$

and

$$
\phi
=
\alpha+\beta.
$$

Because $\alpha>0$ and $\beta>0$ in @eq-beta-pdf,

$$
\alpha+\beta>0,
$$

so

$$
\phi>0.
$$

Also,

$$
0<\alpha<\alpha+\beta,
$$

and dividing all three parts by the positive quantity $\alpha+\beta$ gives

$$
0
<
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
<
1.
$$

Therefore,

$$
0<\mu<1.
$$

Now, we solve explicitly for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ in terms of $\mu$ and $\phi$. Since

$$
\phi=\alpha+\beta,
$$

we have

$$
\alpha+\beta=\phi.
$$

From the definition of $\mu$,

$$
\mu
=
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}.
$$

But $\alpha+\beta=\phi$, so

$$
\mu
=
\frac{\alpha}{\phi}.
$$

Multiplying both sides by $\phi$ gives

$$
\alpha=\mu\phi.
$$

Next, because

$$
\beta
=
\phi-\alpha,
$$

substituting $\alpha=\mu\phi$ gives

$$
\beta
=
\phi-\mu\phi.
$$

Factor out $\phi$:

$$
\beta=(1-\mu)\phi.
$$

Thus, the two parameterizations are related by

$$
\mu=\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta},
\qquad
\phi=\alpha+\beta
$$

and

$$
\alpha=\mu\phi,
\qquad
\beta=(1-\mu)\phi.
$$

This is a one-to-one reparameterization: every $\alpha>0,\beta>0$ corresponds to exactly one pair $0<\mu<1,\phi>0$, and every $0<\mu<1,\phi>0$ produces positive shape parameters because

$$
\mu\phi>0
$$

and

$$
(1-\mu)\phi>0.
$$

Substituting the new expressions for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ into the Beta PDF makes the relationship explicit. Begin with

$$
f(y;\alpha,\beta)
=
\frac{
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
}{
\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
}
y^{\alpha-1}(1-y)^{\beta-1}.
$$

Since

$$
\alpha=\mu\phi,
\qquad
\beta=(1-\mu)\phi,
$$

their sum is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha+\beta
&=
\mu\phi+(1-\mu)\phi
\\
&=
\mu\phi+\phi-\mu\phi
\\
&=
\phi.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
f(y\mid\mu,\phi)
=
\frac{
\Gamma(\phi)
}{
\Gamma(\mu\phi)
\Gamma\left[(1-\mu)\phi\right]
}
y^{\mu\phi-1}
(1-y)^{(1-\mu)\phi-1},
\quad
0<y<1.
$$

Equivalently, we can write

$$
Y
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}
\left(
\mu\phi,\,
(1-\mu)\phi
\right).
$$

The probability distribution has **not changed**. We have only changed the coordinates used to describe it. For example, suppose

$$
\mu=0.70
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\phi=20.
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha
&=
\mu\phi
\\
&=
(0.70)(20)
\\
&=
14,
\end{aligned}
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta
&=
(1-\mu)\phi
\\
&=
(1-0.70)(20)
\\
&=
(0.30)(20)
\\
&=
6.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
Y
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(14,6)
$$

and

$$
Y
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}
\left(
(0.70)(20),\,
(1-0.70)(20)
\right)
$$

describe exactly the same distribution.

This parameterization is especially handy for regression because the two parameters answer two different modelling questions:

1. $\mu$ describes **where the conditional distribution is centred**.
2. $\phi$ describes **how concentrated the conditional distribution is for a fixed value of $\mu$**.

Later, for observational unit $i$, we will allow

$$
\mu_i
=
\mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
$$

to depend on $k$ regressors in vector $\mathbf{x}_i$ through a mean submodel. If the training data provide evidence that a common precision is inadequate, we can also allow

$$
\phi_i
$$

to depend on regressors through a separate precision submodel. This separation is the main reason the $(\mu,\phi)$ form is so useful for Beta regression.

### Mean and Variance {#sec-beta-mean-variance}

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-pixel-cells-reportage-3699342/).](img/reportage.png){width="560"}

The interpretation of $\mu$ and $\phi$ becomes precise once we derive the mean and variance. Start from the shape-parameter form

$$
Y\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\alpha,\beta).
$$

We will use two identities:

$$
B(a,b)
=
\frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}
$$

and the Gamma-function recurrence

$$
\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z).
$$

#### Deriving the Mean

By definition,

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y)
=
\int_0^1 y f(y;\alpha,\beta)\,dy.
$$

Substitute the Beta density:

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y)
=
\int_0^1
y
\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
y^{\alpha-1}
(1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy.
$$

Combine the powers of $y$:

$$
y\cdot y^{\alpha-1}
=
y^\alpha.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y)
=
\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\int_0^1
y^\alpha
(1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy.
$$

The integral is another Beta function:

$$
\int_0^1
y^\alpha
(1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy
=
B(\alpha+1,\beta).
$$

Hence,

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y)
=
\frac{
B(\alpha+1,\beta)
}{
B(\alpha,\beta)
}.
$$

Now use the Gamma representation of each Beta function:

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y)
=
\frac{
\displaystyle
\frac{
\Gamma(\alpha+1)\Gamma(\beta)
}{
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1)
}
}{
\displaystyle
\frac{
\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
}{
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
}
}.
$$

Dividing by a fraction is equivalent to multiplying by its reciprocal:

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y)
=
\left[
\frac{
\Gamma(\alpha+1)\Gamma(\beta)
}{
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1)
}
\right]
\left[
\frac{
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
}{
\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
}
\right].
$$

Use

$$
\Gamma(\alpha+1)
=
\alpha\Gamma(\alpha)
$$

and

$$
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1)
=
(\alpha+\beta)\Gamma(\alpha+\beta).
$$

Then

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y)
=
\left[
\frac{
\alpha\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
}{
(\alpha+\beta)\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
}
\right]
\left[
\frac{
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
}{
\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
}
\right].
$$

Cancel the common Gamma-function factors:

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y)
=
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}.
$$

But by definition,

$$
\mu
=
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y)=\mu.
$$

This is why $\mu$ is called the **mean parameter**.

#### Deriving the Variance

To obtain the variance, first derive the second moment. By definition,

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y^2)
=
\int_0^1 y^2 f(y;\alpha,\beta)\,dy.
$$

Substitute the Beta density:

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y^2)
=
\frac{1}{B(\alpha,\beta)}
\int_0^1
y^{\alpha+1}
(1-y)^{\beta-1}\,dy.
$$

Recognize the integral as

$$
B(\alpha+2,\beta),
$$

so

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y^2)
=
\frac{
B(\alpha+2,\beta)
}{
B(\alpha,\beta)
}.
$$

Using the Gamma representation,

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y^2)
=
\left[
\frac{
\Gamma(\alpha+2)\Gamma(\beta)
}{
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+2)
}
\right]
\left[
\frac{
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
}{
\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
}
\right].
$$

Apply the recurrence twice:

$$
\Gamma(\alpha+2)
=
(\alpha+1)\Gamma(\alpha+1)
=
(\alpha+1)\alpha\Gamma(\alpha),
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+2)
&=
(\alpha+\beta+1)
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+1)
\\
&=
(\alpha+\beta+1)
(\alpha+\beta)
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta).
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y^2)
=
\left[
\frac{
\alpha(\alpha+1)\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
}{
(\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+\beta+1)
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
}
\right]
\left[
\frac{
\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)
}{
\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)
}
\right].
$$

Cancel the common factors:

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y^2)
=
\frac{
\alpha(\alpha+1)
}{
(\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+\beta+1)
}.
$$

Now use

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\mathbb{E}(Y^2)
-
\left[\mathbb{E}(Y)\right]^2.
$$

Substituting the expressions just derived,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{
\alpha(\alpha+1)
}{
(\alpha+\beta)(\alpha+\beta+1)
}
-
\left(
\frac{\alpha}{\alpha+\beta}
\right)^2.
$$

Let

$$
s=\alpha+\beta.
$$

Then

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{\alpha(\alpha+1)}{s(s+1)}
-
\frac{\alpha^2}{s^2}.
$$

Use the common denominator $s^2(s+1)$:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{
\alpha(\alpha+1)s
-
\alpha^2(s+1)
}{
s^2(s+1)
}.
$$

Expand the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha(\alpha+1)s
-
\alpha^2(s+1)
&=
\alpha(\alpha+1)s
-
\alpha^2s
-
\alpha^2
\\
&=
\alpha
\left[
(\alpha+1)s
-
\alpha s
-
\alpha
\right]
\\
&=
\alpha(s-\alpha).
\end{aligned}
$$

Because

$$
s=\alpha+\beta,
$$

we have

$$
s-\alpha
=
\alpha+\beta-\alpha
=
\beta.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{
\alpha\beta
}{
(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)
}.
$$

Now, substitute the mean–precision relationships:

$$
\alpha=\mu\phi,
\qquad
\beta=(1-\mu)\phi,
\qquad
\alpha+\beta=\phi.
$$

The numerator becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha\beta
&=
(\mu\phi)
\left[(1-\mu)\phi\right]
\\
&=
\mu(1-\mu)\phi^2.
\end{aligned}
$$

The denominator becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}
(\alpha+\beta)^2(\alpha+\beta+1)
&=
\phi^2(\phi+1).
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{
\mu(1-\mu)\phi^2
}{
\phi^2(\phi+1)
}.
$$

Because $\phi>0$, we can cancel $\phi^2$:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{
\mu(1-\mu)
}{
1+\phi
}.
$$

Thus, under the mean–precision parameterization,

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y)=\mu,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{\mu(1-\mu)}{1+\phi}.
$$

These formulas are central to the rest of the chapter. In a regression setting, $\mu_i$ determines the **conditional mean**, while the combination of $\mu_i$ and $\phi_i$ determines the **conditional variance**. This is critical in two places later in our workflow:

- First, it matters for **diagnostics**. A fitted Beta regression should reproduce not only the conditional centre of the response but also a plausible amount and pattern of variation around that centre.
- Second, it matters for **probabilistic prediction**. A point prediction based on $\mu_i$ gives only the centre of the predictive distribution. The pair $(\mu_i,\phi_i)$ determines the entire fitted Beta distribution, which is needed for predictive intervals and distribution-based predictive evaluation.

### Understanding the Precision Parameter {#sec-beta-precision}

<br>

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-problem-technology-3974187/).](img/plug-2.png){width="400"}

The word **precision** describes how tightly a Beta distribution is concentrated around its mean when $\mu$ is held fixed. Start from

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{
\mu(1-\mu)
}{
1+\phi
}.
$$

Suppose $\mu$ is fixed. Then $\mu(1-\mu)$ is a positive constant because $0<\mu<1$. Differentiate the variance with respect to $\phi$:

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi}
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi}
\left[
\frac{
\mu(1-\mu)
}{
1+\phi
}
\right].
$$

Write the denominator using a negative power:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\mu(1-\mu)(1+\phi)^{-1}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi}
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
&=
\mu(1-\mu)
(-1)
(1+\phi)^{-2}
\\
&=
-
\frac{
\mu(1-\mu)
}{
(1+\phi)^2
}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\mu(1-\mu)>0
$$

and

$$
(1+\phi)^2>0,
$$

we have

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi}
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
<0.
$$

Thus, **holding the mean fixed**:

- larger $\phi$ means smaller variance and tighter concentration around $\mu$;
- smaller $\phi$ means larger variance and greater dispersion around $\mu$.

For example, hold

$$
\mu=0.70.
$$

Then

$$
\mu(1-\mu)
=
(0.70)(0.30)
=
0.21.
$$

The variance becomes

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{0.21}{1+\phi}.
$$

Three precision values illustrate the effect in @tbl-beta-precision-example.

| $\boldsymbol{\phi}$ | $\boldsymbol{\alpha=\mu\phi}$ | $\boldsymbol{\beta=(1-\mu)\phi}$ | $\boldsymbol{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}$ | **Interpretation** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| $5$ | $3.5$ | $1.5$ | $0.0350$ | Relatively dispersed |
| $20$ | $14$ | $6$ | $0.0100$ | More concentrated |
| $100$ | $70$ | $30$ | $0.0021$ | Highly concentrated around $0.70$ |

: Effect of increasing the Beta precision parameter while holding $\mu=0.70$ fixed. {#tbl-beta-precision-example .striped .hover}

Note that, in @tbl-beta-precision-example, the mean remains exactly $0.70$ in all three cases. Only the concentration around that mean changes. However, this interpretation has an important qualification.

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on why constant precision does not mean constant variance!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
The precision parameter $\phi$ is **not simply the reciprocal of the response variance**. Recall that the variance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{
\mu(1-\mu)
}{
1+\phi
},
$$

so it depends on both $\mu$ and $\phi$.

Suppose precision is common across observations:

$$
\phi_i=\phi.
$$

Then

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
=
\frac{
\mu_i(1-\mu_i)
}{
1+\phi
}.
$$

Even though the denominator is the same for every observation, the numerator can change because $\mu_i$ changes.

To see the pattern mathematically, hold $\phi$ fixed and define

$$
V(\mu)
=
\frac{
\mu(1-\mu)
}{
1+\phi
}.
$$

Differentiate with respect to $\mu$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dV(\mu)}{d\mu}
&=
\frac{
1-2\mu
}{
1+\phi
}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the derivative equal to zero gives

$$
1-2\mu=0,
$$

so

$$
\mu=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

The second derivative is

$$
\frac{d^2V(\mu)}{d\mu^2}
=
-\frac{2}{1+\phi}
<0,
$$

so the variance is maximized at

$$
\mu=0.5.
$$

As $\mu$ moves away from $0.5$ toward either boundary, $\mu(1-\mu)$ decreases, and therefore the response-scale variance decreases even though $\phi$ has not changed.

For example, with the same precision

$$
\phi=20,
$$

a Beta distribution with $\mu=0.50$ has

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{(0.50)(0.50)}{21}
=
\frac{0.25}{21}
\approx
0.01190,
$$

whereas a Beta distribution with $\mu=0.90$ has

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{(0.90)(0.10)}{21}
=
\frac{0.09}{21}
\approx
0.00429.
$$

The precision is identical in both cases, but the response variance is not.
::::
:::

This distinction brings us directly back to the training EDA. The study-time categories have substantially different mean grades, and the higher-study-time groups have means closer to the upper boundary. Under a **common-precision Beta model**, the variance will therefore change automatically as the fitted conditional mean changes.

For the high-mean study-time groups, moving $\mu_i$ closer to $1$ reduces

$$
\mu_i(1-\mu_i),
$$

which tends to reduce the conditional variance even when $\phi$ is held constant. Yet the raw training distributions showed broadly comparable amounts of within-group spread across the four study-time categories. That does not prove that precision must vary. Instead, it gives the common-precision model a concrete characteristic to reproduce. Hence, we will begin with the simpler model,

$$
\phi_i=\phi,
$$

fit it to the training data, and examine whether its fitted conditional distributions reproduce the observed variation adequately.

If they do, a more complicated precision structure is unnecessary. If they do not, the discrepancy will provide a statistical reason to consider a precision submodel rather than adding one automatically.

This is the key role of $\phi$ in the modelling workflow: 

> **It gives us a principled way to distinguish *changes in the conditional mean* from *changes in concentration that cannot be explained by the Beta mean–variance relationship alone*.**

## The Beta Regression Model {#sec-beta-model}

The previous section introduced the Beta distribution in its mean-precision parameterization and showed that

$$
\mathbb{E}(Y)=\mu
$$

and

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)
=
\frac{\mu(1-\mu)}{1+\phi}.
$$

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-nerd-3699334/).](img/feature.png){width="350"}

Beta regression turns this probability distribution into a regression model by allowing the parameters that describe the **conditional distribution of the response** to depend on observed regressors. Hence, the central idea is to separate two modelling tasks. For observation $i$:

- the **mean submodel** describes how the conditional centre $\mu_i$ changes with regressors;
- the **precision submodel** describes how the conditional concentration $\phi_i$ changes with regressors.

These two components jointly determine the conditional Beta distribution. In particular, changing $\mu_i$ can change both the centre and the response-scale variance, whereas changing $\phi_i$ changes concentration while holding $\mu_i$ fixed. This distinction is exactly what we need after the training EDA in @sec-beta-eda-summary and the mean–variance discussion in @sec-beta-precision.

For notation, $\mathbf{x}_i$ will denote the regressors used in the **mean submodel**, while $\mathbf{z}_i$ will denote regressors used in the **precision submodel**. The two sets of regressors do not need to be identical. In the running case, the initial mean submodel will use the `Study Time` indicators defined in @sec-beta-variables, whereas the precision submodel will initially contain only an intercept.

::: {.Tip}
::::{.Tip-header}
Tip on a short history of Beta regression!
::::
::::{.Tip-container}
Regression modelling with Beta-distributed responses predates the now-standard formulation of **Beta regression**. For example, @paolino2001 studied maximum-likelihood regression models with Beta-distributed dependent variables for proportional outcomes in political science. Shortly afterward, @kieschnick2003 compared several approaches for responses observed strictly inside $(0,1)$ and recommended, among the useful alternatives, a parametric regression model based on the Beta distribution.

A particularly influential modern formulation was introduced by @ferrari2004. Their model reparameterized the Beta distribution in terms of a **conditional mean** and a **precision parameter**, related the conditional mean to regressors through a link function, and developed maximum-likelihood estimation, inference, and diagnostic tools. In that formulation, the precision parameter was common across observations.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/daycare-pixel-holding-hands-7464616/).](img/family.png){width="550"}

The framework was subsequently expanded. @smithson2006 developed Beta regression models in which location and dispersion could be described by different sets of predictors, making systematic heteroskedasticity part of the model rather than an afterthought. @simas2010 extended the Ferrari--Cribari-Neto framework to allow regression structures for the precision parameter and nonlinear predictors. Later, @cribari2010 provided a widely used implementation of constant- and variable-precision Beta regression through the [{betareg}](https://cran.r-project.org/package=betareg) package in `R` [@kosmidis2026].

Thus, the model used in this chapter reflects a broader development rather than a single isolated proposal: a **Beta likelihood for continuous bounded responses**, a regression structure for the **conditional mean**, and, when the data require it, a second regression structure for **precision**.
::::
:::

### Conditional Beta Distribution {#sec-beta-random-component}

Let $Y_i$ denote the prepared response for observational unit $i$. As established in @sec-beta-response-preparation,

$$
0<Y_i<1.
$$

In the general Beta regression formulation, we assume

$$
Y_i
\mid
\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}
\left(
\mu_i\phi_i,\,
(1-\mu_i)\phi_i
\right)
$$

for

$$
i=1,\ldots,n,
$$

where

$$
0<\mu_i<1
$$

and

$$
\phi_i>0.
$$

Thus, observation $i$ has the two Beta shape parameters

$$
\alpha_i
=
\mu_i\phi_i
$$

and

$$
\beta_i
=
(1-\mu_i)\phi_i.
$$

Their sum is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha_i+\beta_i
&=
\mu_i\phi_i
+
(1-\mu_i)\phi_i
\\
&=
\mu_i\phi_i
+
\phi_i
-
\mu_i\phi_i
\\
&=
\phi_i.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the mean–precision results from @sec-beta-mean-variance apply observation by observation. The conditional mean is

$$
\mathbb{E}
\left(
Y_i
\mid
\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i
\right)
=
\mu_i,
$$

and the conditional variance is

$$
\operatorname{Var}
\left(
Y_i
\mid
\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i
\right)
=
\frac{
\mu_i(1-\mu_i)
}{
1+\phi_i
}.
$$

These expressions are worth reading together. The conditional mean depends on $\mu_i$, but the conditional variance depends on both $\mu_i$ and $\phi_i$. Consequently, the model does not contain a separate constant response-variance parameter analogous to the $\sigma^2$ of OLS regression.

For the likelihood-based analysis in this chapter, we additionally assume that observations are **conditionally independent given their regressors**. In other words, after conditioning on the information represented by $\mathbf{x}_i$ and $\mathbf{z}_i$, the model treats the remaining random variation in one student's response as independent of the remaining random variation in another student's response. This conditional Beta distribution is the probability component of the model. We now need regression structures that determine $\mu_i$ and, when required, $\phi_i$.

### Mean Submodel {#sec-beta-systematic-component}

The mean submodel describes how the conditional mean of the bounded response changes with regressors. Let

$$
\mathbf{x}_i
=
\left(
x_{i,1},
x_{i,2},
\ldots,
x_{i,k}
\right)^\mathsf{T}
$$

denote the $k$ non-intercept regressors included in a particular mean model. We define the linear predictor

$$
\eta_i
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_{i,1}
+
\beta_2x_{i,2}
+
\cdots
+
\beta_kx_{i,k}.
$$

The linear predictor can take any real value:

$$
-\infty<\eta_i<\infty.
$$

On the other hand, the conditional mean cannot. Because $Y_i$ follows a Beta distribution,

$$
0<\mu_i<1.
$$

Therefore, we do not generally set $\mu_i=\eta_i$ directly. Instead, a **mean link function** $g(\cdot)$ connects the bounded conditional mean to the unrestricted linear predictor:

$$
g(\mu_i)
=
\eta_i
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_{i,1}
+
\cdots
+
\beta_kx_{i,k}.
$$

The link maps

$$
g\text{: }(0,1)\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}.
$$

Applying its inverse gives

$$
\mu_i
=
g^{-1}(\eta_i).
$$

Hence, the regression equation is linear on the **link scale**, not necessarily on the response-mean scale:

$$
\mu_i
=
g^{-1}
\left(
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_{i,1}
+
\cdots
+
\beta_kx_{i,k}
\right).
$$

This distinction lets us use an ordinary linear predictor while ensuring that the fitted conditional mean remains compatible with the support of the response.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-help-assistance-3974184/).](img/fixing.png){width="550"}

For our running case, the initial mean structure uses the three `Study Time` indicators already fixed in @sec-beta-variables and @sec-beta-categorical-coding. With `<1 hour` as the reference category,

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{i,1} = \mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 1-3 hours}\} \\
x_{i,2} = \mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 3-5 hours}\} \\
x_{i,3} = \mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 5+ hours}\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the core mean submodel is

$$
g(\mu_i)
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_{i,1}
+
\beta_2x_{i,2}
+
\beta_3x_{i,3}.
$$

A student in the `<1 hour` reference category has

$$
x_{i,1}=x_{i,2}=x_{i,3}=0,
$$

so that student's linear predictor is simply

$$
\eta_i=\beta_0.
$$

The treatment-coded specification does not assume that the four study-time categories are equally spaced. Each non-reference coefficient instead represents a comparison with the common `<1 hour` baseline on the chosen link scale.

Now, the next question is therefore: 

> **Which link should connect $\mu_i$ to $\eta_i$?**

### Logit Link for the Conditional Mean {#sec-beta-link}

In this chapter, we use the **logit link** for the conditional mean:

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i)
=
\log
\left(
\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}
\right)
=
\eta_i.
$${#eq-beta-logit-link}

This transformation is well defined because

$$
0<\mu_i<1.
$$

Hence,

$$
\mu_i>0
$$

and

$$
1-\mu_i>0,
$$

so

$$
\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}>0.
$$

The logarithm of this positive ratio can take any real value, which makes it suitable for an unrestricted linear predictor.

To return from the linear predictor to the conditional mean, we solve the link equation step by step. Let us begin with

$$
\eta_i
=
\log
\left(
\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}
\right).
$$

Exponentiating both sides gives

$$
\exp(\eta_i)
=
\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}.
$$

Then, we multiply both sides by $1-\mu_i$:

$$
\exp(\eta_i)(1-\mu_i)
=
\mu_i.
$$

Expand the left-hand side:

$$
\exp(\eta_i)
-
\mu_i\exp(\eta_i)
=
\mu_i.
$$

Now, we add $\mu_i\exp(\eta_i)$ to both sides:

$$
\exp(\eta_i)
=
\mu_i
+
\mu_i\exp(\eta_i).
$$

Factor out $\mu_i$ on the right-hand side:

$$
\exp(\eta_i)
=
\mu_i
\left[
1+\exp(\eta_i)
\right].
$$

Finally, divide by $1+\exp(\eta_i)$:

$$
\mu_i
=
\frac{
\exp(\eta_i)
}{
1+\exp(\eta_i)
}.
$$

Dividing the numerator and denominator by $\exp(\eta_i)$ gives the equivalent form

$$
\mu_i
=
\frac{1}{
1+\exp(-\eta_i)
}.
$$

Because

$$
\exp(\eta_i)>0,
$$

the denominator is always larger than the numerator:

$$
1+\exp(\eta_i)
>
\exp(\eta_i).
$$

Therefore,

$$
0
<
\frac{
\exp(\eta_i)
}{
1+\exp(\eta_i)
}
<
1,
$$

so the inverse-logit transformation automatically keeps the fitted conditional mean inside $(0,1)$.

For the running study-time model,

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i)
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_{i,1}
+
\beta_2x_{i,2}
+
\beta_3x_{i,3}.
$$

The four study-time categories therefore have the link-scale conditional means

$$
\begin{aligned}
\eta_{\text{<1 hour}}
&=
\beta_0,
\\
\eta_{\text{1-3 hours}}
&=
\beta_0+\beta_1,
\\
\eta_{\text{3-5 hours}}
&=
\beta_0+\beta_2,
\\
\eta_{\text{5+ hours}}
&=
\beta_0+\beta_3.
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the inverse logit gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_{\text{<1 hour}}
&=
\frac{
\exp(\beta_0)
}{
1+\exp(\beta_0)
},
\\[6pt]
\mu_{\text{1-3 hours}}
&=
\frac{
\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1)
}{
1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_1)
},
\\[6pt]
\mu_{\text{3-5 hours}}
&=
\frac{
\exp(\beta_0+\beta_2)
}{
1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_2)
},
\\[6pt]
\mu_{\text{5+ hours}}
&=
\frac{
\exp(\beta_0+\beta_3)
}{
1+\exp(\beta_0+\beta_3)
}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the coefficients are estimated on the logit scale, while the inverse link returns fitted conditional means to the proportion scale on which the response is modelled. Later, we will also return these means to the original percentage scale for substantive interpretation.

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on the logit link in Beta and Binary Logistic regression!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
The **logit function is the same mathematical transformation used in Binary Logistic regression**, but it operates on a different quantity. In Binary Logistic regression,

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\pi_i)
=
\log
\left(
\frac{\pi_i}{1-\pi_i}
\right),
$$

where $\pi_i$ is the conditional **probability of a binary event**.

On the other hand, in Beta regression,

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i)
=
\log
\left(
\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}
\right),
$$

where

$$
\mu_i
=
\mathbb{E}
\left(
Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i
\right)
$$

is the conditional **mean of a continuous bounded response**.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/laptop-games-jigsaw-puzzle-puzzle-7426707/).](img/generative-model.png){width="300"}

Therefore, the two models use the same link function without modelling the same type of response.

For example, under the running treatment-coded mean model,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_1
&=
\operatorname{logit}
\left(
\mu_{\text{1-3 hours}}
\right)
-
\operatorname{logit}
\left(
\mu_{\text{<1 hour}}
\right)
\\
&=
\log
\left[
\frac{
\mu_{\text{1-3 hours}}/(1-\mu_{\text{1-3 hours}})
}{
\mu_{\text{<1 hour}}/(1-\mu_{\text{<1 hour}})
}
\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

Exponentiating gives

$$
\exp(\beta_1)
=
\frac{
\mu_{\text{1-3 hours}}/(1-\mu_{\text{1-3 hours}})
}{
\mu_{\text{<1 hour}}/(1-\mu_{\text{<1 hour}})
}.
$$

This is a ratio of **odds formed from conditional means**. It is **not an event odds ratio**, because $Y_i$ is not a binary event indicator. For this reason, our substantive interpretation later in the chapter will emphasize fitted conditional means and percentage-point contrasts rather than importing Binary Logistic regression language mechanically.
::::
:::

### Precision Submodel {#sec-beta-precision-submodel}

The mean submodel controls $\mu_i$. Beta regression can also allow the precision parameter $\phi_i$ to change systematically across observations. Thus, in general, let

$$
\mathbf{z}_i
=
\left(
z_{i,1},
z_{i,2},
\ldots,
z_{i,m}
\right)^\mathsf{T}
$$

denote the non-intercept regressors used in the precision submodel. These regressors can be the same as those in the mean submodel, a subset of them, a different set, or absent entirely beyond an intercept.

We introduce a precision linear predictor

$$
\zeta_i
=
\gamma_0
+
\gamma_1z_{i,1}
+
\gamma_2z_{i,2}
+
\cdots
+
\gamma_mz_{i,m}.
$$

Because

$$
\phi_i>0,
$$

we again need a link function that respects the parameter space. In general,

$$
h(\phi_i)
=
\zeta_i
=
\gamma_0
+
\gamma_1z_{i,1}
+
\cdots
+
\gamma_mz_{i,m}.
$$

For the models fitted in this chapter, we use the **log link**:

$$
\log(\phi_i)
=
\gamma_0
+
\gamma_1z_{i,1}
+
\cdots
+
\gamma_mz_{i,m}.
$${#eq-beta-log-link-phi}

To obtain $\phi_i$, exponentiate both sides:

$$
\exp
\left[
\log(\phi_i)
\right]
=
\exp(\zeta_i).
$$

Since $\exp[\log(\phi_i)]=\phi_i$ for $\phi_i>0$,

$$
\phi_i
=
\exp(\zeta_i)
=
\exp
\left(
\gamma_0
+
\gamma_1z_{i,1}
+
\cdots
+
\gamma_mz_{i,m}
\right).
$${#eq-beta-log-link-phi-2}

Because

$$
\exp(\zeta_i)>0
$$

for every real $\zeta_i$, the log link guarantees that every fitted precision is positive.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-group-discussion-3947909/).](img/group-discussion.png){width="440"}

A **constant-precision Beta regression** is the special case in which the precision submodel contains only an intercept:

$$
\log(\phi_i)
=
\gamma_0.
$$

Exponentiating gives

$$
\phi_i
=
\exp(\gamma_0).
$$

Because the right-hand side does not depend on $i$,

$$
\phi_1
=
\phi_2
=
\cdots
=
\phi_n
=
\phi,
$$

where

$$
\phi
=
\exp(\gamma_0).
$$

Thus, constant precision is not a different probability model. It is the **intercept-only special case of the general precision submodel**.

When precision regressors are included, their coefficients have a multiplicative interpretation on the precision scale. Suppose two observations differ by one unit in $z_{i,j}$ while all other precision regressors remain fixed. Their precision linear predictors differ by

$$
\gamma_j.
$$

Hence, the ratio of their fitted precisions is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\phi_{\text{new}}}{\phi_{\text{old}}}
&=
\frac{
\exp(\zeta+\gamma_j)
}{
\exp(\zeta)
}
\\
&=
\exp(\gamma_j).
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\exp(\gamma_j)
$$

is the multiplicative change in fitted precision associated with a one-unit increase in $z_j$, holding the other precision regressors fixed.

Note that this does not translate directly into the reciprocal of a response-variance ratio. As established in @sec-beta-precision,

$$
\operatorname{Var}
\left(
Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i
\right)
=
\frac{
\mu_i(1-\mu_i)
}{
1+\phi_i
},
$$

so response-scale variance depends jointly on the mean and precision.

For the running case, we will deliberately begin with the simpler constant-precision specification,

$$
\log(\phi_i)
=
\gamma_0.
$$

This choice follows the modelling strategy motivated by the EDA: first, determine whether one common precision can reproduce the conditional variation observed across study-time groups whose fitted means differ substantially. Only if the training-stage model checks show a meaningful lack of fit in the conditional spread will we introduce additional structure into the precision submodel.

Thus, the more flexible precision model is available **because the probability model permits it**, but it will be used only if the data provide a modelling reason for that additional complexity.

### Is Beta Regression a GLM? {#sec-beta-glm-clarification}

Beta regression has a structure that should look familiar from generalized linear models (GLMs). It has:

1. a **probability model** for the response conditional on regressors;
2. a **linear predictor**;
3. a **link function** connecting a conditional mean to that linear predictor.

For the mean component,

$$
g(\mu_i)
=
\eta_i
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_{i,1}
+
\beta_2x_{i,2}
+
\cdots
+
\beta_kx_{i,k},
$$

which is exactly the kind of mean-link-linear-predictor structure encountered in a GLM.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/creative-raspberry-pi-circuit-7426704/).](img/creative-2.png){width="450"}

For this reason, Beta regression is often described as **GLM-like** or as using the modelling architecture of a GLM [@ferrari2004; @cribari2010]. Nevertheless, standard Beta regression is **not simply another ordinary GLM family**.

The distinction lies in the probability model. Classical GLMs use response distributions from the **exponential dispersion family**, whose probability structure has a particular relationship among the mean, variance, and dispersion parameter. Although the Beta distribution can be represented as a two-parameter exponential-family distribution, the standard Beta likelihood does not have the exponential-dispersion form required for an ordinary GLM. This is crucial because Beta regression is built from its own specialized likelihood,

$$
Y_i
\mid
\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}
\left(
\mu_i\phi_i,\,
(1-\mu_i)\phi_i
\right),
$$

with

$$
\operatorname{Var}
\left(
Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i
\right)
=
\frac{
\mu_i(1-\mu_i)
}{
1+\phi_i
}.
$$

Moreover, the model can contain a **second linked regression structure for precision**,

$$
h(\phi_i)
=
\gamma_0 +
\gamma_1z_{i,1}
+
\gamma_2z_{i,2}
+
\cdots
+
\gamma_mz_{i,m},
$$

which is not part of the basic one-mean-submodel formulation students usually encounter when first learning GLMs.

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on calling Beta regression a GLM!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
It is useful to recognize the strong family resemblance between Beta regression and GLMs, but we should not let that similarity erase an important distinction. A concise way to remember it is:

> **Beta regression uses a GLM-like mean structure, but it is fitted with a specialized Beta likelihood and may also contain its own precision submodel.**

Accordingly, in `R` foe example, we should not think of standard Beta regression as merely another family passed to the ordinary `glm()` function. In this chapter, the model will be fitted with fitting functions designed specifically for the Beta likelihood and its mean–precision structure.
::::
:::

This distinction also helps organize the remainder of our case study. The **mean submodel** tells us how the centre of the bounded response distribution changes; the **precision submodel** tells us whether its concentration requires additional systematic structure; and the Beta likelihood combines both pieces into one conditional probability distribution. Therefore, the next modelling steps will fit the simpler study-time mean model with common precision first and then evaluate, using the training data, whether either component needs to become more complex.

## Maximum Likelihood Estimation for Beta Regression {#sec-beta-estimation}

The previous section specified the Beta regression model by combining a conditional Beta distribution with separate mean and precision submodels. Now, we need to estimate the unknown coefficients in those submodels from the observed training data. That said, Beta regression is estimated by **maximum likelihood**. The basic principle is the same as in other likelihood-based regression models: among the candidate parameter values allowed by the model, we seek those that make the observed responses most compatible with the assumed conditional probability distribution.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-coffee-3702057/).](img/coffee.png){width="610"}

For compactness in this section, we augment the mean and precision regressor vectors to include their intercepts:

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_{i,1}\\
\vdots\\
x_{i,k}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
z_{i,1}\\
\vdots\\
z_{i,m}
\end{pmatrix}.
$${#eq-beta-augmented-regressor-vectors}

Likewise, collect the corresponding coefficients into

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\beta_0\\
\beta_1\\
\vdots\\
\beta_k
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\gamma}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\gamma_0\\
\gamma_1\\
\vdots\\
\gamma_m
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Under the logit mean link and log precision link used in this chapter,

$$
\eta_i
=
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\qquad
\mu_i
=
\frac{\exp(\eta_i)}
{1+\exp(\eta_i)},
$$

and

$$
\zeta_i
=
\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\gamma},
\qquad
\phi_i
=
\exp(\zeta_i).
$$

Thus, the coefficients do not enter the Beta density directly. They first determine the two linear predictors, which determine $\mu_i$ and $\phi_i$, which in turn determine the two Beta shape parameters. Maximum likelihood estimates the coefficients by following this entire chain.

### Conditional Probability Density Function {#sec-beta-pdf}

For observational unit $i$, recall from @sec-beta-random-component that

$$
Y_i
\mid
\mathbf{x}_i,\mathbf{z}_i
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}
\left(
\mu_i\phi_i,\,
(1-\mu_i)\phi_i
\right).
$$

Define the observation-specific shape parameters

$$
a_i
=
\mu_i\phi_i
$${#eq-beta-compact-a}

and

$$
b_i
=
(1-\mu_i)\phi_i.
$${#eq-beta-compact-b}

Because

$$
a_i+b_i
=
\mu_i\phi_i
+
(1-\mu_i)\phi_i
=
\phi_i,
$$

the conditional probability density function is

$$
f_Y
\left(
y_i;\mu_i,\phi_i
\right)
=
\frac{
\Gamma(\phi_i)
}{
\Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i)
\Gamma\left[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i\right]
}
y_i^{\mu_i\phi_i-1}
(1-y_i)^{(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1},
$$

for $0<y_i<1$. The notation

$$
f_Y
\left(
y_i;\mu_i,\phi_i
\right)
$$

emphasizes that $y_i$ is the observed response value, whereas $\mu_i$ and $\phi_i$ are parameters of its conditional Beta distribution.

Those two parameters are themselves determined by the regression coefficients:

$$
\mu_i
=
\frac{
\exp
\left(
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\beta}
\right)
}{
1+
\exp
\left(
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\beta}
\right)
}
$$

and

$$
\phi_i
=
\exp
\left(
\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\right).
$$

Hence, changing a coefficient in $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ changes the conditional mean and therefore changes the Beta density. Changing a coefficient in $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ changes the precision and also changes the Beta density. Therefore, the likelihood must estimate the two coefficient blocks jointly.

For the initial running model, the precision submodel contains only an intercept. In that special case,

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i
=
1
$$

for every observation and

$$
\phi_i
=
\exp(\gamma_0)
=
\phi.
$$

Thus, all training observations share the same precision, while their conditional means can still differ across study time categories.

### Likelihood {#sec-beta-likelihood}

Suppose the $n$ responses are **conditionally independent given the regressors**, as assumed in @sec-beta-random-component. Then, the joint conditional density is the product of the observation-specific Beta densities. Therefore, the likelihood for the parameter vectors is

$$
\mathcal{L}
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}
f_Y
\left(
y_i;
\mu_i,\phi_i
\right).
$$

where

$$
\mathbf{y}
=
(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^\top
$$

is the vector of observed training responses.

Substituting the Beta density gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{L}
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
&=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}
\Bigg[
\frac{
\Gamma(\phi_i)
}{
\Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i)
\Gamma((1-\mu_i)\phi_i)
} \times
\\
&\qquad\qquad\qquad
y_i^{\mu_i\phi_i-1}
(1-y_i)^{(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1}
\Bigg].
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-beta-likelihood}

Although the density in @eq-beta-likelihood is written in terms of $\mu_i$ and $\phi_i$, the likelihood is ultimately a function of the regression coefficients because

$$
\mu_i
=
g^{-1}
\left(
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\beta}
\right)
$$

and

$$
\phi_i
=
h^{-1}
\left(
\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\right).
$$

For the links used in this chapter,

$$
g^{-1}(\eta_i)
=
\frac{\exp(\eta_i)}
{1+\exp(\eta_i)}
$$

and

$$
h^{-1}(\zeta_i)
=
\exp(\zeta_i).
$$

The maximum likelihood estimators are therefore defined by

$$
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}
\right)
=
\underset{
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma}
}{
\operatorname{arg\,max}
}
\;
\mathcal{L}
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right).
$$

For the initial constant-precision model, the precision parameter vector reduces to the single parameter $\gamma_0$. Hence,

$$
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
\widehat{\gamma}_0
\right)
=
\underset{
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\gamma_0
}{
\operatorname{arg\,max}
}
\;
\mathcal{L}
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\gamma_0;
\mathbf{y}
\right),
$$

where

$$
\phi
=
\exp(\gamma_0).
$$

This formulation is crucial for later model refinement. Allowing precision to depend on study time does not replace the likelihood with a different type of likelihood. It enlarges $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$ and therefore allows $\phi_i$ to vary systematically across observations.

### Log-likelihood {#sec-beta-log-likelihood}

Products of many probability densities can be inconvenient numerically. Maximum-likelihood software therefore works with the **log-likelihood**,

$$
\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
=
\log\left[
\mathcal{L}
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\gamma_0;
\mathbf{y}
\right)\right].
$$

Because the logarithm of a product is a sum,

$$
\log
\left(
\prod_{i=1}^{n} a_i
\right)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log(a_i),
$$

we obtain

$$
\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\ell_i
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
y_i
\right),
$$

where $\ell_i(\cdot)$ is the contribution of observation $i$.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-college-3702064/).](img/plug.png){width="500"}

We start from the conditional density:

$$
f_Y
\left(
y_i;\mu_i,\phi_i
\right)
=
\frac{
\Gamma(\phi_i)
}{
\Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i)
\Gamma((1-\mu_i)\phi_i)
}
y_i^{\mu_i\phi_i-1}
(1-y_i)^{(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1}.
$$

Taking the logarithm gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_i
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
y_i
\right)
&=
\log
\left\{
\frac{
\Gamma(\phi_i)
}{
\Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i)
\Gamma\left[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i\right]
}
\right\} +
\\
&\qquad
\log
\left(
y_i^{\mu_i\phi_i-1}
\right) +
\\
&\qquad \quad
\log
\left[
(1-y_i)^{(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1}
\right].
\end{aligned}
$$

Use

$$
\log\left(\frac{a}{bc}\right)
=
\log(a)-\log(b)-\log(c)
$$

and

$$
\log(a^r)
=
r\log(a).
$$

Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell_i
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
y_i
\right)
&=
\log\left[\Gamma(\phi_i)\right]
-
\log\left[\Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i)\right]
- \\
& \qquad
\log\left\{\Gamma\left[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i\right]\right\} +
\\
&\qquad \quad 
(\mu_i\phi_i-1)\log(y_i) +
\\
&\qquad \quad \quad
[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1]
\log(1-y_i).
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-beta-log-likelihood-i}

Summing over all observations yields

$$
\begin{aligned}
\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
&= 
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\ell_i
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
y_i
\right) \\
&=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\Big\{
\log\left[\Gamma(\phi_i)\right]
-
\log\left[\Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i)\right]
-
\log\left\{\Gamma\left[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i\right]\right\} +
\\
&\qquad
(\mu_i\phi_i-1)\log(y_i) +
\\
&\qquad \quad
[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1]
\log(1-y_i)
\Big\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The dependence on the regression coefficients can be summarized as

$$
\boldsymbol{\beta}
\longrightarrow
\eta_i
=
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\beta}
\longrightarrow
\mu_i
=
\frac{\exp(\eta_i)}
{1+\exp(\eta_i)},
$$

and

$$
\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\longrightarrow
\zeta_i
=
\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\longrightarrow
\phi_i
=
\exp(\zeta_i).
$$

Hence, the resulting $\mu_i$ and $\phi_i$ enter every term of the observation-specific log-likelihood.

Because the logarithm is strictly increasing,

$$
\underset{
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma}
}{
\operatorname{arg\,max}
}
\;
\mathcal{L}
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
=
\underset{
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma}
}{
\operatorname{arg\,max}
}
\;
\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right).
$$

Thus, maximizing the log-likelihood produces exactly the same maximum likelihood estimates as maximizing the likelihood itself, while being substantially more convenient for computation.

### Score and Numerical Estimation {#sec-beta-score}

To locate the maximum of the log-likelihood, we examine how the log-likelihood changes as the parameters change. Hence, we collect all regression coefficients into one vector,

$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\beta}\\
\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The **score vector** is the gradient of the log-likelihood:

$$
\mathbf{U}
\left(
\boldsymbol{\theta};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
=
\frac{
\partial
\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta};
\mathbf{y})
}{
\partial
\boldsymbol{\theta}
}.
$$

At an interior maximum, the score is approximately zero:

$$
\mathbf{U}
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\right)
\approx
\mathbf{0}.
$$

Unlike a simple least-squares normal equation, however, the Beta regression score equations do not reduce to a closed-form solution. To see why, consider representative derivatives of one observation's log-likelihood.

The derivative of the log-Gamma function introduces the **digamma function**,

$$
\psi(t)
=
\frac{d}{dt}
\log\Gamma(t).
$$

::: {.Tip}
::::{.Tip-header}
Tip on the digamma function!
::::
::::{.Tip-container}

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-emotion-upset-6230193/).](img/surprise-2.png){width="300"}

The **digamma function**, also called the **psi function**, is the logarithmic derivative of the Gamma function:

$$
\psi(t)
=
\frac{d}{dt}
\log\Gamma(t)
=
\frac{\Gamma'(t)}{\Gamma(t)}.
$$

The second equality follows from the derivative of a logarithm. Since

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\log[f(t)]
=
\frac{f'(t)}{f(t)},
$$

setting

$$
f(t)=\Gamma(t)
$$

gives

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\log\Gamma(t)
=
\frac{\Gamma'(t)}{\Gamma(t)}.
$$

The digamma function appears naturally in Beta regression because the Beta log-likelihood contains several **log-Gamma terms**. Differentiating those terms when constructing the score therefore produces expressions involving $\psi(\cdot)$.

In our Beta regression model, the arguments at which we evaluate the digamma function include

$$
\phi_i,
\qquad
\mu_i\phi_i,
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(1-\mu_i)\phi_i.
$$

All three are strictly positive because

$$
0<\mu_i<1
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\phi_i>0.
$$

Thus, although the digamma function is defined much more generally, Beta regression requires it here only at **positive real-valued arguments**.

The [NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.2#E2) provides a detailed reference for the Gamma and digamma functions, including their definitions and mathematical properties [@nistdlmf].
::::
:::

For compactness, as indicated in @eq-beta-compact-a and @eq-beta-compact-b, recall

$$
a_i
=
\mu_i\phi_i,
\qquad
b_i
=
(1-\mu_i)\phi_i.
$$

Differentiate $\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)$, see @eq-beta-log-likelihood-i, with respect to $\mu_i$, while holding $\phi_i$ fixed. We proceed term by term. 

Using the digamma identity introduced above,

$$
\frac{d}{dt}\log\Gamma(t)
=
\psi(t),
$$

we can now differentiate each term of $\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)$ with respect to $\mu_i$, while holding $\phi_i$ fixed.
