The first term in $\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)$, again see @eq-beta-log-likelihood-i,

$$
\log[\Gamma(\phi_i)],
$$

does not depend on $\mu_i$, so

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu_i}
\log[\Gamma(\phi_i)]
=
0.
$$

For the second term in @eq-beta-log-likelihood-i,

$$
-\log[\Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i)],
$$

the chain rule gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu_i}
\left\{
-\log[\Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i)]
\right\}
&=
-\psi(\mu_i\phi_i)
\frac{\partial(\mu_i\phi_i)}{\partial\mu_i}
\\
&=
-\phi_i\psi(\mu_i\phi_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

For the third term in @eq-beta-log-likelihood-i,

$$
-\log\left\{\Gamma[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i]\right\},
$$

first note that

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu_i}
[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i]
=
-\phi_i.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu_i}
\left\{
-\log\left\{\Gamma[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i]\right\}
\right\}
&=
-\psi[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i]
(-\phi_i)
\\
&=
\phi_i
\psi[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i].
\end{aligned}
$$

For the fourth term in @eq-beta-log-likelihood-i,

$$
(\mu_i\phi_i-1)\log(y_i),
$$

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu_i}
\left[
(\mu_i\phi_i-1)\log(y_i)
\right]
&=
\phi_i\log(y_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, in @eq-beta-log-likelihood-i, for

$$
[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1]\log(1-y_i),
$$

we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial}{\partial\mu_i}
\left\{
[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i-1]\log(1-y_i)
\right\}
&=
-\phi_i\log(1-y_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the five derivatives together gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)}{\partial\mu_i}
&=
0
-
\phi_i\psi(\mu_i\phi_i)
+
\phi_i\psi[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i] +
\\
&\qquad
\phi_i\log(y_i)
-
\phi_i\log(1-y_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

Every non-zero term contains $\phi_i$, so we can factor it out:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)}{\partial\mu_i}
&=
\phi_i
\left\{
-\psi(\mu_i\phi_i)
+
\psi[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i]
+
\log(y_i)
-
\log(1-y_i)
\right\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\log(y_i)-\log(1-y_i)
=
\log\left(\frac{y_i}{1-y_i}\right),
$$

we finally obtain

$$
\frac{\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)}{\partial\mu_i}
=
\phi_i
\left[
\log\left(\frac{y_i}{1-y_i}\right)
-
\psi(\mu_i\phi_i)
+
\psi[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i]
\right].
$${#eq-beta-first-derivative-mu}

Now, we differentiate @eq-beta-log-likelihood-i with respect to $\phi_i$, holding $\mu_i$ fixed. Term by term,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi_i}
\log\left[\Gamma(\phi_i)\right]
=
\psi(\phi_i),
$$

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi_i}
\left\{
-\log\left[\Gamma(\mu_i\phi_i)\right]
\right\}
=
-\mu_i\psi(\mu_i\phi_i),
$$

and

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\phi_i}
\left\{
-\log\left[\Gamma(1-\mu_i)\phi_i\right]
\right\}
=
-(1-\mu_i)
\psi((1-\mu_i)\phi_i).
$$

The remaining terms contribute

$$
\mu_i\log(y_i)
+
(1-\mu_i)\log(1-y_i).
$$

Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\phi_i
}
&=
\psi(\phi_i)
-
\mu_i\psi(\mu_i\phi_i) -
\\
&\qquad
(1-\mu_i)
\psi((1-\mu_i)\phi_i) +
\\
&\qquad \quad
\mu_i\log(y_i)
+
(1-\mu_i)\log(1-y_i).
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-beta-first-derivative-phi}

@eq-beta-first-derivative-mu and @eq-beta-first-derivative-phi are the first partial derivatives with respect to the distributional parameters $\mu_i$ and $\phi_i$. The regression coefficients enter through the link functions, so we apply the chain rule again.

For mean coefficient $\beta_j$,

$$
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\beta_j
}
=
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\mu_i
}
\times
\frac{
d\mu_i
}{
d\eta_i
}
\times
\frac{
\partial\eta_i
}{
\partial\beta_j
}.
$$

From @eq-beta-logit-link, under the logit mean link,

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i)
=
\eta_i,
$$

so the inverse link is

$$
\mu_i
=
\frac{\exp(\eta_i)}
{1+\exp(\eta_i)}.
$$

To obtain the derivative of $\mu_i$ with respect to the linear predictor $\eta_i$, we differentiate this expression directly. Using the quotient rule,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{d\mu_i}{d\eta_i}
&=
\frac{
\exp(\eta_i)
\left[
1+\exp(\eta_i)
\right]
-
\exp(\eta_i)\exp(\eta_i)
}{
\left[
1+\exp(\eta_i)
\right]^2
}
\\
&=
\frac{
\exp(\eta_i)
+
\exp(2\eta_i)
-
\exp(2\eta_i)
}{
\left[
1+\exp(\eta_i)
\right]^2
}
\\
&=
\frac{
\exp(\eta_i)
}{
\left[
1+\exp(\eta_i)
\right]^2
}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that

$$
\mu_i
=
\frac{
\exp(\eta_i)
}{
1+\exp(\eta_i)
},
$$

while

$$
1-\mu_i
=
1-
\frac{
\exp(\eta_i)
}{
1+\exp(\eta_i)
}.
$$

Putting the terms over a common denominator gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
1-\mu_i
&=
\frac{
1+\exp(\eta_i)
}{
1+\exp(\eta_i)
}
-
\frac{
\exp(\eta_i)
}{
1+\exp(\eta_i)
}
\\
&=
\frac{1}{
1+\exp(\eta_i)
}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mu_i(1-\mu_i)
&=
\left[
\frac{
\exp(\eta_i)
}{
1+\exp(\eta_i)
}
\right]
\left[
\frac{
1
}{
1+\exp(\eta_i)
}
\right]
\\
&=
\frac{
\exp(\eta_i)
}{
\left[
1+\exp(\eta_i)
\right]^2
}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence,

$$
\frac{
d\mu_i
}{
d\eta_i
}
=
\mu_i(1-\mu_i).
$${#eq-beta-first-derivative-mu-2}

Next, recall that the mean linear predictor is

$$
\eta_i
=
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\beta}.
$$

Written in scalar form,

$$
\eta_i
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_{i,1}
+
\beta_2x_{i,2}
+
\cdots
+
\beta_kx_{i,k}.
$$

Using the augmented regressor notation,

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_i
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_{i,1}\\
x_{i,2}\\
\vdots\\
x_{i,k}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

we can write this more compactly as

$$
\eta_i
=
\sum_{j=0}^{k}
\widetilde{x}_{i,j}\beta_j,
$$

where

$$
\widetilde{x}_{i,0}=1.
$$

Now, we differentiate $\eta_i$ with respect to a particular mean-submodel coefficient $\beta_j$. Every term that does not contain $\beta_j$ is constant with respect to $\beta_j$, while

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta_j}
\left(
\widetilde{x}_{i,j}\beta_j
\right)
=
\widetilde{x}_{i,j}.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{
\partial\eta_i
}{
\partial\beta_j
}
=
\widetilde{x}_{i,j}.
$${#eq-beta-first-derivative-eta}

For the intercept coefficient, $j=0$, this becomes

$$
\frac{
\partial\eta_i
}{
\partial\beta_0
}
=
\widetilde{x}_{i,0}
=
1.
$$

For any non-intercept coefficient, $j=1,\ldots,k$;

$$
\frac{
\partial\eta_i
}{
\partial\beta_j
}
=
x_{i,j}.
$$

Via @eq-beta-first-derivative-mu, @eq-beta-first-derivative-mu-2, and @eq-beta-first-derivative-eta; we can now substitute both pieces into the chain rule:

$$
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\beta_j
}
=
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\mu_i
}
\times
\frac{
d\mu_i
}{
d\eta_i
}
\times
\frac{
\partial\eta_i
}{
\partial\beta_j
}.
$$

Since

$$
\frac{
d\mu_i
}{
d\eta_i
}
=
\mu_i(1-\mu_i)
$$

and

$$
\frac{
\partial\eta_i
}{
\partial\beta_j
}
=
\widetilde{x}_{i,j},
$$

we obtain

$$
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\beta_j
}
=
\widetilde{x}_{i,j}
\mu_i(1-\mu_i)
\left[
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\mu_i
}
\right].
$$

Similarly, for a **precision-submodel coefficient $\gamma_j$**, the regression coefficient affects the observation-level log-likelihood through the precision parameter $\phi_i$. Therefore, by the chain rule,

$$
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\gamma_j
}
=
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\phi_i
}
\times
\frac{
d\phi_i
}{
d\zeta_i
}
\times
\frac{
\partial\zeta_i
}{
\partial\gamma_j
}.
$$

We now derive the last two factors separately, so recall @eq-beta-log-link-phi and @eq-beta-log-link-phi-2. Under the log precision link,

$$
\log(\phi_i)
=
\zeta_i.
$$

Applying the exponential function to both sides gives the inverse link,

$$
\phi_i
=
\exp(\zeta_i).
$$

Let us differentiate $\phi_i$ with respect to the precision linear predictor $\zeta_i$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{
d\phi_i
}{
d\zeta_i
}
&=
\frac{
d
}{
d\zeta_i
}
\exp(\zeta_i)
\\
&=
\exp(\zeta_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\phi_i
=
\exp(\zeta_i),
$$

we obtain

$$
\frac{
d\phi_i
}{
d\zeta_i
}
=
\phi_i.
$${#eq-beta-first-derivative-phi-2}

Next, recall that the precision linear predictor is

$$
\zeta_i
=
\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i^\mathsf{T}
\boldsymbol{\gamma}.
$$

Written in scalar form,

$$
\zeta_i
=
\gamma_0
+
\gamma_1z_{i,1}
+
\gamma_2z_{i,2}
+
\cdots
+
\gamma_mz_{i,m}.
$$

Using the augmented precision-regressor vector,

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_i
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
z_{i,1}\\
z_{i,2}\\
\vdots\\
z_{i,m}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

we can write the same linear predictor as

$$
\zeta_i
=
\sum_{j=0}^{m}
\widetilde{z}_{i,j}\gamma_j,
$$

where

$$
\widetilde{z}_{i,0}
=
1.
$$

Now, differentiate $\zeta_i$ with respect to a particular precision-submodel coefficient $\gamma_j$. Every term that does not contain $\gamma_j$ is constant with respect to $\gamma_j$. The only term that contributes to the partial derivative is

$$
\widetilde{z}_{i,j}\gamma_j.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{
\partial\zeta_i
}{
\partial\gamma_j
}
&=
\frac{
\partial
}{
\partial\gamma_j
}
\left(
\widetilde{z}_{i,j}\gamma_j
\right)
\\
&=
\widetilde{z}_{i,j}.
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-beta-first-derivative-zeta}

For the precision intercept, $j=0$, this becomes

$$
\frac{
\partial\zeta_i
}{
\partial\gamma_0
}
=
\widetilde{z}_{i,0}
=
1.
$$

For any non-intercept precision coefficient, $j=1,\ldots,m$,

$$
\frac{
\partial\zeta_i
}{
\partial\gamma_j
}
=
z_{i,j}.
$$

Via @eq-beta-first-derivative-phi, @eq-beta-first-derivative-phi-2, and @eq-beta-first-derivative-zeta, we can now substitute these pieces into the chain rule:

$$
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\gamma_j
}
=
\widetilde{z}_{i,j}
\phi_i
\left[
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\phi_i
}
\right].
$$

Finally, the **full score components** are obtained by summing the observation-level derivatives:

$$
\frac{
\partial\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\beta_j
}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\beta_j
}
$$

and

$$
\frac{
\partial\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\gamma_j
}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\frac{
\partial\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\gamma_j
}.
$$

The resulting score equations contain the **digamma function**, **inverse link functions**, and **parameters** that occur inside one another. Consequently, there is generally no algebraic expression that can be rearranged to give $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ and $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}$ directly. Instead, numerical optimization proceeds iteratively:

1. choose starting values for the parameter vector;
2. compute $\mu_i$ and $\phi_i$ from the current coefficients;
3. evaluate the log-likelihood and its derivatives;
4. update the coefficients in a direction that increases the log-likelihood;
5. repeat until the optimization satisfies its convergence criteria.

Methods, such as **Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (BFGS)** [@fletcher1987], use the score and information about local curvature to search efficiently for the maximum. This is why successful Beta regression fitting is a numerical optimization problem rather than a direct matrix calculation such as the closed-form OLS estimator.

### Information, Covariance, and Model-based Standard Errors {#sec-beta-information}

The score describes the **slope** of the log-likelihood. Moreover, to quantify uncertainty around the maximum likelihood estimator, we also need the **curvature** of the log-likelihood. To do this, we need the matrix of second derivatives which is the **Hessian**:

$$
\mathbf{H}
\left(
\boldsymbol{\theta}
\right)
=
\frac{
\partial^2
\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}; \mathbf{y})
}{
\partial
\boldsymbol{\theta}
\partial
\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathsf{T}}
}.
$$

Since we have **digamma functions** in some of our previous first partial derivatives, second derivatives of the digamma function introduce the **trigamma function**,

$$
\psi_1(t)
=
\frac{d}{dt}\psi(t)
=
\frac{d^2}{dt^2}
\log\Gamma(t).
$$

::: {.Tip}
::::{.Tip-header}
Tip on the trigamma function!
::::
::::{.Tip-container}

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-emotion-pressure-6230208/).](img/surprise.png){width="475"}

The **trigamma function**, denoted by $\psi_1(t)$, is the derivative of the digamma function. Equivalently, it is the **second derivative of the log-Gamma function**:

$$
\psi_1(t)
=
\frac{d}{dt}\psi(t)
=
\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\log\Gamma(t).
$$

The trigamma function is also the **polygamma function of order $1$**. For positive real-valued arguments, it has the series representation

$$
\psi_1(t)
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}
\frac{1}{(t+k)^2},
\qquad
t>0.
$$

Every term in this series is positive. Therefore, $\psi_1(t)>0$ whenever $t>0$.

The trigamma function appears naturally in Beta regression because the **first derivatives** of the log-likelihood contain digamma terms. Differentiating those terms again when constructing the Hessian introduces $\psi_1(\cdot)$.

In our Beta regression model, the relevant trigamma arguments include

$$
\phi_i,
\qquad
\mu_i\phi_i,
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
(1-\mu_i)\phi_i.
$$

All three are strictly positive because $0<\mu_i<1$ and $\phi_i>0$. Hence, the positivity of the trigamma function becomes useful when studying the curvature of the Beta log-likelihood.

The [NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions](https://dlmf.nist.gov/5.15) provides further details on the trigamma function as part of the broader family of **polygamma functions** [@nistdlmf].
::::
:::

For example, holding $\phi_i$ fixed,

$$
\frac{
\partial^2\ell_i\left(\boldsymbol{\beta},\boldsymbol{\gamma};y_i\right)
}{
\partial\mu_i^2
}
=
-
\phi_i^2
\left\{
\psi_1(\mu_i\phi_i)
+
\psi_1\left[(1-\mu_i)\phi_i\right]
\right\}.
$$

The full Hessian must account for curvature involving both the **mean-submodel coefficients** $\boldsymbol{\beta}$ and the **precision-submodel coefficients** $\boldsymbol{\gamma}$. Recall that

$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\beta}\\
\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Therefore, the Hessian can be partitioned according to these two coefficient blocks:

$$
\mathbf{H}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
=
\frac{
\partial^2\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta})
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}
\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
&
\dfrac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
\\[14pt]
\dfrac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
&
\dfrac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The upper-left block,

$$
\frac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf{T}}
},
$$

describes the curvature of the log-likelihood with respect to the mean-submodel coefficients.

The lower-right block,

$$
\frac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\mathsf{T}}
},
$$

describes the curvature with respect to the precision-submodel coefficients.

The two off-diagonal blocks,

$$
\frac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf{T}}
},
$$

describe how changes in the mean and precision coefficient estimates are related through the curvature of the same **Beta log-likelihood**. Under the usual smoothness conditions for the log-likelihood, these cross-derivative blocks are transposes of one another:

$$
\frac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
=
\left[
\frac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
\right]^{\mathsf{T}}.
$$

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-etherpad-group-work-3683373/).](img/interval.png){width="500"}

The **observed information matrix** is defined as the negative Hessian:

$$
\mathbf{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
=
-
\mathbf{H}(\boldsymbol{\theta}).
$$

Hence, its block form is

$$
\mathbf{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
=
-
\begin{pmatrix}
\dfrac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
&
\dfrac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
\\[14pt]
\dfrac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
&
\dfrac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Equivalently, we can denote the four blocks by

$$
\mathbf{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{J}_{\beta\beta}
&
\mathbf{J}_{\beta\gamma}
\\
\mathbf{J}_{\gamma\beta}
&
\mathbf{J}_{\gamma\gamma}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

where, for example,

$$
\mathbf{J}_{\beta\gamma}
=
-
\frac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\mathsf{T}}
}.
$$

The **expected Fisher information matrix** is the expectation of the observed information under the assumed model:

$$
\mathbf{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
=
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\left[
\mathbf{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
\right]
=
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\left[
-
\mathbf{H}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
\right].
$$

Thus,

$$
\mathbf{I}(\boldsymbol{\theta})
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathbf{I}_{\beta\beta}
&
\mathbf{I}_{\beta\gamma}
\\
\mathbf{I}_{\gamma\beta}
&
\mathbf{I}_{\gamma\gamma}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

with

$$
\mathbf{I}_{\beta\beta}
=
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\left[
-
\frac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
\right],
$$

$$
\mathbf{I}_{\beta\gamma}
=
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\left[
-
\frac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
\right],
$$

$$
\mathbf{I}_{\gamma\beta}
=
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\left[
-
\frac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\partial\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
\right],
$$

and

$$
\mathbf{I}_{\gamma\gamma}
=
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\left[
-
\frac{
\partial^2\ell
\left(
\boldsymbol{\beta},
\boldsymbol{\gamma};
\mathbf{y}
\right)
}{
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}
\partial\boldsymbol{\gamma}^{\mathsf{T}}
}
\right].
$$

Now suppose that the true parameter vector is

$$
\boldsymbol{\theta}_0
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\boldsymbol{\beta}_0\\
\boldsymbol{\gamma}_0
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Under the **usual maximum-likelihood regularity conditions** and a **correctly specified model**, the maximum likelihood estimator is asymptotically Normal. More formally,

$$
\sqrt{n}
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
-
\boldsymbol{\theta}_0
\right)
\xrightarrow{d}
\mathcal{N}
\left(
\mathbf{0},
\mathbf{I}_1(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)^{-1}
\right),
$$

where $\mathbf{I}_1(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)$ denotes the Fisher information contributed per observation.

Since the total Fisher information from $n$ observations is

$$
\mathbf{I}_n(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)
=
n\mathbf{I}_1(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0),
$$

the equivalent large-sample approximation is

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\;\dot{\sim}\;
\operatorname{Normal}
\left(
\boldsymbol{\theta}_0,
\mathbf{I}_n(\boldsymbol{\theta}_0)^{-1}
\right).
$$

Here, $\dot{\sim}$ means **approximately distributed as**, rather than exactly distributed as.

Because the true parameter vector $\boldsymbol{\theta}_0$ is unknown, the information matrix is evaluated at the maximum likelihood estimate in practice. Therefore, using the expected Fisher information, a model-based estimator of the covariance matrix of the maximum likelihood estimator is

$$
\widehat{
\operatorname{Cov}
}
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\right)
=
\mathbf{I}_n
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\right)^{-1}.
$$

If the observed information is used instead, then

$$
\widehat{
\operatorname{Cov}
}
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\right)
=
\mathbf{J}
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\right)^{-1}.
$$

Since

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}\\
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

its estimated covariance matrix can also be partitioned according to the mean- and precision-submodel coefficients:

$$
\widehat{
\operatorname{Cov}
}
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\right)
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\beta\beta}
&
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\beta\gamma}
\\
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\gamma\beta}
&
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\gamma\gamma}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The block

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\beta\beta}
$$

contains the estimated variances and covariances of the **mean-submodel coefficient estimators**, whereas

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\gamma\gamma}
$$

contains the estimated variances and covariances of the **precision-submodel coefficient estimators**. The off-diagonal blocks,

$$
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\beta\gamma}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\gamma\beta},
$$

contain the estimated covariances between the two sets of coefficient estimators.

The **model-based SE** of a coefficient estimate is obtained from the corresponding diagonal element of this covariance matrix. Recall that a diagonal element of a covariance matrix is a variance. Therefore, for a mean-submodel coefficient $\widehat{\beta}_j$,

$$
\widehat{
\operatorname{Var}
}
\left(
\widehat{\beta}_j
\right)
=
\left[
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\beta\beta}
\right]_{jj},
$$

and its model-based SE is

$$
\operatorname{SE}
\left(
\widehat{\beta}_j
\right)
=
\sqrt{
\left[
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\beta\beta}
\right]_{jj}
}.
$$

Similarly, for a precision-submodel coefficient $\widehat{\gamma}_j$,

$$
\widehat{
\operatorname{Var}
}
\left(
\widehat{\gamma}_j
\right)
=
\left[
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\gamma\gamma}
\right]_{jj},
$$

so

$$
\operatorname{SE}
\left(
\widehat{\gamma}_j
\right)
=
\sqrt{
\left[
\widehat{\mathbf{V}}_{\gamma\gamma}
\right]_{jj}
}.
$$

More generally, if $\widehat{\theta}_j$ denotes any element of the joint parameter vector $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$, then

$$
\operatorname{SE}
\left(
\widehat{\theta}_j
\right)
=
\sqrt{
\left[
\widehat{
\operatorname{Cov}
}
\left(
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\theta}}
\right)
\right]_{jj}
}.
$$

Thus, the curvature of the Beta log-likelihood provides not only the maximum likelihood estimates themselves but also a model-based measure of how much sampling uncertainty is associated with each estimated mean or precision-submodel coefficient.

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on what "*model-based*" SEs mean!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
The SEs above are called **model-based** because they are obtained from the information matrix implied by the fitted Beta regression model. Thus, they are not assumption-free measures of uncertainty. Their reliability depends on the adequacy of the probability model from which the likelihood and information matrix were derived. In particular, the calculation assumes that:

- the **conditional Beta distribution** provides a reasonable representation of the bounded response;
- the observations can reasonably be treated as **conditionally independent**;
- the **mean submodel** represents the systematic structure in $\mu_i$ adequately; and
- the **precision submodel** represents the systematic structure in $\phi_i$ adequately.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-observation-internship-3974186/).](img/observation.png){width="550"}

Successful numerical optimization does not establish that these assumptions are satisfactory. The optimizer may successfully locate a maximum of the specified likelihood even when that likelihood is too restrictive for the observed data. Hence, this distinction will be crucial in our running case. We will first fit a Beta regression with a **constant precision parameter**. The SEs from that model quantify uncertainty **under that particular mean and precision specification**. They do not, by themselves, establish that constant precision is an adequate description of the conditional variation in final grades.

Therefore, we will assess the fitted model using the training data before relying on its uncertainty estimates for the final analysis. If the precision structure proves inadequate, we will refine that part of the model and obtain SEs from the resulting specification.
::::
:::

### How the Software Fits the Model {#sec-beta-software-estimation}

The previous subsections developed maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) for Beta regression mathematically. Software implements that same likelihood problem by turning the model formulas into a **mean design matrix** and a **precision design matrix**, applying the specified inverse links to obtain $\mu_i$ and $\phi_i$, and numerically maximizing the Beta log-likelihood over the corresponding parameter vectors.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-teaching-to-learn-wiki-3976301/).](img/board.png){width="500"}

The two implementations used in this chapter expose the mean and precision components differently:

- In `R`, [`betareg()`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/betareg/versions/3.2-5/topics/betareg), from the [{betareg}](https://cran.r-project.org/package=betareg) package, uses a two-part formula of the form `response ~ mean regressors | precision regressors` [@cribari2010].
- In `Python`, [`statsmodels.othermod.betareg.BetaModel`](https://www.statsmodels.org/devel/generated/statsmodels.othermod.betareg.BetaModel.html), from [{statsmodels}](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/index.html), receives the mean specification through the main formula and can receive a separate precision specification through `exog_precision_formula`.

Once these designs and links have been supplied, both implementations estimate the coefficients by maximum likelihood and return likelihood-based covariance information for the fitted parameters. Their numerical optimization and covariance calculations need not follow exactly the same computational path, so matched fits should produce closely agreeing estimates even if very small numerical differences remain.

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on software defaults for the precision link!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}

A **constant-precision model** does not guarantee that two software packages will report the precision coefficient on the same scale. In `R`'s `betareg()`, a one-part constant-precision formula can use the identity precision link for backward compatibility, whereas `Python`'s `BetaModel` uses a log precision link by default.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/robotics-robot-programming-7438020/).](img/mice.png){width="625"}

Because this chapter develops the precision submodel using $\log(\phi_i)$, we will **state the mean and precision links explicitly in every fitted model rather than rely on defaults**. This keeps the statistical parameterization aligned across `R` and `Python`.
::::
:::

The next section now applies this general software machinery to the first concrete model in the running case.

## Initial Constant-precision Beta Regression {#sec-beta-simple-model}

We begin model development with a Beta regression fitted only to the **training data**. The mean submodel contains `Study Time`, reflecting the strong ordered shift in grade location observed in @tbl-beta-study-time-summary-r, while the precision submodel initially contains only an intercept.

The constant-precision restriction is a deliberately simple starting point, not a conclusion reached from the EDA. Recall that

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
=
\frac{\mu_i(1-\mu_i)}{1+\phi_i}.
$$

Therefore, the conditional response variance can change as $\mu_i$ changes even when $\phi_i$ is constant. The comparatively similar raw within-category standard deviations observed earlier do not establish that a common precision parameter is adequate. We will test that restriction during the training-stage model-adequacy assessment.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/daycare-pixel-holding-hands-7464616/).](img/juggling.png){width="300"}


### Model Specification {#sec-beta-simple-specification}

Recall that `<1 hour` is the treatment-coding reference category fixed in @sec-beta-categorical-coding. Define the three non-reference `Study Time` indicators as

$$
\begin{aligned}
x_{i,1}
&=
\mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 1–3 hours}\},\\
x_{i,2}
&=
\mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 3–5 hours}\},\\
x_{i,3}
&=
\mathbb{1}\{\text{Study Time is 5+ hours}\}.
\end{aligned}
$$

All three indicators equal zero for a student in the `<1 hour` reference category. The initial conditional-mean submodel is

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i)
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_{i,1}
+
\beta_2x_{i,2}
+
\beta_3x_{i,3}.
$${#eq-beta-simple-mean}

Thus, $\beta_0$ is the logit of the conditional mean for the `<1 hour` category, while $\beta_1$, $\beta_2$, and $\beta_3$ are logit-mean contrasts between their respective categories and that reference group. Treatment coding does not impose equal spacing or a linear trend across the four study-time categories.

For the initial precision submodel,

$$
\log(\phi_i)
=
\gamma_0,
$${#eq-beta-simple-precision}

so

$$
\phi_i
=
\exp(\gamma_0)
=
\phi
$${#eq-beta-simple-common-precision}

for every training observation. Combining @eq-beta-simple-mean and @eq-beta-simple-common-precision gives

$$
Y_i
\mid
\mathbf{x}_i
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}
\left(
\mu_i\phi,\,
(1-\mu_i)\phi
\right).
$$

The model therefore allows the conditional mean to differ across `Study Time` categories while imposing one common precision parameter. The adequacy of that restriction remains to be assessed.

### `R` and `Python` Fitting {#sec-beta-simple-fitting}

The following code implements @eq-beta-simple-mean and @eq-beta-simple-precision in the two software environments. The response preparation and category coding were already fixed earlier in the workflow, so this step only fits the specified model.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-constant-fit-r
#| lst-cap: "Fitting the initial constant-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_model <- betareg(
  grade_beta ~ `Study Time` | 1,
  data = training_data,
  link = "logit", link.phi = "log",
  type = "ML", dist = "beta",
  control = betareg.control(method = "BFGS")
)
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-constant-fit-py
#| lst-cap: "Fitting the initial constant-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

import statsmodels.api as sm
from statsmodels.othermod.betareg import BetaModel

beta_constant_model = BetaModel.from_formula(
    'grade_beta ~ C(Q("Study Time"), Treatment(reference="<1 hour"))',
    data=training_data,
    exog_precision_formula="1",
    link=sm.families.links.Logit(),
    link_precision=sm.families.links.Log(),
).fit(method="bfgs", maxiter=1000, disp=False)
```

:::

In `R` (@lst-beta-constant-fit-r), the expression before `|` specifies the mean submodel and `| 1` specifies an intercept-only precision submodel. On the other hand, in `Python` (@lst-beta-constant-fit-py), the main formula supplies the same treatment-coded mean design and `exog_precision_formula="1"` supplies the precision intercept. The explicit logit and log links enforce the common parameterization established in @sec-beta-simple-specification.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-techbot-teach-o-bot-3947912/).](img/bot.png){width="550"}

Note that the `R` call also sets `dist = "beta"` explicitly because `grade_beta` was prepared in @sec-beta-boundary-strategy to lie strictly inside $(0,1)$; hence, the intended likelihood is the classical Beta likelihood developed in @sec-beta-pdf. Both fits use MLE with BFGS optimization.

### Initial Coefficient Output {#sec-beta-simple-output}

Before assessing model adequacy, we record the coefficient estimates and model-based SEs from the training fit. These quantities document what the fitted model estimated; they are **not yet the basis for final inferential conclusions**.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-simple-coefficients-r
#| tbl-cap: "Training-stage coefficient estimates for the initial constant-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_parameters <- unname(coef(beta_constant_model))
beta_constant_standard_errors <- unname(
  sqrt(diag(vcov(beta_constant_model)))
)
stopifnot(
  length(beta_constant_parameters) == 5L,
  length(beta_constant_standard_errors) == 5L
)

beta_constant_phi <- exp(beta_constant_parameters[5])

beta_constant_coefficients <- tibble(
  Component = c(rep("Mean", 4), "Precision"),
  Term = c(
    "Intercept (<1 hour)",
    "Study Time: 1–3 hours vs <1 hour",
    "Study Time: 3–5 hours vs <1 hour",
    "Study Time: 5+ hours vs <1 hour",
    "Intercept"
  ),
  Estimate = beta_constant_parameters,
  `Model-based SE` = beta_constant_standard_errors
)

beta_constant_coefficients_display <- beta_constant_coefficients |>
  mutate(across(c(Estimate, `Model-based SE`),
    ~ formatC(.x, format = "f", digits = 4)))

beta_constant_coefficients_display |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_parameters = np.asarray(beta_constant_model.params)
beta_constant_standard_errors = np.asarray(beta_constant_model.bse)
assert (
    beta_constant_parameters.size == 5
    and beta_constant_standard_errors.size == 5
)

beta_constant_phi = np.exp(beta_constant_parameters[4])

beta_constant_coefficients = pd.DataFrame({
    "Component": ["Mean"] * 4 + ["Precision"],
    "Term": [
        "Intercept (<1 hour)",
        "Study Time: 1–3 hours vs <1 hour",
        "Study Time: 3–5 hours vs <1 hour",
        "Study Time: 5+ hours vs <1 hour",
        "Intercept",
    ],
    "Estimate": beta_constant_parameters,
    "Model-based SE": beta_constant_standard_errors,
})

beta_constant_coefficients_display = beta_constant_coefficients.copy()
for column in ["Estimate", "Model-based SE"]:
    beta_constant_coefficients_display[column] = (
        beta_constant_coefficients_display[column]
        .map(lambda value: f"{value:.4f}"))

beta_constant_coefficients_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_constant_coefficients_display)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-simple-coefficients-py
#| tbl-cap: "Training-stage coefficient estimates for the initial constant-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_constant_coefficients_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

The first four rows in @tbl-beta-simple-coefficients-r correspond to the mean-submodel parameters in @eq-beta-simple-mean, while the final row is the precision intercept $\widehat{\gamma}_0$ from @eq-beta-simple-precision. As anticipated in @sec-beta-software-estimation, the matched `R` and `Python` fits agree extremely closely: both the coefficient estimates and their model-based SEs are identical to the **four decimal places displayed** in @tbl-beta-simple-coefficients-r and @tbl-beta-simple-coefficients-py. This agreement provides a useful implementation check that the two software specifications are representing the same fitted Beta regression model.

The estimated precision intercept is $\widehat{\gamma}_0= \text{`r formatC(beta_constant_parameters[5], format = "f", digits = 4)`}$. Because the precision submodel uses the log link,

$$
\widehat{\phi}
=
\exp(\widehat{\gamma}_0)
=
\text{`r formatC(beta_constant_phi, format = "f", digits = 3)`},
$$

the value `r formatC(beta_constant_phi, format = "f", digits = 3)` is the fitted **common precision parameter** of the conditional Beta distributions. It is not a probability, a grade percentage, or a standard deviation. Under the mean–precision parameterization introduced in @sec-beta-mean-precision, each fitted conditional distribution has shape parameters

$$
\widehat{\alpha}_i
=
\widehat{\mu}_i\widehat{\phi},
\qquad
\widehat{\beta}_i
=
(1-\widehat{\mu}_i)\widehat{\phi},
$$

so that $\widehat{\alpha}_i+\widehat{\beta}_i=\widehat{\phi}$. Because the current precision submodel contains only an intercept, the **same value** `r formatC(beta_constant_phi, format = "f", digits = 3)` is used for every student, while the fitted conditional mean $\widehat{\mu}_i$ changes across the `Study Time` categories. For any given conditional mean, a larger value of $\phi$ corresponds to a Beta distribution that is more concentrated around that mean. However, the conditional variance still depends on both quantities,

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
=
\frac{
\widehat{\mu}_i(1-\widehat{\mu}_i)
}{
1+\widehat{\phi}
},
$$

so a common value of $\widehat{\phi}$ does not imply equal conditional variances across the four study-time groups.

At this stage, the coefficient table should still be read only on the scales defined by the model. The three non-intercept mean coefficients are contrasts relative to `<1 hour` on the **logit-mean scale**, while the precision intercept is on the **log-precision scale**. Likewise, the model-based SEs quantify uncertainty under the current mean and constant-precision assumptions. Therefore, we postpone grade-scale interpretation, Wald $p$-values, CIs, and final inferential statements until the model specification has passed its training-stage goodness-of-fit checks.

## Goodness of Fit and Model Adequacy for the Constant-precision Model {#sec-beta-simple-gof}

Fitting a Beta regression using the proper coding syntax is only the beginning of the modelling stage. We now ask whether the fitted model provides a reasonable description of the **training data** before using it for substantive interpretation or freezing the specification.

The checks below target different aspects of adequacy:

- **numerical stability** asks whether the likelihood optimization produced a usable solution;
- **observed-versus-fitted conditional means** assesses whether the mean submodel reproduces the group centres;
- **quantile residuals** assess the fitted conditional distributions more broadly;
- the **precision-structure check** asks whether one common value of $\phi$ can reproduce the observed within-group dispersion across the four fitted mean levels of our case study; and
- **influence screening** checks whether the conclusions are being driven by a small number of unusual training observations.

Note that these checks are complementary. A model can fit the conditional means well while still representing the conditional spread poorly, and successful numerical convergence does not imply distributional adequacy.

::: {.Heads-up}
::::{.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on diagnostics versus hypothesis tests!
::::
::::{.Heads-up-container}
We do not turn every goodness-of-fit diagnostic into a significance test. Quantile residuals are designed to provide a standard-Normal reference for graphical model checking. For a continuous response, Dunn and Smyth indicate that the residuals are standard Normal apart from sampling variability arising from estimated model parameters, and that their distribution converges to standard Normal when those parameters are consistently estimated [@dunn1996]. In the specific context of Beta regression, Pereira likewise emphasizes this asymptotic result and studies the finite-sample behaviour of quantile residuals through Monte Carlo simulation [@pereira2019].

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-feedback-to-learn-3699331/).](img/thumbs-up-down.png){width="500"}

Accordingly, we use the residual-versus-fitted and Normal Q-Q plots below as **diagnostic tools** rather than treating a generic Normality test of the fitted residual vector as a standalone goodness-of-fit test for the complete Beta regression specification. Likewise, the groupwise dispersion comparison introduced later is used descriptively; the formal test of whether `Study Time` should enter the precision submodel will come from the explicitly nested Beta regression models in @sec-beta-refinement.
::::
:::

### Convergence and Numerical Stability {#sec-beta-simple-stability}

The first check is computational. MLE can fail or become unstable when the likelihood is poorly behaved, the design is nearly redundant, or the fitted parameters move toward problematic regions. Therefore, before interpreting any diagnostic, we verify that the optimizer reports convergence, that all coefficient estimates and model-based standard errors are finite, and that the fitted conditional means remain strictly inside the Beta support.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-simple-stability-r
#| tbl-cap: "Numerical-stability checks for the initial constant-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_converged <- isTRUE(beta_constant_model$converged)
beta_constant_parameters_finite <- all(is.finite(beta_constant_parameters))
beta_constant_se_finite <- all(is.finite(beta_constant_standard_errors))

beta_constant_fitted_mean <- predict(beta_constant_model, type = "response")
beta_constant_fitted_precision <- predict(beta_constant_model, type = "precision")

beta_grade_scale_factor <- 100 * full_sample_n / (full_sample_n - 1)
beta_grade_scale_offset <- -50 / (full_sample_n - 1)
beta_constant_fitted_grade <-
  beta_grade_scale_factor * beta_constant_fitted_mean + beta_grade_scale_offset

stopifnot(
  beta_constant_converged,
  beta_constant_parameters_finite,
  beta_constant_se_finite,
  all(beta_constant_fitted_mean > 0 & beta_constant_fitted_mean < 1),
  all(beta_constant_fitted_precision > 0)
)

beta_constant_stability <- tibble(
  Check = c("Optimizer converged", "All coefficient estimates finite",
    "All model-based SEs finite", "Minimum fitted conditional mean (%)",
    "Maximum fitted conditional mean (%)", "Fitted common precision"),
  Result = c("Yes", "Yes", "Yes",
    formatC(min(beta_constant_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2),
    formatC(max(beta_constant_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2),
    formatC(beta_constant_phi, format = "f", digits = 3))
)

beta_constant_stability |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_converged = bool(beta_constant_model.mle_retvals["converged"])
beta_constant_parameters_finite = np.isfinite(beta_constant_parameters).all()
beta_constant_se_finite = np.isfinite(beta_constant_standard_errors).all()

beta_constant_fitted_mean = beta_constant_model.model.predict(
    beta_constant_model.params, which="mean")
beta_constant_fitted_precision = beta_constant_model.model.predict(
    beta_constant_model.params, which="precision")

beta_grade_scale_factor = 100 * full_sample_n / (full_sample_n - 1)
beta_grade_scale_offset = -50 / (full_sample_n - 1)
beta_constant_fitted_grade = (
    beta_grade_scale_factor * beta_constant_fitted_mean
    + beta_grade_scale_offset)

assert beta_constant_converged
assert beta_constant_parameters_finite and beta_constant_se_finite
assert ((beta_constant_fitted_mean > 0) & (beta_constant_fitted_mean < 1)).all()
assert (beta_constant_fitted_precision > 0).all()

    "Check": [
        "Optimizer converged",

        "Minimum fitted conditional mean (%)",
        "Maximum fitted conditional mean (%)",
        "Fitted common precision",

        "Yes", "Yes", "Yes",

beta_constant_stability_html = scrollable_table_html(beta_constant_stability)
```

:::

The stability checks pass in both implementations. The **fitted conditional means** range from `r formatC(min(beta_constant_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2)`% to `r formatC(max(beta_constant_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2)`%, so the fitted means remain well inside the grade scale after reversing the boundary transformation. Hence, the model is numerically usable. This tells us that the specified likelihood was optimized successfully; **it does not yet tell us whether the constant-precision distributional assumption is adequate**.

### Observed Versus Fitted Conditional Means {#sec-beta-simple-observed-fitted}

Because `Study Time` is the only regressor in the mean submodel, the model produces one fitted conditional mean for each of its four categories. A direct calibration check is therefore to compare each fitted group mean with the corresponding observed training mean on the original grade-percentage scale.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-simple-mean-calibration-r
#| tbl-cap: "Observed and fitted conditional mean grades by study time category."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_mean_calibration <- training_data |>
  mutate(`Fitted mean grade (%)` = beta_constant_fitted_grade) |>
  group_by(`Study Time`) |>
  summarise(
    `Observed mean grade (%)` = mean(`Final Grade (%)`),
    `Fitted mean grade (%)` = mean(`Fitted mean grade (%)`),
    `Observed - fitted (percentage points)` =
      `Observed mean grade (%)` - `Fitted mean grade (%)`,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

beta_constant_mean_max_gap <- max(
  abs(beta_constant_mean_calibration[["Observed - fitted (percentage points)"]])
)

beta_constant_mean_calibration |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ formatC(.x, format = "f", digits = 2))) |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_mean_calibration = training_data[[
    "Study Time", "Final Grade (%)"
]].copy()
beta_constant_mean_calibration["Fitted mean grade (%)"] = (
    beta_constant_fitted_grade)

beta_constant_mean_calibration = (
    beta_constant_mean_calibration.groupby("Study Time", observed=True)
    .agg(
        **{
            "Observed mean grade (%)": ("Final Grade (%)", "mean"),
            "Fitted mean grade (%)": ("Fitted mean grade (%)", "mean"),
        })
    .reset_index()
)
beta_constant_mean_calibration["Observed - fitted (percentage points)"] = (
    beta_constant_mean_calibration["Observed mean grade (%)"]
    - beta_constant_mean_calibration["Fitted mean grade (%)"])

beta_constant_mean_max_gap = np.abs(
    beta_constant_mean_calibration[
        "Observed - fitted (percentage points)"]).max()

beta_constant_mean_calibration_display = beta_constant_mean_calibration.copy()
for column in beta_constant_mean_calibration_display.columns[1:]:
    beta_constant_mean_calibration_display[column] = (
        beta_constant_mean_calibration_display[column]
        .map(lambda value: f"{value:.2f}"))

beta_constant_mean_calibration_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_constant_mean_calibration_display)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-simple-mean-calibration-py
#| tbl-cap: "Observed and fitted conditional mean grades by study time category."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_constant_mean_calibration_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

In @tbl-beta-simple-mean-calibration-r, the fitted conditional means track the observed training means closely across all four study-time categories. For the **first three categories**, the observed and fitted means differ by less than `r formatC(max(abs(beta_constant_mean_calibration[["Observed - fitted (percentage points)"]][1:3])), format = "f", digits = 2)` percentage points. The **largest discrepancy** occurs for the `5+ hours` group, where the fitted mean is `r formatC(abs(beta_constant_mean_calibration[["Observed - fitted (percentage points)"]][4]), format = "f", digits = 2)` percentage points higher than the observed group mean. Even this largest difference is small relative to the approximately `r formatC(study_time_mean_span, format = "f", digits = 1)`-percentage-point separation between the lowest and highest observed study-time means documented during the EDA.

Thus, the initial `Study Time` mean submodel is reproducing the **conditional centres** of the training response well. In particular, the substantial upward shift in final grades across the four study-time categories is already captured without adding further regressors to the mean submodel. This is useful descriptive evidence about the **mean structure**, but it does not establish adequacy of the complete Beta regression model.

A Beta regression specifies an entire conditional distribution, not only its conditional mean. Hence, a model can reproduce the group centres closely while still representing the conditional spread or distributional shape poorly. We next use quantile residuals to compare each observed response with the fitted conditional Beta distribution and determine whether the constant-precision specification is adequate beyond its fitted means.

### Quantile Residual Diagnostics {#sec-beta-simple-residuals}

For a continuous fitted distribution with cumulative distribution function (CDF) $F_i(\cdot)$, the **quantile residual** proposed by @dunn1996 is obtained by mapping the fitted cumulative probability of the observation through the standard-Normal quantile function:

$$
r_i^{(q)}
=
\Phi^{-1}
\left[
F_i(y_i)
\right],
$$

where $\Phi(\cdot)$ denotes the CDF of a standard-Normal random variable,

$$
\Phi(z)
=
\Pr(Z\leq z),
\qquad
Z\sim\operatorname{Normal}(0,1),
$$

and $\Phi^{-1}(\cdot)$ is its corresponding quantile function. Thus, $F_i(y_i)$ first expresses the observed response as a cumulative probability under its fitted conditional distribution, and $\Phi^{-1}(\cdot)$ then places that probability on the standard-Normal scale.

For the current Beta regression,

$$
F_i(y_i)
=
F_{\operatorname{Beta}}
\left(
y_i;\,
\widehat{\mu}_i\widehat{\phi},\,
(1-\widehat{\mu}_i)\widehat{\phi}
\right).
$$

Because the standard Beta distribution is continuous, the quantile residual is obtained directly from the fitted cumulative probability $F_i(y_i)$. The additional Uniform randomization introduced by Dunn and Smyth is required for non-continuous response distributions, where the fitted CDF has jumps [@dunn1996]. Then, if the fitted conditional distributions are adequate and their parameters were known, the probability-integral transform motivates a standard-Normal reference for these residuals. In a fitted regression, however, $\widehat{\mu}_i$ and $\widehat{\phi}$ are estimated from the same data, so the resulting residuals should be regarded as **approximately**, not exactly, standard Normal. Simulation work specifically for Beta regression has found quantile residuals to have useful Normal-reference behaviour for diagnostic purposes [@pereira2019]. The current [{betareg}](https://cran.r-project.org/package=betareg) implementation also uses quantile residuals as its default residual type.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-digital-3704070/).](img/pinned-notes.png){width="500"}

Now, we calculate the same residual definition explicitly in both languages.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-simple-residual-summary-r
#| tbl-cap: "Quantile-residual summaries by study time category for the constant-precision model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_alpha <- beta_constant_fitted_mean * beta_constant_fitted_precision
beta_constant_beta <-
  (1 - beta_constant_fitted_mean) * beta_constant_fitted_precision

beta_constant_cdf <- pbeta(
  training_data$grade_beta,
  shape1 = beta_constant_alpha,
  shape2 = beta_constant_beta
)
beta_constant_cdf <- pmin(
  pmax(beta_constant_cdf, .Machine$double.eps),
  1 - .Machine$double.eps
)
beta_constant_quantile_residuals <- qnorm(beta_constant_cdf)

beta_constant_residual_data <- training_data |>
  transmute(
    `Study Time`, `Final Grade (%)`, grade_beta,
    fitted_mean_beta = beta_constant_fitted_mean,
    `Fitted mean grade (%)` = beta_constant_fitted_grade,
    quantile_residual = beta_constant_quantile_residuals
  )

beta_constant_residual_summary <- beta_constant_residual_data |>
  group_by(`Study Time`) |>
  summarise(
    Students = n(),
    `Mean residual` = mean(quantile_residual),
    `Residual SD` = sd(quantile_residual),
    `Residual IQR` = IQR(quantile_residual),
    `|Residual| > 2` = sum(abs(quantile_residual) > 2),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

beta_constant_residual_sd_min <- min(beta_constant_residual_summary$`Residual SD`)
beta_constant_residual_sd_max <- max(beta_constant_residual_summary$`Residual SD`)
beta_constant_residual_sd_ratio <-
  beta_constant_residual_sd_max / beta_constant_residual_sd_min

beta_constant_residual_summary |>
  mutate(across(c(`Mean residual`, `Residual SD`, `Residual IQR`),
    ~ formatC(.x, format = "f", digits = 3))) |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_alpha = beta_constant_fitted_mean * beta_constant_fitted_precision
beta_constant_beta = (
    (1 - beta_constant_fitted_mean) * beta_constant_fitted_precision)

beta_constant_cdf = stats.beta.cdf(
    training_data["grade_beta"],
    beta_constant_alpha,
    beta_constant_beta,
)
beta_constant_cdf = np.clip(
    beta_constant_cdf, np.finfo(float).eps, 1 - np.finfo(float).eps)
beta_constant_quantile_residuals = stats.norm.ppf(beta_constant_cdf)

beta_constant_residual_data = training_data[[
    "Study Time", "Final Grade (%)", "grade_beta"
]].copy()
beta_constant_residual_data["fitted_mean_beta"] = beta_constant_fitted_mean
beta_constant_residual_data["Fitted mean grade (%)"] = beta_constant_fitted_grade
beta_constant_residual_data["quantile_residual"] = (
    beta_constant_quantile_residuals)

beta_constant_residual_summary = (
    beta_constant_residual_data.groupby("Study Time", observed=True)
    .agg(
        Students=("quantile_residual", "size"),
        **{
            "Mean residual": ("quantile_residual", "mean"),
            "Residual SD": ("quantile_residual", "std"),
            "Residual IQR": (
                "quantile_residual",
                lambda x: x.quantile(0.75) - x.quantile(0.25)),
            "|Residual| > 2": (
                "quantile_residual",
                lambda x: (np.abs(x) > 2).sum()),
        })
    .reset_index()
)

beta_constant_residual_sd_min = beta_constant_residual_summary[
    "Residual SD"].min()
beta_constant_residual_sd_max = beta_constant_residual_summary[
    "Residual SD"].max()
beta_constant_residual_sd_ratio = (
    beta_constant_residual_sd_max / beta_constant_residual_sd_min)

beta_constant_residual_summary_display = beta_constant_residual_summary.copy()
for column in ["Mean residual", "Residual SD", "Residual IQR"]:
    beta_constant_residual_summary_display[column] = (
        beta_constant_residual_summary_display[column]
        .map(lambda value: f"{value:.3f}"))

beta_constant_residual_summary_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_constant_residual_summary_display)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-simple-residual-summary-py
#| tbl-cap: "Quantile-residual summaries by study time category for the constant-precision model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_constant_residual_summary_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

The residual summaries in @tbl-beta-simple-residual-summary-r reveal more than the fitted conditional means did. First, the **mean quantile residuals remain close to zero in all four study-time groups**, so there is little evidence here of a systematic location bias within any one category. The more important pattern appears in the **residual spread**. The **group-specific residual standard deviations** increase from `r formatC(beta_constant_residual_summary[["Residual SD"]][1], format = "f", digits = 3)` for `<1 hour` and `r formatC(beta_constant_residual_summary[["Residual SD"]][2], format = "f", digits = 3)` for `1–3 hours` to `r formatC(beta_constant_residual_summary[["Residual SD"]][3], format = "f", digits = 3)` for `3–5 hours` and `r formatC(beta_constant_residual_summary[["Residual SD"]][4], format = "f", digits = 3)` for `5+ hours`. Overall, the largest residual SD is therefore `r formatC(beta_constant_residual_sd_ratio, format = "f", digits = 2)` times the smallest.

The **IQRs** reinforce the same pattern: residual spread is narrower in the two lower-study-time groups and wider in the two higher-study-time groups. The **counts of observations with $|r_i^{(q)}|>2$** also increase from `r beta_constant_residual_summary[["|Residual| > 2"]][1]` and `r beta_constant_residual_summary[["|Residual| > 2"]][2]` in the first two categories to `r beta_constant_residual_summary[["|Residual| > 2"]][3]` and `r beta_constant_residual_summary[["|Residual| > 2"]][4]` in the last two. These counts are descriptive rather than a formal goodness-of-fit test, but they point in the same direction as the SD and IQR comparisons.

Under a well-calibrated fitted conditional distribution, the quantile residuals should have broadly comparable spread across fitted mean levels. Instead, the residual dispersion increases systematically with `Study Time`. This suggests that the **mean structure is capturing the group centres reasonably well, while the constant-precision assumption is not reproducing the conditional spread equally well across the four categories**. The next diagnostics examine that precision mismatch more directly.

The residual-versus-fitted plot in @fig-beta-simple-residuals-fitted-r (or @fig-beta-simple-residuals-fitted-py) makes that comparison visible.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-beta-simple-residuals-fitted-r
#| fig-cap: "Quantile residuals versus fitted conditional mean grades for the constant-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

beta_constant_residual_y_limits <- c(
  floor(min(beta_constant_quantile_residuals)),
  ceiling(max(beta_constant_quantile_residuals))
)
beta_constant_residual_y_breaks <- seq(
  2 * ceiling(beta_constant_residual_y_limits[1] / 2),
  2 * floor(beta_constant_residual_y_limits[2] / 2), by = 2
)
beta_constant_residual_fitted_x_limits <- c(
  5 * floor((min(beta_constant_fitted_grade) - 0.5) / 5),
  5 * ceiling((max(beta_constant_fitted_grade) + 0.5) / 5)
)
beta_constant_residual_fitted_x_breaks <- seq(
  beta_constant_residual_fitted_x_limits[1],
  beta_constant_residual_fitted_x_limits[2], by = 5
)

beta_constant_residual_fitted_plot <- ggplot(
  beta_constant_residual_data,
  aes(x = `Fitted mean grade (%)`, y = quantile_residual)
) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.25, height = 0, seed = 551),
    alpha = 0.45, colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-2, 2), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = beta_constant_residual_fitted_x_limits,
    breaks = beta_constant_residual_fitted_x_breaks,
    expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = beta_constant_residual_y_limits,
    breaks = beta_constant_residual_y_breaks,
    expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 15.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 20),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(x = "\n Fitted conditional mean grade (%)",
    y = "Quantile residual\n")

beta_constant_residual_fitted_plot
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-beta-simple-residuals-fitted-py
#| fig-cap: "Quantile residuals versus fitted conditional mean grades for the constant-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

beta_constant_residual_y_limits = (
    np.floor(beta_constant_quantile_residuals.min()),
    np.ceil(beta_constant_quantile_residuals.max()),
)
beta_constant_residual_y_breaks = np.arange(
    2 * np.ceil(beta_constant_residual_y_limits[0] / 2),
    2 * np.floor(beta_constant_residual_y_limits[1] / 2) + 1, 2)
beta_constant_residual_fitted_x_limits = (
    5 * np.floor((beta_constant_fitted_grade.min() - 0.5) / 5),
    5 * np.ceil((beta_constant_fitted_grade.max() + 0.5) / 5),
)
beta_constant_residual_fitted_x_breaks = np.arange(
    beta_constant_residual_fitted_x_limits[0],
    beta_constant_residual_fitted_x_limits[1] + 1, 5)

beta_constant_residual_plot_rng = np.random.default_rng(551)
beta_constant_residual_plot_x = (
    beta_constant_fitted_grade
    + beta_constant_residual_plot_rng.uniform(
        -0.25, 0.25, len(beta_constant_fitted_grade)))

beta_constant_residual_fitted_plot, beta_constant_residual_fitted_axis = (
    plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 8)))

_ = beta_constant_residual_fitted_axis.scatter(
    beta_constant_residual_plot_x, beta_constant_quantile_residuals,
    alpha=0.45, color="#0072B2")
_ = beta_constant_residual_fitted_axis.axhline(
    0, linewidth=0.8, color="black")
for reference in (-2, 2):
    _ = beta_constant_residual_fitted_axis.axhline(
        reference, linestyle="--", linewidth=0.7, color="black")

_ = beta_constant_residual_fitted_axis.set_xlim(
    beta_constant_residual_fitted_x_limits)
_ = beta_constant_residual_fitted_axis.set_xticks(
    beta_constant_residual_fitted_x_breaks)
_ = beta_constant_residual_fitted_axis.set_ylim(
    beta_constant_residual_y_limits)
_ = beta_constant_residual_fitted_axis.set_yticks(
    beta_constant_residual_y_breaks)
_ = beta_constant_residual_fitted_axis.set_xlabel(
    "\n Fitted conditional mean grade (%)", fontsize=20)
_ = beta_constant_residual_fitted_axis.set_ylabel(
    "Quantile residual\n", fontsize=20)
beta_constant_residual_fitted_axis.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=15.5)
beta_constant_residual_fitted_plot.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

In @fig-beta-simple-residuals-fitted-r, because the fitted mean model contains only the four study-time categories, the horizontal axis has four fitted mean locations. Hence, the diagnostic question is whether the vertical residual distributions look similarly centred and dispersed at those locations. The plot shows that the residual spread changes across the fitted means rather than remaining roughly comparable, which points toward a distributional issue that is not visible from the group means alone.

A Normal Q-Q plot provides a complementary view of the residual distribution.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-beta-simple-residuals-qq-r
#| fig-cap: "Normal Q-Q plot of quantile residuals from the constant-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

beta_constant_qq_probabilities <- (
  seq_along(beta_constant_quantile_residuals) - 0.5
) / length(beta_constant_quantile_residuals)
beta_constant_qq_data <- tibble(
  theoretical = qnorm(beta_constant_qq_probabilities),
  observed = sort(beta_constant_quantile_residuals)
)
beta_constant_qq_x_limits <- c(
  floor(min(beta_constant_qq_data$theoretical)),
  ceiling(max(beta_constant_qq_data$theoretical))
)
beta_constant_qq_x_breaks <- seq(
  2 * ceiling(beta_constant_qq_x_limits[1] / 2),
  2 * floor(beta_constant_qq_x_limits[2] / 2), by = 2
)
beta_constant_qq_y_limits <- c(
  floor(min(beta_constant_quantile_residuals)),
  ceiling(max(beta_constant_quantile_residuals))
)
beta_constant_qq_y_breaks <- seq(
  2 * ceiling(beta_constant_qq_y_limits[1] / 2),
  2 * floor(beta_constant_qq_y_limits[2] / 2), by = 2
)

beta_constant_residual_qq_plot <- ggplot(
  beta_constant_qq_data, aes(x = theoretical, y = observed)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = beta_constant_qq_x_limits,
    breaks = beta_constant_qq_x_breaks,
    expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = beta_constant_qq_y_limits,
    breaks = beta_constant_qq_y_breaks,
    expand = expansion(mult = 0)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 15.5),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 20),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "\n Theoretical standard-Normal quantiles",
    y = "Observed quantile residuals\n"

beta_constant_residual_qq_plot
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-beta-simple-residuals-qq-py
#| fig-cap: "Normal Q-Q plot of quantile residuals from the constant-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

#| fig.width: 14

beta_constant_qq_probabilities = (
    np.arange(1, len(beta_constant_quantile_residuals) + 1) - 0.5
) / len(beta_constant_quantile_residuals)
beta_constant_qq_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "theoretical": stats.norm.ppf(beta_constant_qq_probabilities),
    "observed": np.sort(beta_constant_quantile_residuals),
})
beta_constant_qq_x_limits = (
    np.floor(beta_constant_qq_data["theoretical"].min()),
    np.ceil(beta_constant_qq_data["theoretical"].max()),
)
beta_constant_qq_x_breaks = np.arange(
    2 * np.ceil(beta_constant_qq_x_limits[0] / 2),
    2 * np.floor(beta_constant_qq_x_limits[1] / 2) + 1, 2)
beta_constant_qq_y_limits = (
    np.floor(beta_constant_quantile_residuals.min()),
    np.ceil(beta_constant_quantile_residuals.max()),
)
beta_constant_qq_y_breaks = np.arange(
    2 * np.ceil(beta_constant_qq_y_limits[0] / 2),
    2 * np.floor(beta_constant_qq_y_limits[1] / 2) + 1, 2)

beta_constant_residual_qq_plot, beta_constant_residual_qq_axis = (
    plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 8)))

_ = beta_constant_residual_qq_axis.scatter(
    beta_constant_qq_data["theoretical"],
    beta_constant_qq_data["observed"],
    alpha=0.55, color="#0072B2")
_ = beta_constant_residual_qq_axis.plot(
    beta_constant_qq_x_limits, beta_constant_qq_x_limits,
    linestyle="--", color="black")

_ = beta_constant_residual_qq_axis.set_xlim(beta_constant_qq_x_limits)
_ = beta_constant_residual_qq_axis.set_xticks(beta_constant_qq_x_breaks)
_ = beta_constant_residual_qq_axis.set_ylim(beta_constant_qq_y_limits)
_ = beta_constant_residual_qq_axis.set_yticks(beta_constant_qq_y_breaks)
_ = beta_constant_residual_qq_axis.set_xlabel(
    "\n Theoretical standard-Normal quantiles", fontsize=20)
_ = beta_constant_residual_qq_axis.set_ylabel(
    "Observed quantile residuals\n", fontsize=20)
beta_constant_residual_qq_axis.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=15.5)
beta_constant_residual_qq_plot.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

The Normal Q-Q plot, in @fig-beta-simple-residuals-qq-r (or @fig-beta-simple-residuals-qq-py), provides a complementary view of the residual distribution. Through most of the central range, the quantile residuals follow the reference line reasonably closely, indicating that the bulk of the fitted residual distribution is not grossly inconsistent with the standard-Normal reference. The more noticeable departures occur in the tails, especially in the **upper tail**, where several of the largest residuals lie well above the reference line. This pattern indicates that the fitted constant-precision model assigns too little probability to some comparatively large positive departures from the fitted conditional means.

This tail behaviour is consistent with the groupwise summaries rather than being an isolated graphical feature. As shown in @tbl-beta-simple-residual-summary-r and @fig-beta-simple-residuals-fitted-r, residual dispersion increases with `Study Time`, with the largest spread and the largest number of residuals beyond $|r_i^{(q)}|=2$ occurring in the higher-study-time categories. Thus, the Q-Q plot reinforces the conclusion that the principal inadequacy is not a broad failure of the `Study Time` mean structure, which already reproduces the group centres closely, but rather a mismatch in the **conditional dispersion represented by the constant-precision assumption**.

Nevertheless, the Q-Q plot should be interpreted as a diagnostic rather than a formal goodness-of-fit test. Its role here is to reveal where the fitted conditional distribution departs from its reference behaviour and to be considered together with the residual-versus-fitted plot and the groupwise residual summaries. Taken together, these diagnostics motivate examining the precision structure directly in the next subsection.


### Precision-structure Check {#sec-beta-simple-precision}

This is the **central adequacy check** for the initial model. The training EDA showed that the raw within-category grade standard deviations are fairly similar across the four `Study Time` groups (see @tbl-beta-study-time-summary-r). However, under the mean–precision parameterization of Beta regression [@ferrari2004; @cribari2010],

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
=
\frac{\mu_i(1-\mu_i)}{1+\phi}.
$${#eq-beta-constant-precision-variance}

Because the fitted conditional means increase substantially across the study-time categories and move toward the upper boundary, the factor $\mu_i(1-\mu_i)$ decreases in @eq-beta-constant-precision-variance. Thus, a single common $\phi$ forces the model-implied response standard deviation to shrink as the fitted mean approaches $1$. Importantly, **constant precision does not imply constant response-scale variance**: even when $\phi$ is fixed, the conditional variance changes with $\mu_i$ through the term $\mu_i(1-\mu_i)$ [@ferrari2004; @cribari2010].

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-action-bound-3704046/).](img/magnifying-glass-2.png){width="420"}

Having said that, we compare the observed within-group standard deviation with the standard deviation implied by the fitted constant-precision Beta distribution. To make the discrepancy easier to interpret, we also construct a **variance-matching implied precision** for each study-time category.

If $s_g^2$ is the observed sample variance of `grade_beta` in category $g$ and $\widehat{\mu}_g$ is its fitted conditional mean, we algebraically rearrange the Beta variance relationship,

$$
s_g^2
\approx
\frac{\widehat{\mu}_g(1-\widehat{\mu}_g)}{1+\phi_g},
$$

to obtain

$$
\widetilde{\phi}_g
=
\frac{\widehat{\mu}_g(1-\widehat{\mu}_g)}{s_g^2}-1.
$${#eq-beta-variance-matching-precision}

This quantity answers a diagnostic question:

> **What precision would reproduce the observed group variance if the fitted mean were held fixed?**

The quantity in @eq-beta-variance-matching-precision is a **diagnostic algebraic rearrangement of the Beta variance function**, not a literature-defined test statistic or an alternative maximum-likelihood estimate. Thus, we do not assign it a reference sampling distribution or a $p$-value. Its purpose is descriptive: if the values of $\widetilde{\phi}_g$ differ substantially across the study-time categories, then the common-precision assumption is unlikely to reproduce the observed within-group dispersion equally well across those categories.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-simple-precision-diagnostic-r
#| tbl-cap: "Observed and model-implied within-group dispersion under constant precision."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_precision_diagnostic <- beta_constant_residual_data |>
  group_by(`Study Time`) |>
  summarise(observed_sd_grade = sd(`Final Grade (%)`), observed_variance_beta = var(grade_beta),
    fitted_mean_beta = first(fitted_mean_beta), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(model_sd_grade = beta_grade_scale_factor * sqrt(
      fitted_mean_beta * (1 - fitted_mean_beta) / (1 + beta_constant_phi)),
    sd_ratio = observed_sd_grade / model_sd_grade,
    variance_matching_phi = fitted_mean_beta * (1 - fitted_mean_beta) /
      observed_variance_beta - 1)

beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_min <- min(beta_constant_precision_diagnostic$variance_matching_phi)
beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_max <- max(beta_constant_precision_diagnostic$variance_matching_phi)
beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_ratio <- beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_max /
  beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_min

beta_constant_precision_diagnostic |>
  transmute(`Study Time`, `Observed SD (percentage points)` = observed_sd_grade,
    `Model-implied SD (percentage points)` = model_sd_grade,
    `Observed / implied SD` = sd_ratio, `Variance-matching precision` = variance_matching_phi,
    `Fitted common precision` = beta_constant_phi) |>
  kable(digits = 2, align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_precision_diagnostic = (beta_constant_residual_data.groupby(
    "Study Time", observed=True).agg(observed_sd_grade=("Final Grade (%)", "std"),
        observed_variance_beta=("grade_beta", "var"),
        fitted_mean_beta=("fitted_mean_beta", "first")).reset_index())
beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["model_sd_grade"] = beta_grade_scale_factor * np.sqrt(
    beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["fitted_mean_beta"]
    * (1 - beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["fitted_mean_beta"])
    / (1 + beta_constant_phi))
beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["sd_ratio"] = (beta_constant_precision_diagnostic[
    "observed_sd_grade"] / beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["model_sd_grade"])
beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["variance_matching_phi"] = (
    beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["fitted_mean_beta"]
    * (1 - beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["fitted_mean_beta"])
    / beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["observed_variance_beta"] - 1)

beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_min = beta_constant_precision_diagnostic[
    "variance_matching_phi"].min()
beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_max = beta_constant_precision_diagnostic[
    "variance_matching_phi"].max()
beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_ratio = (beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_max /
    beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_min)

beta_constant_precision_display = beta_constant_precision_diagnostic[["Study Time",
    "observed_sd_grade", "model_sd_grade", "sd_ratio", "variance_matching_phi"]].rename(
    columns={"observed_sd_grade": "Observed SD (percentage points)",
        "model_sd_grade": "Model-implied SD (percentage points)",
        "sd_ratio": "Observed / implied SD",
        "variance_matching_phi": "Variance-matching precision"}).copy()
beta_constant_precision_display["Fitted common precision"] = beta_constant_phi
beta_constant_precision_diagnostic_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_constant_precision_display, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.2f}")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-simple-precision-diagnostic-py
#| tbl-cap: "Observed and model-implied within-group dispersion under constant precision."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_constant_precision_diagnostic_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

Now, the response-scale mismatch is easier to see graphically. The next figure compares the observed within-group grade SD with the SD implied by the fitted constant-precision model.

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{r}
#| label: fig-beta-simple-precision-diagnostic-r
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-beta-simple-precision-diagnostic-py
#| fig-cap: "Observed and model-implied within-group grade standard deviations under the constant-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

beta_constant_precision_plot_y_max = np.ceil(max(
    beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["observed_sd_grade"].max(),
    beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["model_sd_grade"].max()))
beta_constant_precision_plot_x = np.arange(len(study_time_levels))
beta_constant_precision_plot_width = 0.34
beta_constant_precision_plot, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 8))

_ = ax.bar(beta_constant_precision_plot_x - beta_constant_precision_plot_width / 2,
    beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["observed_sd_grade"],
    beta_constant_precision_plot_width, label="Observed", color="#0072B2")
_ = ax.bar(beta_constant_precision_plot_x + beta_constant_precision_plot_width / 2,
    beta_constant_precision_diagnostic["model_sd_grade"],
    beta_constant_precision_plot_width, label="Model-implied", color="#D55E00")
_ = ax.set_xlim(-0.6, len(study_time_levels) - 0.4)
_ = ax.set_ylim(0, beta_constant_precision_plot_y_max)
_ = ax.set_xticks(beta_constant_precision_plot_x, study_time_levels)
_ = ax.set_yticks(np.arange(0, beta_constant_precision_plot_y_max + 1, 1))
_ = ax.set_xlabel("\n Study Time", fontsize=20)
_ = ax.set_ylabel("Within-group SD (percentage points)\n", fontsize=20)
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=15.5)
_ = ax.legend(title="Dispersion", loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.14),
    ncol=2, frameon=False, fontsize=16, title_fontsize=18)
beta_constant_precision_plot.tight_layout()
beta_constant_precision_plot.subplots_adjust(bottom=0.22)
```
