
:::

The mismatch shown in @fig-beta-simple-precision-diagnostic-r (or @fig-beta-simple-precision-diagnostic-py) is systematic. The **observed within-group grade SDs range** from `r formatC(min(beta_constant_precision_diagnostic$observed_sd_grade), format = "f", digits = 2)` to `r formatC(max(beta_constant_precision_diagnostic$observed_sd_grade), format = "f", digits = 2)` percentage points, whereas the **model-implied SD** declines from `r formatC(beta_constant_precision_diagnostic$model_sd_grade[1], format = "f", digits = 2)` percentage points for `<1 hour` to `r formatC(beta_constant_precision_diagnostic$model_sd_grade[4], format = "f", digits = 2)` percentage points for `5+ hours`. Thus, the figure makes visible the variance pattern imposed by one common precision parameter: as the fitted mean rises toward the upper boundary, the model increasingly compresses the conditional distribution even though the observed grade-scale spread remains comparatively stable.

The same issue appears on the **precision scale**. The fitted model uses the **common value** `r formatC(beta_constant_phi, format = "f", digits = 3)` for all four categories, but the **category-specific variance-matching implied precisions** range from `r formatC(beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_min, format = "f", digits = 2)` to `r formatC(beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_max, format = "f", digits = 2)`, a largest-to-smallest ratio of `r formatC(beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_ratio, format = "f", digits = 2)`. The observed-versus-implied SD ratios, in @tbl-beta-simple-precision-diagnostic-r, express the same mismatch from the response-scale perspective.

This is exactly the distinction anticipated in @sec-beta-precision: the conditional means can be modelled well while the common-precision restriction imposes the wrong pattern of conditional spread. This diagnostic does not by itself establish a formal alternative model. Instead, it provides a concrete reason to fit a variable-precision specification and then compare the nested models using an explicitly defined likelihood-ratio test.

### Influence and Leverage {#sec-beta-simple-influence}

A model can also appear inadequate because a small number of unusual observations exert disproportionate influence. Beta regression diagnostics include residual and leverage measures developed specifically for this modelling framework [@ferrari2004; @cribari2010]. However, the current `R` and `Python` implementations do not expose identical influence quantities. In particular, the official [{statsmodels} documentation for `BetaResults.get_influence()`](https://www.statsmodels.org/stable/generated/statsmodels.othermod.betareg.BetaResults.get_influence.html) notes that multi-link influence support is experimental and that its generalized leverage differs from the linear-approximation leverage used by `betareg()`.

Therefore, we avoid presenting differently defined Cook's-distance or generalized-leverage quantities as though they were numerically interchangeable. Instead, we use a transparent two-part screen that can be reproduced in both languages:

1. inspect the ordinary **mean-design leverage** to identify unusual `Study Time` design configurations; and
2. for the five observations with the largest absolute quantile residuals, refit the same model after deleting one observation at a time and record the maximum change in the four fitted conditional means and the relative change in the common precision.

This is a **sensitivity screen**, not a hypothesis test or an automatic deletion rule.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-simple-influence-r
#| tbl-cap: "Targeted case-deletion sensitivity screen for the constant-precision model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_mean_design <- model.matrix(~ `Study Time`, data = training_data)
beta_constant_design_leverage <- rowSums(
  (beta_constant_mean_design %*% solve(crossprod(beta_constant_mean_design))) *
    beta_constant_mean_design)
beta_constant_screen_positions <- head(
  order(abs(beta_constant_quantile_residuals), decreasing = TRUE), 5)

beta_constant_reference_data <- tibble(
  `Study Time` = factor(study_time_levels, levels = study_time_levels))
beta_constant_reference_means <- predict(
  beta_constant_model, newdata = beta_constant_reference_data, type = "response")

beta_constant_influence_screen <- bind_rows(lapply(
  beta_constant_screen_positions, function(position) {
    beta_constant_reduced_model <- update(
      beta_constant_model, data = training_data[-position, , drop = FALSE])
    beta_constant_reduced_means <- predict(
      beta_constant_reduced_model, newdata = beta_constant_reference_data,
      type = "response")
    beta_constant_reduced_phi <- predict(
      beta_constant_reduced_model, type = "precision")[1]

    tibble(`Training row` = position,
      `Study Time` = as.character(training_data$`Study Time`[position]),
      `Final grade (%)` = training_data$`Final Grade (%)`[position],
      `|Quantile residual|` = abs(beta_constant_quantile_residuals[position]),
      `Design leverage` = beta_constant_design_leverage[position],
      `Max fitted-mean change (percentage points)` = beta_grade_scale_factor *
        max(abs(beta_constant_reduced_means - beta_constant_reference_means)),
      `Absolute relative precision change (%)` =
        100 * abs(beta_constant_reduced_phi / beta_constant_phi - 1))
  }))

beta_constant_max_design_leverage <- max(beta_constant_design_leverage)
beta_constant_max_mean_sensitivity <- max(
  beta_constant_influence_screen[["Max fitted-mean change (percentage points)"]])
beta_constant_max_phi_sensitivity <- max(
  beta_constant_influence_screen[["Absolute relative precision change (%)"]])

beta_constant_influence_screen |>
  kable(digits = 3, align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_constant_mean_design = beta_constant_model.model.exog
beta_constant_design_leverage = np.einsum(
    "ij,jk,ik->i", beta_constant_mean_design,
    np.linalg.inv(beta_constant_mean_design.T @ beta_constant_mean_design),
    beta_constant_mean_design)
beta_constant_screen_positions = np.argsort(
    np.abs(beta_constant_quantile_residuals))[-5:][::-1]

beta_constant_reference_data = pd.DataFrame({"Study Time": pd.Categorical(
    study_time_levels, categories=study_time_levels, ordered=False)})
beta_constant_reference_means = np.asarray(beta_constant_model.predict(
    exog=beta_constant_reference_data, which="mean"))

beta_constant_influence_rows = []
for position in beta_constant_screen_positions:
    beta_constant_reduced_data = training_data.drop(training_data.index[position])
    beta_constant_reduced_model = BetaModel.from_formula(
        'grade_beta ~ C(Q("Study Time"), Treatment(reference="<1 hour"))',
        data=beta_constant_reduced_data, exog_precision_formula="1",
        link=sm.families.links.Logit(), link_precision=sm.families.links.Log(),
    ).fit(method="bfgs", maxiter=1000, disp=False)
    beta_constant_reduced_means = np.asarray(beta_constant_reduced_model.predict(
        exog=beta_constant_reference_data, which="mean"))
    beta_constant_reduced_phi = float(beta_constant_reduced_model.model.predict(
        beta_constant_reduced_model.params, which="precision")[0])

    beta_constant_influence_rows.append({
        "Training row": int(position + 1),
        "Study Time": str(training_data.iloc[position]["Study Time"]),
        "Final grade (%)": training_data.iloc[position]["Final Grade (%)"],
        "|Quantile residual|": abs(beta_constant_quantile_residuals[position]),
        "Design leverage": beta_constant_design_leverage[position],
        "Max fitted-mean change (percentage points)": beta_grade_scale_factor *
            np.max(np.abs(beta_constant_reduced_means - beta_constant_reference_means)),
        "Absolute relative precision change (%)":
            100 * abs(beta_constant_reduced_phi / beta_constant_phi - 1),
    })

beta_constant_influence_screen = pd.DataFrame(beta_constant_influence_rows)
beta_constant_max_design_leverage = beta_constant_design_leverage.max()
beta_constant_max_mean_sensitivity = beta_constant_influence_screen[
    "Max fitted-mean change (percentage points)"].max()
beta_constant_max_phi_sensitivity = beta_constant_influence_screen[
    "Absolute relative precision change (%)"].max()
beta_constant_influence_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_constant_influence_screen, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.3f}")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-simple-influence-py
#| tbl-cap: "Targeted case-deletion sensitivity screen for the constant-precision model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_constant_influence_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

The ordinary mean-design leverage is uniformly low because the mean submodel contains only the four well-represented `Study Time` categories. In this factor-only design, observations within the same category share the same leverage, and the largest value is only `r formatC(beta_constant_max_design_leverage, format = "f", digits = 4)`. Thus, none of the screened observations is unusual because of its regressor configuration.

The case-deletion results provide a more direct sensitivity check. The five largest absolute quantile residuals are concentrated near the upper response boundary, but deleting any one of these observations changes the **four fitted conditional means** by at most `r formatC(beta_constant_max_mean_sensitivity, format = "f", digits = 3)` percentage points. The **common fitted precision** is somewhat more sensitive: its largest absolute relative change is `r formatC(beta_constant_max_phi_sensitivity, format = "f", digits = 2)`%. This distinction is useful. The fitted mean structure is highly stable to these individual cases, whereas the dispersion parameter reacts more noticeably to an extreme response.

These are sensitivity measures rather than universal cutoff statistics, so they do not provide a formal rule for retaining or deleting observations. More importantly, the dispersion problem identified earlier is a **repeated across-group pattern**, whereas this screen perturbs the model one observation at a time. Hence, the case-deletion results do not suggest that the inadequate constant-precision structure can be explained away by a single influential observation. We retain all observations and address the dispersion pattern through the model specification itself.

### Constant-precision Model Adequacy Summary {#sec-beta-simple-gof-summary}

<br>

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-group-discussion-3947909/).](img/group-discussion.png){width="440"}

All together, the training-stage diagnostics give a consistent picture of what the initial model captures well and where its main inadequacy lies.

| **Diagnostic layer** | **Training-stage finding** | **Implication for the workflow** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Numerical stability | Optimization converges, the coefficient estimates and model-based SEs are finite, and all fitted conditional means remain inside the response support. | The fitted solution is numerically usable, so the remaining concerns are about model adequacy rather than optimization failure. |
| Conditional means | The **largest absolute observed-versus-fitted group-mean difference** is `r formatC(beta_constant_mean_max_gap, format = "f", digits = 2)` percentage points. | The `Study Time` mean submodel already represents the conditional centres well. |
| Quantile residuals | **Group-specific residual SDs** range from `r formatC(beta_constant_residual_sd_min, format = "f", digits = 3)` to `r formatC(beta_constant_residual_sd_max, format = "f", digits = 3)`, with greater spread in the higher-study-time categories and noticeable upper-tail Q-Q departures. | The fitted conditional distributions do not reproduce the residual spread equally well across the four fitted mean levels. |
| Precision structure | **Variance-matching implied precisions** range from `r formatC(beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_min, format = "f", digits = 2)` to `r formatC(beta_constant_variance_matching_phi_max, format = "f", digits = 2)`, whereas the fitted model imposes $\widehat{\phi}=$ `r formatC(beta_constant_phi, format = "f", digits = 3)` for every category. | One common precision cannot reconcile the Beta variance function with the comparatively stable observed grade-scale spread across `Study Time` categories. |
| Influence screen | The **largest mean-design leverage** is `r formatC(beta_constant_max_design_leverage, format = "f", digits = 4)`. Deleting any one of the five largest absolute quantile-residual cases changes the fitted group means by at most `r formatC(beta_constant_max_mean_sensitivity, format = "f", digits = 3)` percentage points and the common precision by at most `r formatC(beta_constant_max_phi_sensitivity, format = "f", digits = 2)`%. | The mean structure is highly stable to these individual cases. Precision is somewhat more sensitive, but no single screened observation explains the repeated across-group dispersion pattern. |

: Adequacy summary for the initial constant-precision Beta regression. {#tbl-beta-simple-gof-summary .striped .hover}

Therefore, the central conclusion is not that the `Study Time` mean structure has failed. The fitted conditional means reproduce the observed group centres closely, and the case-deletion screen shows that those fitted means are highly stable even for the observations with the largest absolute quantile residuals. The main inadequacy lies instead in the **constant-precision restriction**.

Under one common $\phi$, the Beta variance function forces the conditional spread to decrease as the fitted mean moves toward the upper boundary. The training data do not follow that pattern: their observed within-category grade SDs remain comparatively stable, while the quantile-residual spread increases across the higher-study-time categories. The variance-matching diagnostic makes the same disagreement visible on the precision scale. Although the fitted common precision is somewhat sensitive to the most extreme individual responses, the mismatch is repeated across categories rather than attributable to a single influential observation.

The next modelling step is targeted rather than exploratory. We retain the existing `Study Time` mean submodel and allow the **precision parameter to vary by `Study Time`**. We will then compare this variable-precision specification with the current constant-precision model using a formally defined nested-model likelihood-ratio test. After that comparison, we will repeat the core adequacy checks before deciding whether the revised specification is suitable to freeze for the subsequent inferential and predictive analyses.

## Variable-precision Beta Regression {#sec-beta-extended-model}

The constant-precision model gave us a useful starting point: its `Study Time` mean submodel reproduced the observed group centres closely, but its conditional spread was not equally adequate across the four study-time categories. Hence, the next model changes **only the part of the specification implicated by the diagnostics**. We retain the existing conditional-mean structure and allow the precision parameter to vary with `Study Time`. This is a targeted refinement rather than a search for a more complicated model. All decisions in this section continue to use the **training data only**; the testing responses remain untouched.

### Why Model Precision? {#sec-beta-adjustment-rationale}

The motivation comes directly from the adequacy checks in @sec-beta-simple-gof. Under the constant-precision fit, the conditional means were reproduced closely, so there is no diagnostic reason to replace the `Study Time` mean structure. The problem appeared instead in the conditional spread: quantile-residual dispersion increased across the higher-study-time categories, and the variance-matching implied precisions differed substantially even though the fitted model imposed one common value of $\phi$.

This distinction follows from the Beta mean–variance relationship,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
=
\frac{\mu_i(1-\mu_i)}{1+\phi_i}.
$$

When $\phi_i$ is held constant, changes in $\mu_i$ alone determine how the model variance changes across observations. In our training data, that restriction forces the fitted distribution to become increasingly concentrated as the conditional mean approaches the upper boundary, while the observed grade-scale spread remains comparatively stable. **Allowing $\phi_i$ to vary** provides the model with the flexibility needed to address that specific mismatch [@cribari2010].

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-group-3702061/).](img/sample-piece.png){width="350"}

Accordingly, the refinement is

$$
\text{mean}\sim\texttt{Study Time},
\qquad
\text{precision}\sim\texttt{Study Time}.
$$

The precision submodel should be interpreted primarily as **distributional structure**. It helps the conditional Beta distributions reproduce the observed amount of variation; it is not being introduced as a separate causal or behavioural model of why some students have more variable grades.

### Mathematical Specification {#sec-beta-extended-specification}

The conditional-mean submodel remains exactly the same as in @eq-beta-simple-mean. With `<1 hour` as the reference category,

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i)
=
\beta_0
+
\beta_1x_{i,1}
+
\beta_2x_{i,2}
+
\beta_3x_{i,3},
$${#eq-beta-variable-mean}

where $x_{i,1}$, $x_{i,2}$, and $x_{i,3}$ are the treatment-coded indicators for `1–3 hours`, `3–5 hours`, and `5+ hours`, respectively.

We now use those **same three indicator regressors** in the precision submodel:

$$
\log(\phi_i)
=
\gamma_0
+
\gamma_1x_{i,1}
+
\gamma_2x_{i,2}
+
\gamma_3x_{i,3}.
$${#eq-beta-variable-precision}

Hence,

$$
\phi_i
=
\exp\left(
\gamma_0+\gamma_1x_{i,1}+\gamma_2x_{i,2}+\gamma_3x_{i,3}
\right)
>0.
$$

For the `<1 hour` reference category, $\phi_i=\exp(\gamma_0)$. For the other categories, $\exp(\gamma_j)$ is the multiplicative precision ratio relative to `<1 hour`, holding the coding of the remaining indicators fixed. These ratios describe differences in the **concentration of the fitted conditional distributions**, not event odds or causal effects.

The resulting model is

$$
Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}
\left(
\mu_i\phi_i,\,
(1-\mu_i)\phi_i
\right),
$$

with both $\mu_i$ and $\phi_i$ allowed to differ across `Study Time` categories. The model contains four mean parameters and four precision parameters. Relative to the constant-precision model, the only additions are $\gamma_1$, $\gamma_2$, and $\gamma_3$.

### `R`/`Python` Fit {#sec-beta-extended-fitting}

The following code fits the same variable-precision specification in both languages. The mean formula is unchanged; only the precision formula is expanded from an intercept to the three `Study Time` indicators.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-variable-fit-r
#| lst-cap: "Fitting the variable-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_variable_model <- betareg(
  grade_beta ~ `Study Time` | `Study Time`, data = training_data,
  link = "logit", link.phi = "log", type = "ML", dist = "beta",
  control = betareg.control(method = "BFGS")
)
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-variable-fit-py
#| lst-cap: "Fitting the variable-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_variable_model = BetaModel.from_formula(
    'grade_beta ~ C(Q("Study Time"), Treatment(reference="<1 hour"))',
    data=training_data,
    exog_precision_formula=
        'C(Q("Study Time"), Treatment(reference="<1 hour"))',
    link=sm.families.links.Logit(), link_precision=sm.families.links.Log(),
).fit(method="bfgs", maxiter=1000, disp=False)
```

:::

In @lst-beta-variable-fit-r for `R`, the formula to the left of `|` remains the mean submodel, while the formula to the right now lets precision depend on `Study Time`. The `Python` fit in @lst-beta-variable-fit-py uses the same treatment-coded factor in `exog_precision_formula`. Thus, both implementations estimate the same eight-parameter model: **four coefficients for the conditional mean** and **four for the log precision**. We do not interpret the new precision coefficients substantively at this point. First, we ask whether the added precision flexibility produces a statistically meaningful improvement over the nested constant-precision model.

### Training-stage Likelihood-ratio Test {#sec-beta-refinement}

The constant- and variable-precision models differ only in the precision submodel:

- **Reduced model:** `Study Time` mean with constant precision;
- **Full model:** `Study Time` mean with `Study Time`-dependent precision.

The models are **nested** because the full model reduces exactly to the constant-precision model when

$$
\gamma_1=\gamma_2=\gamma_3=0.
$$

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-protocol-exchange-3947913/).](img/test.png){width="420"}

The likelihood-ratio test therefore evaluates

$$
\begin{gathered}
H_0\text{: }\gamma_1=\gamma_2=\gamma_3=0,\\
\text{versus}\\
H_1\text{: }\text{at least one of }\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\gamma_3\neq0.
\end{gathered}
$$

Under $H_0$, `Study Time` does not contribute to the precision submodel beyond the common precision intercept. Note that the mean regression terms and the precision intercept are **nuisance parameters for this test** and are estimated by maximum likelihood under both competing models.

::: {#Definition-nuisance-parameter .definition}
:::: {.definition-header}
Definition of nuisance parameter
::::
:::: {.definition-container}
A **nuisance parameter** is a model parameter that must be estimated to specify the likelihood function correctly, but is **not the parameter or set of parameters directly targeted by the hypothesis testing or inferential question**.

In the likelihood-ratio test considered here, the parameters of interest are the additional precision coefficients

$$
\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\gamma_3,
$$

because the test asks whether `Study Time` contributes to the precision submodel. The mean-submodel coefficients and the precision intercept $\gamma_0$ are nuisance parameters for this particular test. They are still estimated under both the reduced and full models so that the two maximized likelihoods are compared appropriately.
::::
:::

Let $\ell_R$ and $\ell_F$ denote the maximized training-data log-likelihoods under the reduced and full models, respectively. The observed likelihood-ratio statistic is

$$
G^2_{\phi}
=
2(\ell_F-\ell_R).
$$

Because the full model adds exactly three precision coefficients, under $H_0$ and the usual large-sample regularity conditions,

$$
G^2_{\phi}
\mathrel{\dot{\sim}}
\chi^2_3.
$$

The corresponding $p$-value is the upper-tail probability

$$
\Pr\left(\chi^2_3\geq G^2_{\phi,\mathrm{obs}}\right).
$$

Thus, a small $p$-value provides evidence that the common-precision restriction is too restrictive relative to this prespecified `Study Time`-dependent alternative. This is a **training-stage model-development test**, not the final inferential test concerning the conditional mean.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-precision-lrt-r
#| tbl-cap: "Training-stage likelihood-ratio test for study time-dependent precision."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_precision_reduced_loglik <- as.numeric(logLik(beta_constant_model))
beta_precision_full_loglik <- as.numeric(logLik(beta_variable_model))
beta_precision_lr_statistic <- 2 * (
  beta_precision_full_loglik - beta_precision_reduced_loglik)
beta_precision_lr_df <- attr(logLik(beta_variable_model), "df") -
  attr(logLik(beta_constant_model), "df")
beta_precision_lr_p_value <- pchisq(
  beta_precision_lr_statistic, df = beta_precision_lr_df, lower.tail = FALSE)
stopifnot(beta_precision_lr_df == 3L)

beta_precision_lrt <- tibble(
  `Reduced log-likelihood` = beta_precision_reduced_loglik,
  `Full log-likelihood` = beta_precision_full_loglik,
  `LR statistic` = beta_precision_lr_statistic,
  `Degrees of freedom` = beta_precision_lr_df,
  `p-value` = beta_precision_lr_p_value)

beta_precision_lrt |>
  mutate(across(1:3, ~ round(.x, 3)),
    `p-value` = formatC(`p-value`, format = "g", digits = 4)) |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_precision_reduced_loglik = beta_constant_model.llf
beta_precision_full_loglik = beta_variable_model.llf
beta_precision_lr_statistic = 2 * (
    beta_precision_full_loglik - beta_precision_reduced_loglik)
beta_precision_lr_df = int(
    beta_variable_model.params.size - beta_constant_model.params.size)
beta_precision_lr_p_value = stats.chi2.sf(
    beta_precision_lr_statistic, beta_precision_lr_df)
assert beta_precision_lr_df == 3

beta_precision_lrt = pd.DataFrame({
    "Reduced log-likelihood": [beta_precision_reduced_loglik],
    "Full log-likelihood": [beta_precision_full_loglik],
    "LR statistic": [beta_precision_lr_statistic],
    "Degrees of freedom": [beta_precision_lr_df],
    "p-value": [beta_precision_lr_p_value],
})
beta_precision_lrt_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_precision_lrt, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.4g}")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-precision-lrt-py
#| tbl-cap: "Training-stage likelihood-ratio test for study time-dependent precision."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_precision_lrt_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

For the canonical training split, the **likelihood-ratio statistic** is `r formatC(beta_precision_lr_statistic, format = "f", digits = 3)` with `r beta_precision_lr_df` degrees of freedom, giving a $p$-value of `r formatC(beta_precision_lr_p_value, format = "g", digits = 4)`. At the conventional $\alpha=0.05$ level, this result `r ifelse(beta_precision_lr_p_value < 0.05, "leads us to reject the constant-precision null hypothesis. The training data provide evidence that allowing precision to differ across the study time categories improves the fitted Beta distribution beyond the common-precision specification", "does not lead us to reject the constant-precision null hypothesis. The training data do not provide sufficient evidence that the study time-dependent precision specification improves upon the common-precision model")`.

The modelling consequence is correspondingly targeted. `r ifelse(beta_precision_lr_p_value < 0.05, "We retain the variable-precision model as the working specification and next reassess its numerical and distributional adequacy.", "We would not retain the additional precision terms solely on the basis of this comparison; the adequacy evidence would need to be reconsidered before proceeding.")` The test does not tell us that precision differences are causal, nor does it establish that this is the only possible precision structure. It asks whether the **specific three-parameter extension motivated by the preceding diagnostics** improves the training-data likelihood enough to reject the constant-precision restriction.

### Optional Mean-model Complexity Check {#sec-beta-mean-complexity-check}

The precision refinement addresses the inadequacy identified by the diagnostics, but it does not automatically justify making the **mean submodel** more complicated. Recall from @sec-beta-eda-secondary and @tbl-beta-eda-summary that the nine remaining candidate variables showed comparatively small descriptive mean-grade differences after the dominant `Study Time` pattern was removed. We now complete the pre-specified training-stage check anticipated there.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-tutor-helper-e-learning-3974185/).](img/tutor.png){width="500"}

The reduced model for this comparison is the variable-precision model just fitted:

$$
\text{mean}\sim\texttt{Study Time},
\qquad
\text{precision}\sim\texttt{Study Time}.
$$

The larger candidate keeps the **same precision submodel** but expands the mean to the complete 21-column candidate design basis defined in @tbl-beta-variable-dictionary. In other words, it adds the 18 non-`Study Time` mean coefficients associated with café location, year in school, hobbies, primary sport, living arrangement, part-time work hours, study-group participation, hours of sleep, and tutor status.

Using the coefficient indexing fixed earlier, the joint hypotheses are

$$
\begin{gathered}
H_0\text{: }\beta_4=\beta_5=\cdots=\beta_{21}=0,\\
\text{versus}\\
H_1\text{: }\text{at least one of }\beta_4,\ldots,\beta_{21}\neq0.
\end{gathered}
$$

The two models are nested because setting those 18 additional mean coefficients to zero recovers the focused `Study Time` mean model, while the precision structure remains identical. Consequently,

$$
G^2_{\mu}
=
2(\ell_{\mathrm{larger}}-\ell_{\mathrm{focused}})
\mathrel{\dot{\sim}}
\chi^2_{18}
$$

under $H_0$ and the usual large-sample likelihood-ratio regularity conditions. All retained mean and precision parameters are re-estimated in both models; the test concerns only the **joint contribution of the 18 additional mean coefficients**.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-mean-complexity-lrt-r
#| tbl-cap: "Training-stage likelihood-ratio check for additional mean-submodel complexity."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_mean_full_model <- betareg(
  grade_beta ~ `Study Time` + `Café Location` + `Year in School` + Hobbies +
    `Primary Sport` + `Living Arrangement` + `Part-time Work Hours` +
    `Study Group Participation` + `Hours of Sleep per Night` + `Has a Tutor` |
    `Study Time`,
  data = training_data, link = "logit", link.phi = "log",
  type = "ML", dist = "beta", control = betareg.control(method = "BFGS")
)

beta_mean_lr_statistic <- 2 * (
  as.numeric(logLik(beta_mean_full_model)) - as.numeric(logLik(beta_variable_model)))
beta_mean_lr_df <- attr(logLik(beta_mean_full_model), "df") -
  attr(logLik(beta_variable_model), "df")
beta_mean_lr_p_value <- pchisq(
  beta_mean_lr_statistic, df = beta_mean_lr_df, lower.tail = FALSE)
stopifnot(beta_mean_lr_df == 18L)

beta_mean_lrt <- tibble(
  `Focused log-likelihood` = as.numeric(logLik(beta_variable_model)),
  `Larger log-likelihood` = as.numeric(logLik(beta_mean_full_model)),
  `LR statistic` = beta_mean_lr_statistic,
  `Degrees of freedom` = beta_mean_lr_df,
  `p-value` = beta_mean_lr_p_value)

beta_mean_lrt |>
  mutate(across(1:3, ~ round(.x, 3)),
    `p-value` = formatC(`p-value`, format = "g", digits = 4)) |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_mean_full_model = BetaModel.from_formula(
    'grade_beta ~ C(Q("Study Time"), Treatment(reference="<1 hour")) + '
    'C(Q("Café Location"), Treatment(reference="AMS Nest")) + '
    'C(Q("Year in School"), Treatment(reference="1st Year")) + '
    'C(Hobbies, Treatment(reference="Gaming")) + '
    'C(Q("Primary Sport"), Treatment(reference="None")) + '
    'C(Q("Living Arrangement"), Treatment(reference="Alone")) + '
    'Q("Part-time Work Hours") + '
    'C(Q("Study Group Participation"), Treatment(reference="No")) + '
    'Q("Hours of Sleep per Night") + C(Q("Has a Tutor"), Treatment(reference="No"))',
    data=training_data,
    exog_precision_formula=
        'C(Q("Study Time"), Treatment(reference="<1 hour"))',
    link=sm.families.links.Logit(), link_precision=sm.families.links.Log(),
).fit(method="bfgs", maxiter=1000, disp=False)

beta_mean_lr_statistic = 2 * (
    beta_mean_full_model.llf - beta_variable_model.llf)
beta_mean_lr_df = int(
    beta_mean_full_model.params.size - beta_variable_model.params.size)
beta_mean_lr_p_value = stats.chi2.sf(beta_mean_lr_statistic, beta_mean_lr_df)
assert beta_mean_lr_df == 18

beta_mean_lrt = pd.DataFrame({
    "Focused log-likelihood": [beta_variable_model.llf],
    "Larger log-likelihood": [beta_mean_full_model.llf],
    "LR statistic": [beta_mean_lr_statistic],
    "Degrees of freedom": [beta_mean_lr_df],
    "p-value": [beta_mean_lr_p_value],
})
beta_mean_lrt_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_mean_lrt, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.4g}")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-mean-complexity-lrt-py
#| tbl-cap: "Training-stage likelihood-ratio check for additional mean-submodel complexity."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_mean_lrt_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

For the canonical training split, the larger mean model gives a **likelihood-ratio statistic** of `r formatC(beta_mean_lr_statistic, format = "f", digits = 0)` with `r beta_mean_lr_df` degrees of freedom and a $p$-value of `r formatC(beta_mean_lr_p_value, format = "g", digits = 4)`. At $\alpha=0.05$, this result `r ifelse(beta_mean_lr_p_value < 0.05, "provides evidence that the 18 additional mean coefficients improve the training-data likelihood jointly beyond the focused study time mean submodel", "does not provide strong evidence that the 18 additional mean coefficients improve the training-data likelihood jointly beyond the focused study time mean submodel")`. `r ifelse(beta_mean_lr_p_value < 0.05, "A statistically detectable likelihood improvement would not, by itself, justify automatically adopting all 18 additional coefficients; the larger specification would require its own adequacy and parsimony assessment.", "Accordingly, we do not retain the additional mean terms. The working mean submodel remains focused on study time, while the study time-dependent precision structure is carried forward.")`

This conclusion is deliberately narrow. Failing to reject the joint null would not establish that every secondary variable is unrelated to final grade, just as rejecting it would not identify which individual terms should be retained. The comparison asks whether the pre-specified block of secondary mean terms, **taken together**, provides enough additional training-data likelihood to justify expanding the focused mean structure. It is therefore a parsimony check, not an automated variable-selection procedure.

## Goodness of Fit and Model Adequacy for the Variable-precision Model {#sec-beta-extended-gof}

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-teacher-acrobatics-3974168/).](img/sequence.png){width="700"}

The training-stage likelihood-ratio test in @sec-beta-refinement supported allowing precision to vary by `Study Time`, while the optional complexity check in @sec-beta-mean-complexity-check did **not** support expanding the mean submodel beyond `Study Time`. Thus, our working model is the focused specification

$$
\text{mean}\sim\texttt{Study Time},
\qquad
\text{precision}\sim\texttt{Study Time}.
$$

Before freezing that specification, we repeat the same diagnostic layers used for the constant-precision model. This is important because a better likelihood does not, by itself, establish practical adequacy. We again check numerical stability, conditional means, quantile residuals, the fitted precision structure, and sensitivity to unusual observations using the **training data only**.

### Convergence and Numerical Stability {#sec-beta-extended-stability}

We first verify that the variable-precision fit is computationally usable. Adding a precision submodel introduces three additional parameters, so convergence and finite model-based standard errors should be checked again rather than inherited from the simpler fit.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-extended-stability-r
#| tbl-cap: "Numerical-stability checks for the variable-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_variable_parameters <- coef(beta_variable_model)
beta_variable_standard_errors <- sqrt(diag(vcov(beta_variable_model)))
beta_variable_converged <- isTRUE(beta_variable_model$converged)
beta_variable_parameters_finite <- all(is.finite(beta_variable_parameters))
beta_variable_se_finite <- all(is.finite(beta_variable_standard_errors))

beta_variable_fitted_mean <- predict(beta_variable_model, type = "response")
beta_variable_fitted_precision <- predict(beta_variable_model, type = "precision")
beta_variable_fitted_grade <- beta_grade_scale_factor * beta_variable_fitted_mean +
  beta_grade_scale_offset

stopifnot(beta_variable_converged, beta_variable_parameters_finite,
  beta_variable_se_finite,
  all(beta_variable_fitted_mean > 0 & beta_variable_fitted_mean < 1),
  all(beta_variable_fitted_precision > 0))

beta_variable_stability <- tibble(
  Check = c("Optimizer converged", "All coefficient estimates finite",
    "All model-based SEs finite", "Minimum fitted conditional mean (%)",
    "Maximum fitted conditional mean (%)", "Minimum fitted precision",
    "Maximum fitted precision"),
  Result = c("Yes", "Yes", "Yes",
    formatC(min(beta_variable_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2),
    formatC(max(beta_variable_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2),
    formatC(min(beta_variable_fitted_precision), format = "f", digits = 3),
    formatC(max(beta_variable_fitted_precision), format = "f", digits = 3)))

beta_variable_stability |>
  kable(align = c("c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_variable_parameters = np.asarray(beta_variable_model.params)
beta_variable_standard_errors = np.asarray(beta_variable_model.bse)
beta_variable_converged = bool(beta_variable_model.mle_retvals["converged"])
beta_variable_parameters_finite = np.isfinite(beta_variable_parameters).all()
beta_variable_se_finite = np.isfinite(beta_variable_standard_errors).all()

beta_variable_fitted_mean = beta_variable_model.model.predict(
    beta_variable_model.params, which="mean")
beta_variable_fitted_precision = beta_variable_model.model.predict(
    beta_variable_model.params, which="precision")
beta_variable_fitted_grade = (
    beta_grade_scale_factor * beta_variable_fitted_mean + beta_grade_scale_offset)

assert beta_variable_converged
assert beta_variable_parameters_finite and beta_variable_se_finite
assert ((beta_variable_fitted_mean > 0) & (beta_variable_fitted_mean < 1)).all()
assert (beta_variable_fitted_precision > 0).all()

beta_variable_stability = pd.DataFrame({
    "Check": [
        "Optimizer converged", "All coefficient estimates finite",
        "All model-based SEs finite", "Minimum fitted conditional mean (%)",
        "Maximum fitted conditional mean (%)", "Minimum fitted precision",
        "Maximum fitted precision",
    ],
    "Result": [
        "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", f"{beta_variable_fitted_grade.min():.2f}",
        f"{beta_variable_fitted_grade.max():.2f}",
        f"{beta_variable_fitted_precision.min():.3f}",
        f"{beta_variable_fitted_precision.max():.3f}",
    ],
})
beta_variable_stability_html = scrollable_table_html(beta_variable_stability)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-extended-stability-py
#| tbl-cap: "Numerical-stability checks for the variable-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_variable_stability_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

The stability checks pass in both implementations. The **fitted conditional means** range from `r formatC(min(beta_variable_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2)`% to `r formatC(max(beta_variable_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2)`%, while the **fitted precisions remain positive throughout**. Hence, the additional precision flexibility has not produced an obvious numerical failure. Hence, we can now assess whether it resolves the distributional problem identified under constant precision.

### Observed Versus Fitted Conditional Means {#sec-beta-extended-observed-fitted}

The mean submodel still contains only `Study Time`, but its parameter estimates are re-estimated jointly with the new precision parameters. That said, we recompute the observed-versus-fitted mean comparison rather than assuming that it is unchanged.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-extended-mean-calibration-r
#| tbl-cap: "Observed and fitted conditional mean grades under the variable-precision model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_variable_mean_calibration <- training_data |>
  mutate(`Fitted mean grade (%)` = beta_variable_fitted_grade) |>
  group_by(`Study Time`) |>
  summarise(`Observed mean grade (%)` = mean(`Final Grade (%)`),
    `Fitted mean grade (%)` = mean(`Fitted mean grade (%)`),
    `Observed - fitted (percentage points)` =
      `Observed mean grade (%)` - `Fitted mean grade (%)`, .groups = "drop")

beta_variable_mean_max_gap <- max(abs(
  beta_variable_mean_calibration[["Observed - fitted (percentage points)"]]))

beta_variable_mean_calibration |>
  kable(digits = 2, align = c("c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_variable_mean_calibration = training_data[[
    "Study Time", "Final Grade (%)"]].copy()
beta_variable_mean_calibration["Fitted mean grade (%)"] = beta_variable_fitted_grade
beta_variable_mean_calibration = (
    beta_variable_mean_calibration.groupby("Study Time", observed=True)
    .agg(**{
        "Observed mean grade (%)": ("Final Grade (%)", "mean"),
        "Fitted mean grade (%)": ("Fitted mean grade (%)", "mean"),
    }).reset_index())
beta_variable_mean_calibration["Observed - fitted (percentage points)"] = (
    beta_variable_mean_calibration["Observed mean grade (%)"]
    - beta_variable_mean_calibration["Fitted mean grade (%)"])
beta_variable_mean_max_gap = np.abs(beta_variable_mean_calibration[
    "Observed - fitted (percentage points)"]).max()

beta_variable_mean_calibration_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_variable_mean_calibration, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.2f}")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-extended-mean-calibration-py
#| tbl-cap: "Observed and fitted conditional mean grades under the variable-precision model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_variable_mean_calibration_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

As shown in @tbl-beta-extended-mean-calibration-r, the mean fit remains strong. The **largest absolute observed-versus-fitted group-mean difference** is `r formatC(beta_variable_mean_max_gap, format = "f", digits = 2)` percentage points, compared with `r formatC(beta_constant_mean_max_gap, format = "f", digits = 2)` percentage points under constant precision. Thus, allowing precision to vary has not required abandoning the focused `Study Time` mean structure. This is also consistent with the parsimony check in @sec-beta-mean-complexity-check, which did not support retaining the additional 18 mean coefficients.

### Quantile Residual Diagnostics {#sec-beta-extended-residuals}

<br>

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-social-network-3704049/).](img/paint.png){width="525"}

Now, we recompute the quantile residuals using the same definition introduced in @sec-beta-simple-residuals, but with the fitted observation-specific precision $\widehat{\phi}_i$:

$$
r_i^{(q)}
=
\Phi^{-1}\left[
F_{\operatorname{Beta}}\left(
y_i;\,
\widehat{\mu}_i\widehat{\phi}_i,\,
(1-\widehat{\mu}_i)\widehat{\phi}_i
\right)
\right].
$$

The standard-Normal reference remains a graphical diagnostic rather than a standalone goodness-of-fit test [@dunn1996; @pereira2019].

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-extended-residual-summary-r
#| tbl-cap: "Quantile-residual summaries by study time category for the variable-precision model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_variable_alpha <- beta_variable_fitted_mean * beta_variable_fitted_precision
beta_variable_beta <- (1 - beta_variable_fitted_mean) *
  beta_variable_fitted_precision
beta_variable_cdf <- pbeta(training_data$grade_beta, beta_variable_alpha,
  beta_variable_beta)
beta_variable_cdf <- pmin(pmax(beta_variable_cdf, .Machine$double.eps),
  1 - .Machine$double.eps)
beta_variable_quantile_residuals <- qnorm(beta_variable_cdf)

beta_variable_residual_data <- training_data |>
  transmute(`Study Time`, `Final Grade (%)`, grade_beta,
    fitted_mean_beta = beta_variable_fitted_mean,
    fitted_precision = beta_variable_fitted_precision,
    `Fitted mean grade (%)` = beta_variable_fitted_grade,
    quantile_residual = beta_variable_quantile_residuals)

beta_variable_residual_summary <- beta_variable_residual_data |>
  group_by(`Study Time`) |>
  summarise(Students = n(), `Mean residual` = mean(quantile_residual),
    `Residual SD` = sd(quantile_residual), `Residual IQR` = IQR(quantile_residual),
    `|Residual| > 2` = sum(abs(quantile_residual) > 2), .groups = "drop")

beta_variable_residual_sd_min <- min(beta_variable_residual_summary$`Residual SD`)
beta_variable_residual_sd_max <- max(beta_variable_residual_summary$`Residual SD`)
beta_variable_residual_sd_ratio <- beta_variable_residual_sd_max /
  beta_variable_residual_sd_min

beta_variable_residual_summary |>
  kable(digits = 3, align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_variable_alpha = beta_variable_fitted_mean * beta_variable_fitted_precision
beta_variable_beta = (
    (1 - beta_variable_fitted_mean) * beta_variable_fitted_precision)
beta_variable_cdf = stats.beta.cdf(
    training_data["grade_beta"], beta_variable_alpha, beta_variable_beta)
beta_variable_cdf = np.clip(
    beta_variable_cdf, np.finfo(float).eps, 1 - np.finfo(float).eps)
beta_variable_quantile_residuals = stats.norm.ppf(beta_variable_cdf)

beta_variable_residual_data = training_data[[
    "Study Time", "Final Grade (%)", "grade_beta"]].copy()
beta_variable_residual_data["fitted_mean_beta"] = beta_variable_fitted_mean
beta_variable_residual_data["fitted_precision"] = beta_variable_fitted_precision
beta_variable_residual_data["Fitted mean grade (%)"] = beta_variable_fitted_grade
beta_variable_residual_data["quantile_residual"] = beta_variable_quantile_residuals

beta_variable_residual_summary = (
    beta_variable_residual_data.groupby("Study Time", observed=True)
    .agg(Students=("quantile_residual", "size"), **{
        "Mean residual": ("quantile_residual", "mean"),
        "Residual SD": ("quantile_residual", "std"),
        "Residual IQR": ("quantile_residual",
            lambda x: x.quantile(0.75) - x.quantile(0.25)),
        "|Residual| > 2": ("quantile_residual",
            lambda x: (np.abs(x) > 2).sum()),
    }).reset_index())
beta_variable_residual_sd_min = beta_variable_residual_summary[
    "Residual SD"].min()
beta_variable_residual_sd_max = beta_variable_residual_summary[
    "Residual SD"].max()
beta_variable_residual_sd_ratio = (
    beta_variable_residual_sd_max / beta_variable_residual_sd_min)

beta_variable_residual_summary_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_variable_residual_summary, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.3f}")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-extended-residual-summary-py
#| tbl-cap: "Quantile-residual summaries by study time category for the variable-precision model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_variable_residual_summary_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

According to @tbl-beta-extended-residual-summary-r, the improvement in **residual spread across groups** is substantial. Under the constant-precision model, see @tbl-beta-simple-residual-summary-r, the **largest group-specific residual SD** was `r formatC(beta_constant_residual_sd_ratio, format = "f", digits = 2)` times the smallest. After allowing precision to vary with `Study Time`, that ratio falls to only `r formatC(beta_variable_residual_sd_ratio, format = "f", digits = 2)`. More specifically, the **residual SDs** are now `r formatC(beta_variable_residual_summary[["Residual SD"]][1], format = "f", digits = 3)` for `<1 hour`, `r formatC(beta_variable_residual_summary[["Residual SD"]][2], format = "f", digits = 3)` for `1–3 hours`, `r formatC(beta_variable_residual_summary[["Residual SD"]][3], format = "f", digits = 3)` for `3–5 hours`, and `r formatC(beta_variable_residual_summary[["Residual SD"]][4], format = "f", digits = 3)` for `5+ hours`. In the training split, these are essentially all equal to $1$, ranging only from `r formatC(beta_variable_residual_sd_min, format = "f", digits = 3)` to `r formatC(beta_variable_residual_sd_max, format = "f", digits = 3)`.

The residual means are also close to zero in every category, so there is little evidence of systematic location bias within any study-time group. Therefore, these results contrast sharply with the increasing residual dispersion seen under constant precision. The added precision submodel has addressed the main across-group distributional mismatch identified in @sec-beta-simple-residuals: the fitted conditional distributions now produce quantile residuals with **approximately comparable scale across all four fitted mean levels**.

The residual-versus-fitted plot provides the corresponding visual check.

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{r}
beta_variable_residual_y_limits <- c(

beta_variable_residual_y_breaks <- seq(
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-beta-extended-residuals-fitted-py
#| fig-cap: "Quantile residuals versus fitted conditional mean grades for the variable-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

beta_variable_residual_y_limits = (
    np.floor(beta_variable_quantile_residuals.min()),
    np.ceil(beta_variable_quantile_residuals.max()))
beta_variable_residual_y_breaks = np.arange(
    2 * np.ceil(beta_variable_residual_y_limits[0] / 2),
    2 * np.floor(beta_variable_residual_y_limits[1] / 2) + 1, 2)
beta_variable_residual_fitted_x_limits = (
    5 * np.floor((beta_variable_fitted_grade.min() - 0.5) / 5),
    5 * np.ceil((beta_variable_fitted_grade.max() + 0.5) / 5))
beta_variable_residual_fitted_x_breaks = np.arange(
    beta_variable_residual_fitted_x_limits[0],
    beta_variable_residual_fitted_x_limits[1] + 1, 5)

beta_variable_residual_plot_rng = np.random.default_rng(551)
beta_variable_residual_plot_x = beta_variable_fitted_grade + (
    beta_variable_residual_plot_rng.uniform(
        -0.25, 0.25, len(beta_variable_fitted_grade)))
beta_variable_residual_fitted_plot, beta_variable_residual_fitted_axis = (
    plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 8)))
_ = beta_variable_residual_fitted_axis.scatter(
    beta_variable_residual_plot_x, beta_variable_quantile_residuals,
    alpha=0.45, color="#0072B2")
_ = beta_variable_residual_fitted_axis.axhline(0, linewidth=0.8, color="black")
for reference in (-2, 2):
    _ = beta_variable_residual_fitted_axis.axhline(
        reference, linestyle="--", linewidth=0.7, color="black")
_ = beta_variable_residual_fitted_axis.set_xlim(
    beta_variable_residual_fitted_x_limits)
_ = beta_variable_residual_fitted_axis.set_xticks(
    beta_variable_residual_fitted_x_breaks)
_ = beta_variable_residual_fitted_axis.set_ylim(beta_variable_residual_y_limits)
_ = beta_variable_residual_fitted_axis.set_yticks(beta_variable_residual_y_breaks)
_ = beta_variable_residual_fitted_axis.set_xlabel(
    "\n Fitted conditional mean grade (%)", fontsize=20)
_ = beta_variable_residual_fitted_axis.set_ylabel(
    "Quantile residual\n", fontsize=20)
beta_variable_residual_fitted_axis.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=15.5)
beta_variable_residual_fitted_plot.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

As before, the horizontal axis contains four fitted mean locations because `Study Time` is the only regressor retained in the mean submodel. The important change is in the **vertical spread of the residual clouds**. Under the constant-precision model in @fig-beta-simple-residuals-fitted-r, the two higher-study-time groups show visibly greater dispersion than the first two groups, including several large positive residuals. This produces the systematic increase in residual spread already quantified in @tbl-beta-simple-residual-summary-r.

That pattern is largely removed in @fig-beta-extended-residuals-fitted-r. The main residual clouds at all four fitted mean locations are now centred close to zero and have very similar vertical spread, consistent with the group-specific residual SDs being approximately $1$ throughout. Some isolated upper-tail observations remain—most visibly in the `3–5 hours` and `5+ hours` groups, but they no longer form part of a broader pattern in which residual dispersion increases with the fitted conditional mean. Thus, the variable-precision model has addressed the **systematic across-group dispersion mismatch** that motivated the refinement, while leaving a small number of individual tail departures for the Q-Q and influence diagnostics to examine separately.

A Normal Q-Q plot gives a complementary assessment of the overall residual distribution.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}

#| warning: false
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

beta_variable_qq_probabilities <- (
  seq_along(beta_variable_quantile_residuals) - 0.5
) / length(beta_variable_quantile_residuals)
beta_variable_qq_data <- tibble(
  theoretical = qnorm(beta_variable_qq_probabilities),
  observed = sort(beta_variable_quantile_residuals))
beta_variable_qq_x_limits <- c(
  floor(min(beta_variable_qq_data$theoretical)),
  ceiling(max(beta_variable_qq_data$theoretical)))
beta_variable_qq_x_breaks <- seq(
  2 * ceiling(beta_variable_qq_x_limits[1] / 2),
  2 * floor(beta_variable_qq_x_limits[2] / 2), by = 2)
beta_variable_qq_y_limits <- c(
  floor(min(beta_variable_quantile_residuals)),
  ceiling(max(beta_variable_quantile_residuals)))

  2 * ceiling(beta_variable_qq_y_limits[1] / 2),
  2 * floor(beta_variable_qq_y_limits[2] / 2), by = 2)
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-beta-extended-residuals-qq-py

#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

beta_variable_qq_probabilities = (
    np.arange(1, len(beta_variable_quantile_residuals) + 1) - 0.5
) / len(beta_variable_quantile_residuals)
beta_variable_qq_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "theoretical": stats.norm.ppf(beta_variable_qq_probabilities),
    "observed": np.sort(beta_variable_quantile_residuals),
})
beta_variable_qq_x_limits = (
    np.floor(beta_variable_qq_data["theoretical"].min()),
    np.ceil(beta_variable_qq_data["theoretical"].max()))
beta_variable_qq_x_breaks = np.arange(
    2 * np.ceil(beta_variable_qq_x_limits[0] / 2),
    2 * np.floor(beta_variable_qq_x_limits[1] / 2) + 1, 2)
beta_variable_qq_y_limits = (
    np.floor(beta_variable_quantile_residuals.min()),
    np.ceil(beta_variable_quantile_residuals.max()))
beta_variable_qq_y_breaks = np.arange(
    2 * np.ceil(beta_variable_qq_y_limits[0] / 2),
    2 * np.floor(beta_variable_qq_y_limits[1] / 2) + 1, 2)

beta_variable_residual_qq_plot, beta_variable_residual_qq_axis = (
    plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 8)))
_ = beta_variable_residual_qq_axis.scatter(
    beta_variable_qq_data["theoretical"], beta_variable_qq_data["observed"],
    alpha=0.55, color="#0072B2")
_ = beta_variable_residual_qq_axis.plot(
    beta_variable_qq_x_limits, beta_variable_qq_x_limits,
    linestyle="--", color="black")
_ = beta_variable_residual_qq_axis.set_xlim(beta_variable_qq_x_limits)
_ = beta_variable_residual_qq_axis.set_xticks(beta_variable_qq_x_breaks)
_ = beta_variable_residual_qq_axis.set_ylim(beta_variable_qq_y_limits)
_ = beta_variable_residual_qq_axis.set_yticks(beta_variable_qq_y_breaks)
_ = beta_variable_residual_qq_axis.set_xlabel(
    "\n Theoretical standard-Normal quantiles", fontsize=20)
_ = beta_variable_residual_qq_axis.set_ylabel(
    "Observed quantile residuals\n", fontsize=20)
beta_variable_residual_qq_axis.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=15.5)
beta_variable_residual_qq_plot.tight_layout()

```

:::

The Normal Q-Q plot in @fig-beta-extended-residuals-qq-r shows a clear improvement over the constant-precision diagnostic in @fig-beta-simple-residuals-qq-r. Across most of the central range, the quantile residuals now follow the standard-Normal reference line closely. The lower tail also tracks the reference more closely than under constant precision, where a more systematic departure was visible.

The most important remaining discrepancy is in the **upper tail**. Several positive residuals still rise above the reference line, including one particularly large observation, so the variable-precision model has not eliminated all tail departures. However, the pronounced upper-tail distortion under the constant-precision model has been substantially reduced: the remaining departures are more localized rather than accompanying the broader across-group dispersion pattern seen previously.

This distinction is critical for the adequacy assessment. Together with the nearly equal group-specific residual SDs and the much more comparable residual clouds in @fig-beta-extended-residuals-fitted-r, the Q-Q plot indicates that modelling precision by `Study Time` has corrected the **main systematic distributional inadequacy** of the initial model. The remaining upper-tail observations should therefore be examined as localized departures in the subsequent influence analysis rather than interpreted, by themselves, as evidence that the revised specification is globally inadequate.

As before, the Q-Q plot is a diagnostic rather than a formal acceptance test. We use it together with the groupwise residual summaries, residual-versus-fitted plot, precision diagnostic, and influence screen to judge whether any remaining departure is sufficiently systematic to justify further model refinement.

### Precision-structure Check {#sec-beta-extended-precision}

The variable-precision model now estimates a separate fitted precision for each `Study Time` category. Recall that, holding $\mu_i$ fixed, a **larger $\phi_i$ means a more concentrated conditional Beta distribution**, whereas a **smaller $\phi_i$ means a broader conditional distribution**. Because both $\mu_i$ and $\phi_i$ enter the Beta variance function, the fitted precision values should be interpreted together with the corresponding fitted means rather than in isolation.

We compare the fitted category-specific precisions with the variance-matching diagnostic introduced in @sec-beta-simple-precision and, on the original grade scale, compare the observed group SDs with the SDs implied by the variable-precision model.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-extended-precision-r
#| tbl-cap: "Observed and model-implied dispersion under study time-dependent precision."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_variable_precision_diagnostic <- beta_variable_residual_data |>
  group_by(`Study Time`) |>
  summarise(observed_sd_grade = sd(`Final Grade (%)`),
    observed_variance_beta = var(grade_beta),
    fitted_mean_beta = first(fitted_mean_beta),
    fitted_precision = first(fitted_precision), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(model_sd_grade = beta_grade_scale_factor * sqrt(
      fitted_mean_beta * (1 - fitted_mean_beta) / (1 + fitted_precision)),
    sd_ratio = observed_sd_grade / model_sd_grade,
    variance_matching_phi = fitted_mean_beta * (1 - fitted_mean_beta) /
      observed_variance_beta - 1)

beta_variable_sd_ratio_min <- min(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$sd_ratio)
beta_variable_sd_ratio_max <- max(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$sd_ratio)

beta_variable_precision_diagnostic |>
  transmute(`Study Time`, `Fitted precision` = fitted_precision,
    `Variance-matching precision` = variance_matching_phi,
    `Observed SD (percentage points)` = observed_sd_grade,
    `Model-implied SD (percentage points)` = model_sd_grade,
    `Observed / implied SD` = sd_ratio) |>
  kable(digits = 2, align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_variable_precision_diagnostic = (
    beta_variable_residual_data.groupby("Study Time", observed=True)
    .agg(observed_sd_grade=("Final Grade (%)", "std"),
        observed_variance_beta=("grade_beta", "var"),
        fitted_mean_beta=("fitted_mean_beta", "first"),
        fitted_precision=("fitted_precision", "first")).reset_index())
beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["model_sd_grade"] = beta_grade_scale_factor * np.sqrt(
    beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["fitted_mean_beta"]
    * (1 - beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["fitted_mean_beta"])
    / (1 + beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["fitted_precision"]))
beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["sd_ratio"] = (
    beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["observed_sd_grade"]
    / beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["model_sd_grade"])
beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["variance_matching_phi"] = (
    beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["fitted_mean_beta"]
    * (1 - beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["fitted_mean_beta"])
    / beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["observed_variance_beta"] - 1)

beta_variable_sd_ratio_min = beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["sd_ratio"].min()
beta_variable_sd_ratio_max = beta_variable_precision_diagnostic["sd_ratio"].max()

beta_variable_precision_display = beta_variable_precision_diagnostic[[
    "Study Time", "fitted_precision", "variance_matching_phi",
    "observed_sd_grade", "model_sd_grade", "sd_ratio"]].rename(columns={
        "fitted_precision": "Fitted precision",
        "variance_matching_phi": "Variance-matching precision",
        "observed_sd_grade": "Observed SD (percentage points)",
        "model_sd_grade": "Model-implied SD (percentage points)",
        "sd_ratio": "Observed / implied SD"})
beta_variable_precision_diagnostic_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_variable_precision_display, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.2f}")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-extended-precision-py
#| tbl-cap: "Observed and model-implied dispersion under study time-dependent precision."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_variable_precision_diagnostic_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

The **fitted precision values** now vary substantially across `Study Time` in @tbl-beta-extended-precision-r for the study time-dependent precision model, decreasing from `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$fitted_precision[1], format = "f", digits = 2)` for `<1 hour` to `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$fitted_precision[4], format = "f", digits = 2)` for `5+ hours`. This decline counteracts the reduction in $\widehat{\mu}_g(1-\widehat{\mu}_g)$ as the fitted conditional mean approaches the upper boundary, allowing the model to maintain considerably more conditional spread than the constant-precision specification could.

The response-scale comparison shows that this adjustment is not identical across all four categories. For `<1 hour` and `1–3 hours`, the fitted precisions are very close to their variance-matching counterparts, and the **observed-to-implied SD ratios** are both approximately `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$sd_ratio[1], format = "f", digits = 2)`. For `3–5 hours` and `5+ hours`, however, the fitted precisions are lower than the corresponding variance-matching values, producing somewhat broader fitted distributions: the observed-to-implied SD ratios fall to `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$sd_ratio[3], format = "f", digits = 2)` and `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$sd_ratio[4], format = "f", digits = 2)`, respectively. In the training split, this means that the model-implied SDs exceed the observed SDs in the two highest-study-time groups.

This remaining discrepancy should not be interpreted as a failure to reproduce the variance-matching quantities exactly. Those quantities are descriptive moment-based diagnostics, whereas the fitted precisions are maximum-likelihood estimates chosen to represent the **entire conditional Beta distribution**. The more important result is that allowing precision to vary has moved the model in the required direction and, as shown by the nearly unit quantile-residual SDs in @tbl-beta-extended-residual-summary-r, has substantially removed the systematic across-group dispersion pattern that was present under constant precision.

The same comparison is shown graphically below.

::: {.panel-tabset}

```{r}
  transmute(`Study Time`, Observed = observed_sd_grade,
```

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-beta-extended-precision-py
#| fig-cap: "Observed and model-implied within-group grade standard deviations under the variable-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.height: 8
#| fig.width: 14

beta_variable_precision_plot_y_max = np.ceil(max(

beta_variable_precision_plot_x = np.arange(len(study_time_levels))

_ = beta_variable_precision_axis.bar(
```

:::

@fig-beta-extended-precision-r (or @fig-beta-extended-precision-py) makes the effect of the variable-precision specification more concrete. For `<1 hour`, the **observed** and **model-implied within-group SDs** are `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$observed_sd_grade[1], format = "f", digits = 2)` and `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$model_sd_grade[1], format = "f", digits = 2)` percentage points, respectively; for `1–3 hours`, they are `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$observed_sd_grade[2], format = "f", digits = 2)` and `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$model_sd_grade[2], format = "f", digits = 2)`. Thus, the paired bars for the **first two study-time categories** nearly coincide. The agreement is less exact for the **two higher-study-time categories**. For `3–5 hours`, the model-implied SD is `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$model_sd_grade[3], format = "f", digits = 2)` percentage points compared with an observed SD of `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$observed_sd_grade[3], format = "f", digits = 2)`; for `5+ hours`, the corresponding values are `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$model_sd_grade[4], format = "f", digits = 2)` and `r formatC(beta_variable_precision_diagnostic$observed_sd_grade[4], format = "f", digits = 2)`. The fitted conditional distributions are therefore somewhat broader than the raw within-group spread in these two categories. Nevertheless, this adjustment is in the direction required to correct the much stronger under-dispersion imposed by the constant-precision model (see @fig-beta-simple-precision-diagnostic-r), and it is consistent with the nearly unit quantile-residual SDs obtained after the refinement.

The fitted precision values themselves should not be interpreted as targets that must reproduce each raw group SD exactly. They are maximum-likelihood estimates chosen jointly with the mean parameters to represent the **entire conditional Beta distribution**. Holding the fitted mean fixed, a larger $\phi_g$ corresponds to a more concentrated conditional distribution and a smaller $\phi_g$ to a broader one. In the present model, the substantial decline in fitted precision across the study-time categories supplies the additional dispersion needed near the upper response boundary. These differences are features of the fitted conditional distribution; they should not be interpreted as evidence that study time causally changes the variability of student performance.

### Influence and Leverage {#sec-beta-extended-influence}

We finish the adequacy screen by repeating the targeted case-deletion analysis for the revised model. Because `Study Time` supplies the same four-category design basis to both the mean and precision submodels, the ordinary design leverage remains simple. The more informative question is whether one of the largest quantile-residual cases materially changes either the four fitted means or the four fitted category-specific precisions.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-reflection-mirror-image-3947915/).](img/mirror.png){width="275"}

As before, this is a **sensitivity screen**, not a hypothesis test or an automatic deletion rule.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-extended-influence-r
#| tbl-cap: "Targeted case-deletion sensitivity screen for the variable-precision model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_variable_mean_design <- model.matrix(~ `Study Time`, data = training_data)
beta_variable_design_leverage <- rowSums(
  (beta_variable_mean_design %*% solve(crossprod(beta_variable_mean_design))) *
    beta_variable_mean_design)
beta_variable_screen_positions <- head(
  order(abs(beta_variable_quantile_residuals), decreasing = TRUE), 5)

beta_variable_reference <- beta_variable_residual_data |>
  group_by(`Study Time`) |>
  summarise(fitted_mean = first(fitted_mean_beta),
    fitted_precision = first(fitted_precision), .groups = "drop")

beta_variable_influence_screen <- bind_rows(lapply(
  beta_variable_screen_positions, function(position) {
    beta_variable_reduced_data <- training_data[-position, , drop = FALSE]
    beta_variable_reduced_model <- update(
      beta_variable_model, data = beta_variable_reduced_data)
    beta_variable_reduced_mean <- predict(
      beta_variable_reduced_model, type = "response")
    beta_variable_reduced_precision <- predict(
      beta_variable_reduced_model, type = "precision")
    beta_variable_reduced_reference <- beta_variable_reduced_data |>
      mutate(fitted_mean = beta_variable_reduced_mean,
        fitted_precision = beta_variable_reduced_precision) |>
      group_by(`Study Time`) |>
      summarise(fitted_mean = first(fitted_mean),
        fitted_precision = first(fitted_precision), .groups = "drop")

    tibble(`Training row` = position,
      `Study Time` = as.character(training_data$`Study Time`[position]),
      `Final grade (%)` = training_data$`Final Grade (%)`[position],
      `|Quantile residual|` = abs(beta_variable_quantile_residuals[position]),
      `Design leverage` = beta_variable_design_leverage[position],
      `Max fitted-mean change (percentage points)` = beta_grade_scale_factor *
        max(abs(beta_variable_reduced_reference$fitted_mean -
          beta_variable_reference$fitted_mean)),
      `Max absolute relative precision change (%)` = 100 * max(abs(
        beta_variable_reduced_reference$fitted_precision /
          beta_variable_reference$fitted_precision - 1)))
  }))

beta_variable_max_design_leverage <- max(beta_variable_design_leverage)
beta_variable_max_mean_sensitivity <- max(
  beta_variable_influence_screen[["Max fitted-mean change (percentage points)"]])
beta_variable_max_phi_sensitivity <- max(
  beta_variable_influence_screen[["Max absolute relative precision change (%)"]])

beta_variable_influence_screen |>
  kable(digits = 3, align = c("c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_variable_mean_design = beta_variable_model.model.exog
beta_variable_design_leverage = np.einsum(
    "ij,jk,ik->i", beta_variable_mean_design,
    np.linalg.inv(beta_variable_mean_design.T @ beta_variable_mean_design),
    beta_variable_mean_design)
beta_variable_screen_positions = np.argsort(
    np.abs(beta_variable_quantile_residuals))[-5:][::-1]

beta_variable_reference = beta_variable_residual_data.groupby(
    "Study Time", observed=True).agg(
        fitted_mean=("fitted_mean_beta", "first"),
        fitted_precision=("fitted_precision", "first")).reindex(study_time_levels)

beta_variable_influence_rows = []
for position in beta_variable_screen_positions:
    beta_variable_reduced_data = training_data.drop(training_data.index[position])
    beta_variable_reduced_model = BetaModel.from_formula(
        'grade_beta ~ C(Q("Study Time"), Treatment(reference="<1 hour"))',
        data=beta_variable_reduced_data,
        exog_precision_formula=
            'C(Q("Study Time"), Treatment(reference="<1 hour"))',
        link=sm.families.links.Logit(), link_precision=sm.families.links.Log(),
    ).fit(method="bfgs", maxiter=1000, disp=False)
    beta_variable_reduced_mean = beta_variable_reduced_model.model.predict(
        beta_variable_reduced_model.params, which="mean")
    beta_variable_reduced_precision = beta_variable_reduced_model.model.predict(
        beta_variable_reduced_model.params, which="precision")
    beta_variable_reduced_reference = beta_variable_reduced_data[
        ["Study Time"]].copy()
    beta_variable_reduced_reference["fitted_mean"] = beta_variable_reduced_mean
    beta_variable_reduced_reference["fitted_precision"] = (
        beta_variable_reduced_precision)
    beta_variable_reduced_reference = beta_variable_reduced_reference.groupby(
        "Study Time", observed=True).agg(
            fitted_mean=("fitted_mean", "first"),
            fitted_precision=("fitted_precision", "first")).reindex(study_time_levels)

    beta_variable_influence_rows.append({
        "Training row": int(position + 1),
        "Study Time": str(training_data.iloc[position]["Study Time"]),
        "Final grade (%)": training_data.iloc[position]["Final Grade (%)"],
        "|Quantile residual|": abs(beta_variable_quantile_residuals[position]),
        "Design leverage": beta_variable_design_leverage[position],
        "Max fitted-mean change (percentage points)": beta_grade_scale_factor *
            np.max(np.abs(beta_variable_reduced_reference["fitted_mean"]
                - beta_variable_reference["fitted_mean"])),
        "Max absolute relative precision change (%)": 100 * np.max(np.abs(
            beta_variable_reduced_reference["fitted_precision"]
            / beta_variable_reference["fitted_precision"] - 1)),
    })

beta_variable_influence_screen = pd.DataFrame(beta_variable_influence_rows)
beta_variable_max_design_leverage = beta_variable_design_leverage.max()
beta_variable_max_mean_sensitivity = beta_variable_influence_screen[
    "Max fitted-mean change (percentage points)"].max()
beta_variable_max_phi_sensitivity = beta_variable_influence_screen[
    "Max absolute relative precision change (%)"].max()
beta_variable_influence_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_variable_influence_screen, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.3f}")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-extended-influence-py
#| tbl-cap: "Targeted case-deletion sensitivity screen for the variable-precision model."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_variable_influence_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

The **ordinary mean-design leverage** remains **uniformly low**. Its **largest value** is only `r formatC(beta_variable_max_design_leverage, format = "f", digits = 4)`, which is expected because the retained model uses the same four well-represented `Study Time` categories in both submodels. Hence, in @tbl-beta-extended-influence-r, none of the five screened observations is unusual because of its regressor configuration. Instead, they are selected because their responses are unusual relative to their fitted conditional Beta distributions.

The case-deletion results show a clear difference between the stability of the **conditional means** and the stability of the **precision parameters**. Deleting any one of the five observations changes the four fitted mean grades by at most `r formatC(beta_variable_max_mean_sensitivity, format = "f", digits = 3)` percentage points, so the **fitted mean structure** is **extremely stable**. The **largest sensitivity** occurs for the `3–5 hours` observation with the **most extreme positive quantile residual**: removing that single case changes at least one fitted category-specific precision by as much as `r formatC(beta_variable_max_phi_sensitivity, format = "f", digits = 2)`%. The remaining screened cases produce appreciably smaller precision changes.

Note that this distinction is substantively important. The revised model's **mean component is not being driven by a handful of unusual observations**, but the precision component is understandably more responsive to observations near the upper response boundary because it governs the concentration of the conditional distribution. In particular, the largest precision sensitivity is associated with an observation receiving a final grade of 100% in a category where such a response lies far into the fitted upper tail. This is consistent with the localized upper-tail departure that remained visible in the variable-precision Q-Q plot (see @fig-beta-extended-residuals-qq-r).

These sensitivity values do not have universal cutoff thresholds, and a comparatively large relative change in one fitted precision is not, by itself, a reason to delete the corresponding observation. More importantly, the broader diagnostic evidence does not disappear because of this case: the fitted means remain stable, the group-specific quantile-residual SDs are now approximately equal, and the systematic increase in residual dispersion seen under constant precision has been substantially removed. Thus, we retain all observations and interpret the case-deletion result as evidence of **localized precision sensitivity**, not as evidence that the overall variable-precision refinement is being driven by a single case.

### Variable-precision Model Practical Adequacy Summary {#sec-beta-extended-gof-summary}

The repeated training-stage diagnostics now assess the **focused `Study Time` mean + `Study Time` precision model** selected in @sec-beta-refinement and retained after the parsimony check in @sec-beta-mean-complexity-check. The summarized diagnostic conclusions are shown in @tbl-beta-extended-gof-summary.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-seminar-conference-3974170/).](img/meeting-2.png){width="500"}

| **Diagnostic layer** | **Training-stage finding** | **Implication for the workflow** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Numerical stability | Optimization converges, all estimates and model-based SEs are finite, fitted means remain inside the response support, and all fitted precisions are positive. | The revised fitted solution is numerically usable. |
| Conditional means | The **largest absolute observed-versus-fitted group-mean difference** is `r formatC(beta_variable_mean_max_gap, format = "f", digits = 2)` percentage points. | The focused `Study Time` mean submodel continues to reproduce the group centres well after precision is allowed to vary. |
| Quantile residuals | **Group-specific residual SDs** range only from `r formatC(beta_variable_residual_sd_min, format = "f", digits = 3)` to `r formatC(beta_variable_residual_sd_max, format = "f", digits = 3)`, giving a **largest-to-smallest ratio** of `r formatC(beta_variable_residual_sd_ratio, format = "f", digits = 2)`, compared with `r formatC(beta_constant_residual_sd_ratio, format = "f", digits = 2)` under constant precision.
