The main residual clouds are similarly dispersed, although some localized upper-tail departures remain. | The systematic increase in residual dispersion across the four fitted mean levels has been substantially removed. The remaining departures are localized rather than evidence of the same broad across-group mismatch. |
| Precision structure | Fitted precision decreases markedly across `Study Time`. **Observed-to-implied group SD ratios** range from `r formatC(beta_variable_sd_ratio_min, format = "f", digits = 2)` to `r formatC(beta_variable_sd_ratio_max, format = "f", digits = 2)`: agreement is very close for the first two categories, while the fitted distributions remain somewhat broader than the observed spread for `3–5 hours` and `5+ hours`. | The variable-precision structure moves the model in the direction required to reconcile the Beta variance function with the training data, without requiring exact reproduction of the descriptive variance-matching quantities. |
| Influence screen | The **largest design leverage** is `r formatC(beta_variable_max_design_leverage, format = "f", digits = 4)`. Targeted deletion changes fitted group means by at most `r formatC(beta_variable_max_mean_sensitivity, format = "f", digits = 3)` percentage points, while the **largest relative change** in a fitted category-specific precision is `r formatC(beta_variable_max_phi_sensitivity, format = "f", digits = 2)`%. | The mean structure is extremely stable. One extreme upper-tail case produces noticeable localized precision sensitivity, but it does not explain the broader improvement in residual dispersion across groups. |

: Adequacy summary for the variable-precision Beta regression. {#tbl-beta-extended-gof-summary .striped .hover}

Taken together, the diagnostics show that the targeted precision refinement addresses the **main structural inadequacy** of the initial model without introducing unsupported complexity into the mean submodel. The conditional means remain well represented, and the group-specific quantile-residual SDs are now essentially equal across the four `Study Time` categories. This is a substantial improvement over the constant-precision model, where residual dispersion increased systematically with the fitted conditional mean.

The revised model is not diagnostically perfect. The Q-Q plot, from @fig-beta-extended-residuals-qq-r, still shows several localized upper-tail departures, and the response-scale precision diagnostic shows that the fitted distributions for `3–5 hours` and `5+ hours` are somewhat broader than their raw within-group grade spread. In addition, the case-deletion screen identifies one extreme observation for which a fitted precision is noticeably sensitive. These remaining features are important to report, but they do not reproduce the systematic across-group failure that motivated the refinement: the fitted means remain highly stable, the residual spreads are now approximately comparable, and the overall dispersion pattern is no longer driven by the constant-precision restriction.

The likelihood-ratio test in @sec-beta-refinement provides formal training-stage evidence in favour of allowing precision to depend on `Study Time`, while the separate mean-complexity test in @sec-beta-mean-complexity-check does not support retaining the additional 18 mean coefficients. The diagnostic evidence is therefore coherent with the model-development decisions: retain the focused `Study Time` mean structure, retain `Study Time`-dependent precision, and **do not reopen the larger mean model**.

No finite collection of diagnostics can establish that a fitted model is literally correct. The practical question is whether any remaining departure is sufficiently large, systematic, or structurally interpretable to justify another round of model development before examining the testing outcomes. Here, the remaining issues are **localized rather than systematic**, and no comparably strong unresolved pattern emerges that would motivate another specification change.

Thus, we judge the **`Study Time` mean + `Study Time` precision** Beta regression to be adequate enough to **freeze** as the final specification. From this point onward, the response transformation, mean and precision structures, links, treatment coding, and prediction targets should remain fixed. The frozen model can now be carried forward to the final inferential analysis and the held-out predictive evaluation without using the testing outcomes to alter the specification.

## Freezing the Final Specification {#sec-beta-freeze}

At this point, the training-stage model-development process is complete. The variable-precision model addressed the main distributional inadequacy of the initial constant-precision fit, while the separate complexity check did not support expanding the mean submodel beyond `Study Time`. Thus, we **freeze the complete analysis specification before examining the testing outcomes**.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-social-network-3704066/).](img/privacy.png){width="500"}

Freezing applies to more than the regression formula. It also fixes the response definition, links, category coding, predictive baseline, evaluation scales, predictive metrics, interval level, and distributional calibration diagnostic. The testing responses may later be used to evaluate the pre-specified inferential and predictive questions, but they cannot be used to revise any of these choices.

| **Component** | **Frozen choice** |
|:---:|:---:|
| Response used by the Beta model | `grade_beta`, obtained from the fixed Smithson--Verkuilen interior transformation defined in @sec-beta-boundary-strategy using the full-sample value of $n$ fixed before splitting |
| Mean submodel | `Study Time` treatment indicators |
| Precision submodel | `Study Time` treatment indicators |
| Mean link | Logit as in @eq-beta-logit-link |
| Precision link | Log as in @eq-beta-log-link-phi |
| Reference category | `<1 hour` |
| Training-fitted model carried into prediction | The variable-precision Beta regression from @sec-beta-extended-specification fitted in @sec-beta-extended-fitting |
| Predictive baseline | **Intercept-only Beta regression**, with intercept-only mean and precision submodels, fitted using the training data only |
| Point-prediction target | Held-out final grade reported on the original percentage scale |
| Point-prediction metrics | **Mean error (ME)**, **mean absolute error (MAE)**, and **root mean squared error (RMSE)** |
| Probabilistic predictive score | **Mean negative log predictive density (NLPD)** |
| Predictive intervals | Equal-tailed 90% plug-in predictive intervals |
| Predictive-interval summaries | Empirical 90% coverage and average 90% interval width, with width reported in percentage points |
| Distributional calibration diagnostic | **Probability integral transform (PIT)** histogram using ten equal-width bins on $[0,1]$ |

: Frozen Beta-regression specification and held-out evaluation plan. {#tbl-beta-frozen-specification .striped .hover}

The distinction between the **modelling scale** and the **reporting scale** is critical. The Beta likelihood, NLPD, and PIT calculations use the transformed response `grade_beta`, because this is the response on $(0,1)$ for which the fitted Beta distribution is defined. By contrast, conditional-mean point predictions and predictive-interval endpoints will be translated back to the original grade-percentage scale for interpretation. Because the boundary transformation was fixed before the split, neither the final model nor the baseline may use a different transformation after the testing outcomes are examined.

### Pre-specified Point-Prediction Assessment {#sec-beta-pre-specified-point-assessment} 

For a held-out student $i$, let $g_i$ denote the observed final grade in percentage points and let $\widehat{g}_i$ denote the conditional-mean prediction obtained from the **training-fitted variable-precision model** after reversing the fixed boundary transformation. If

$$
e_i
=
g_i-\widehat{g}_i,
$$

then the point-prediction metrics are

$$
\operatorname{ME}
=
\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}}e_i,
$${#eq-beta-predictive-me}

$$
\operatorname{MAE}
=
\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}}|e_i|,
$${#eq-beta-predictive-mae}

and

$$
\operatorname{RMSE}
=
\sqrt{
\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}}e_i^2
}.
$${#eq-beta-predictive-rmse}

All three quantities are evaluated on the original grade-percentage scale. With the sign convention in @eq-beta-predictive-me, a positive ME indicates average **underprediction**, whereas a negative ME indicates average **overprediction**. MAE describes the typical absolute size of the prediction error, while RMSE gives comparatively greater weight to larger errors. MAE and RMSE therefore assess the accuracy of the predicted conditional mean; they do not assess whether the fitted Beta distribution represents predictive dispersion appropriately.

The inverse transformation used to recover the percentage-scale point prediction is also frozen. If $\widehat{\mu}_i$ is the predicted conditional mean on the transformed Beta scale and $n$ is the full-sample value fixed in @sec-beta-boundary-strategy, then

$$
\widehat{g}_i
=
100
\left(
\frac{n\widehat{\mu}_i-0.5}{n-1}
\right).
$${#eq-beta-predictive-inverse-transform}


### Pre-specified Probabilistic Predictive Assessment {#sec-beta-pre-specified-prob-assessment} 

Beta regression provides an entire fitted conditional distribution, not only $\widehat{\mu}_i$. For each held-out student, the frozen training model will produce

$$
\widehat{\mu}_i,
\qquad
\widehat{\phi}_i,
$$

and therefore the fitted Beta shape parameters

$$
\widehat{\alpha}_i
=
\widehat{\mu}_i\widehat{\phi}_i,
\qquad
\widehat{\beta}_i
=
(1-\widehat{\mu}_i)\widehat{\phi}_i.
$$

::: {#Definition-plugin-predictive-distribution .definition}
:::: {.definition-header}
Definition of plug-in predictive distribution
::::
:::: {.definition-container}
A **plug-in predictive distribution** uses parameter estimates obtained from the training data and then treats those fitted values as fixed when predicting or evaluating new observations. Here, the training-fitted values $\widehat{\mu}_i$ and $\widehat{\phi}_i$ determine a Beta distribution for each held-out student.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-emotion-proud-6230200/).](img/king.png){width="400"}

This distribution represents **conditional response variability under the fitted model**, but it does not integrate over uncertainty in the estimated regression coefficients or precision parameters. Hence, it is different from a Bayesian posterior predictive distribution, which averages over parameter uncertainty.
::::
:::

Our **primary probabilistic score** will be NLPD. For the transformed held-out response $y_i=\texttt{grade\_beta}_i$,

$$
\operatorname{NLPD}_i
=
-\log
f_{\operatorname{Beta}}
\left(
y_i;
\widehat{\alpha}_i,
\widehat{\beta}_i
\right),
$${#eq-beta-nlpd-observation}

and the testing-set summary is

$$
\overline{\operatorname{NLPD}}
=
-\frac{1}{n_{\mathrm{test}}}
\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_{\mathrm{test}}}
\log
f_{\operatorname{Beta}}
\left(
y_i;
\widehat{\alpha}_i,
\widehat{\beta}_i
\right).
$${#eq-beta-mean-nlpd}

Unlike MAE and RMSE, NLPD evaluates the **entire fitted conditional Beta distribution** through the predictive density assigned to the response that actually occurs. More precisely, the observation-specific quantity in @eq-beta-nlpd-observation is the negative of the **logarithmic score**. For a predictive density $p(\cdot)$ and realized outcome $\omega$, @gneiting2007 define the logarithmic score as $\operatorname{LogS}(p,\omega)=\log p(\omega)$ and show that it is **strictly proper**. Strict propriety means that, in expectation, the score is optimized by issuing the predictive distribution that corresponds to the data-generating distribution rather than a different one.

In our loss-oriented formulation, NLPD changes the sign of the logarithmic score, so **smaller values are better**. Consequently, a fitted Beta distribution receives a larger penalty when it assigns little density to a response that actually occurs. This can happen because its conditional mean is poorly located or because its dispersion is poorly represented: an overly concentrated distribution may assign very little density to even a modest departure from its fitted mean, whereas an unnecessarily diffuse distribution spreads its density more broadly.

In our frequentist setting, we apply NLPD to the **plug-in held-out predictive distributions** produced by the frozen training model. Thus, the fitted parameters are estimated from the training data and then treated as fixed when the testing responses are evaluated. When competing models are assessed on the **same held-out observations, response definition, and transformation**, a smaller mean NLPD indicates better probabilistic predictive performance.

::: {.Heads-up}
:::: {.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on interpreting NLPD!
::::
:::: {.Heads-up-container}
A negative NLPD is possible because NLPD uses a **probability density**, not a probability. Let us recall that a probability must lie between $0$ and $1$. However, a PDF is a height of a density curve and can be greater than $1$. What must equal $1$ is the **total area under the PDF curve**, not its maximum height. This is especially easy to encounter for distributions defined on a short interval such as the Beta distribution on $(0,1)$. For example, suppose the fitted Beta distribution assigns density

$$
f_{\operatorname{Beta}}(y_i;\widehat{\alpha}_i,\widehat{\beta}_i)=3
$$

to an observed held-out response. Then

$$
\operatorname{NLPD}_i
=
-\log(3)
\approx
-1.10.
$$

The negative value does not mean that the model assigned a negative probability. It means that the observed response occurred at a location where the fitted continuous density was relatively high. Conversely, if the fitted density at the observed response were only $0.01$, then

$$
-\log(0.01)\approx 4.61,
$$

which is much larger and indicates that the model assigned very little predictive density to what actually occurred.

Thus, NLPD is **not bounded below by $0$** for continuous responses, and a negative observation-specific or mean NLPD is not a computational error. This follows because NLPD is the negative logarithm of a **density**, and a continuous density can exceed $1$.

The key interpretation is comparative:

> **Smaller NLPD is better when models are evaluated on the same held-out observations, using the same response definition and transformation**.

@gneiting2007 define the logarithmic score for predictive densities as $\operatorname{LogS}(p,\omega)=\log p(\omega)$ and show that it is strictly proper; they also emphasize that average scores for competing forecasting procedures are directly comparable when they refer to the same set of forecast situations.

Finally, testing NLPD should not be confused with the negative training log-likelihood used to estimate the model. Their mathematical forms are similar, but the training likelihood is evaluated on observations used for estimation, whereas held-out NLPD evaluates new responses using the already-frozen training-derived model. Gneiting and Raftery's discussion of plug-in maximum-likelihood scoring and cross-validation provides the corresponding predictive-scoring framework [@gneiting2007].
::::
:::

The full model will be compared with the pre-specified **intercept-only Beta baseline**. Both models will be fitted using the training data only and evaluated on exactly the same testing observations. The baseline has no `Study Time` terms in either submodel, so it provides one training-derived conditional mean and one training-derived precision. It therefore supplies a deliberately simple reference for both point prediction and full-distribution prediction.

### Pre-specified Predictive Intervals and Calibration {#sec-beta-pre-specified-pred-int-calibration}

NLPD is complemented by a direct assessment of predictive uncertainty. For each held-out student, the frozen model will produce the equal-tailed 90% plug-in predictive interval

$$
\left[
F_{\operatorname{Beta}}^{-1}
\left(
0.05;
\widehat{\alpha}_i,
\widehat{\beta}_i
\right),
\,
F_{\operatorname{Beta}}^{-1}
\left(
0.95;
\widehat{\alpha}_i,
\widehat{\beta}_i
\right)
\right].
$${#eq-beta-predictive-interval}

The endpoints will be transformed back to the original grade-percentage scale for reporting. We will summarize the intervals using **empirical coverage**, the proportion of held-out grades falling inside their intervals, and **average interval width**, reported in percentage points. Coverage and width must be interpreted together: very wide intervals can attain high coverage while still providing weak predictive resolution.

Finally, predictive calibration will be assessed using the **PIT**. For a continuous random variable with CDF $F(\cdot)$, evaluating the CDF at a realization from that distribution produces a $\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$ random variable. @rosenblatt1952 formalized a multivariate extension of this transformation, mapping an absolutely continuous multivariate distribution to a Uniform distribution on the unit hypercube. In predictive-distribution evaluation, Diebold, Gunther, and Tay used the PIT as the basis of a general framework for assessing density forecasts [@diebold1998], and Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery subsequently placed PIT diagnostics within a broader framework for assessing probabilistic calibration [@gneiting2007calibration].

For each held-out observation,

$$
\operatorname{PIT}_i
=
F_{\operatorname{Beta}}
\left(
y_i;
\widehat{\alpha}_i,
\widehat{\beta}_i
\right).
$${#eq-beta-pit}

If the frozen conditional predictive distributions represent the held-out responses well, their PIT values should be approximately $\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1)$. Diebold, Gunther, and Tay show that correctly specified continuous conditional density forecasts generate Uniform PIT values, while Gneiting, Balabdaoui, and Raftery relate PIT Uniformity directly to probabilistic calibration [@diebold1998; @gneiting2007calibration].

Departures from Uniformity can therefore reveal aspects of predictive-distribution miscalibration. The **shape** of the PIT histogram can also be informative about the nature of those departures. However, PIT Uniformity should not be treated as a standalone model-acceptance criterion: a Uniform PIT distribution is a necessary but not sufficient condition for an ideal probabilistic forecast, and apparently Uniform PIT histograms can occur even for defective forecasting procedures [@gneiting2007calibration]. Accordingly, we interpret the PIT histogram as one diagnostic component of the broader held-out predictive assessment rather than converting it into a single accept-or-reject test [@diebold1998].

We pre-specify a PIT histogram with **ten equal-width bins** on $[0,1]$ as the main held-out calibration diagnostic. @gneiting2007calibration note that 10 or 20 bins generally provide an adequate display for PIT histograms. Our use of ten bins is therefore a pre-specified visualization choice, not a claim that ten is a theoretically optimal number of bins.

@tbl-beta-frozen-predictive-assessment summarizes the complementary roles of the frozen predictive criteria.

| **Assessment** | **Uses** | **Primary question** | **Direction / reference** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| ME | Predicted conditional mean | Is there systematic average over- or underprediction? | Values near $0$ indicate little average signed bias |
| MAE | Predicted conditional mean | How large are absolute point-prediction errors on average? | Smaller is better |
| RMSE | Predicted conditional mean | How large are point-prediction errors when larger misses receive extra weight? | Smaller is better |
| Mean NLPD | Entire fitted conditional Beta density | How much predictive density does the model assign to the held-out responses that occur? | Smaller is better on the same cases and response scale |
| 90% coverage | Predictive interval | How often do held-out responses fall inside their predictive intervals? | Interpret relative to the nominal 90% level |
| Average 90% width | Predictive interval | How concentrated are those intervals in practical grade units? | Narrower is useful only when considered together with coverage |
| PIT histogram | Entire fitted conditional Beta distribution | Do held-out responses have approximately the expected rank behaviour within their predictive distributions? | Approximately Uniform$(0,1)$ |

: Roles of the pre-specified held-out predictive assessments. {#tbl-beta-frozen-predictive-assessment .striped .hover}

The freeze is now complete. Testing outcomes cannot be used to change the response transformation, model terms, links, reference category, baseline, point metrics, probabilistic score, predictive-interval level, or calibration diagnostic. For prediction, the current training-fitted variable-precision model will remain fixed when the testing regressors are supplied. For inference, the **same frozen model specification** may later be refitted to the testing data for the protected inferential analysis, but those results will not reopen model development.

## Interpreting Beta Regression Coefficients {#sec-beta-interpretation}

The final Beta regression specification is now frozen, but its coefficients still require careful interpretation. In particular, the logit link used for the **conditional mean** creates algebra that resembles [Binary Logistic regression](#sec-binary-logistic) while referring to a fundamentally different quantity. Here,

$$
\mu_i
=
\mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
$$

is the conditional mean of a continuous response on $(0,1)$; **it is not the probability of a binary event**.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-problem-technology-3974187/).](img/plug-2.png){width="400"}

The frozen model contains `Study Time` in both submodels. This section focuses on the mean-submodel coefficients $\beta_0,\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_3$, because the chapter's inferential inquiry concerns differences in **conditional mean final grade**. The precision coefficients $\gamma_0,\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_3$ retain the distributional interpretation established in @sec-beta-extended-specification: after exponentiation, they describe multiplicative differences in fitted precision, not changes in the conditional mean.

To keep the split workflow intact, the numerical examples below use the **already fitted training model** `beta_variable_model`. They illustrate how to read the frozen specification; **they are not the chapter's final inferential estimates**. As established in @sec-beta-testing-roles, the protected coefficient estimates, model-based SEs, CIs, and original-scale inferential contrasts will later come from the same frozen specification refitted to the testing data.

### Logit-mean Scale {#sec-beta-logit-mean-interpretation}

For the frozen mean submodel,

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i)
=
\log\left(
\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}
\right)
=
\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i,1}+\beta_2x_{i,2}+\beta_3x_{i,3},
$${#eq-beta-interpretation-mean}


where the three indicators represent `1–3 hours`, `3–5 hours`, and `5+ hours`, with `<1 hour` as the reference category. Thus,

$$
\beta_0
=
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_{<1}),
$$

while

$$
\begin{aligned}
\beta_1
&=
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_{1\text{–}3})
-
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_{<1}),\\
\beta_2
&=
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_{3\text{–}5})
-
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_{<1}),\\
\beta_3
&=
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_{5+})
-
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_{<1}).
\end{aligned}
$$

Because `Study Time` is the **only regressor in the frozen mean submodel**, these are direct category contrasts. There are no additional mean regressors that need to be held fixed when describing the three comparisons.

::: {.Heads-up}
:::: {.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on interpreting continuous regressors!
::::
:::: {.Heads-up-container}
Although the running model contains no continuous mean regressor, the same coefficient logic is important more generally. Suppose a Beta-regression mean submodel contains a continuous regressor $x_j$ **linearly and without an interaction or nonlinear transformation**:

$$
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i)
=
\beta_0+\beta_jx_{i,j}+\cdots.
$$

Then, comparing two otherwise model-comparable observations whose values of $x_j$ differ by $\Delta$,

$$
\Delta\operatorname{logit}(\mu)
=
\beta_j\Delta.
$$

For a one-unit increase, $\Delta=1$, so the fitted logit of the conditional mean changes by $\beta_j$, **holding the other included regressors fixed**. The meaning of one unit is determined by how the regressor enters the model; if it has been rescaled, the coefficient must be interpreted in those rescaled units.

This interpretation does not automatically carry over when the systematic component is more complicated. If the same continuous regressor also appears through a quadratic term, another nonlinear transformation, or an interaction, its fitted change generally depends on its starting value and/or the value of the interacting regressor. In that setting, a meaningful finite contrast should be constructed from the **complete linear predictor** rather than interpreting one coefficient in isolation.
::::
:::


### Exponentiated Coefficients {#sec-beta-exponentiated-coefficient}

Exponentiating @eq-beta-interpretation-mean gives

$$
\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}
=
\exp\left(
\beta_0+\beta_1x_{i,1}+\beta_2x_{i,2}+\beta_3x_{i,3}
\right).
$${#eq-beta-conditional-mean-odds}

The quantity

$$
\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}
$$

is the ratio of the conditional mean proportion to its complement. We will refer to this transformation as the **conditional-mean odds** for convenience. For a treatment-coded category $g$ relative to the reference category,

$$
\frac{
\mu_g/(1-\mu_g)
}{
\mu_{<1}/(1-\mu_{<1})
}
=
\exp(\beta_g).
$${#eq-beta-exponentiated-category}

Therefore, $\exp(\beta_g)$ is the multiplicative factor relating the two categories on the conditional-mean-odds scale.

The same result applies to a continuous regressor that enters linearly and without interactions. For a change of $\Delta$ units in $x_j$,

$$
\frac{
\mu(x_j+\Delta)/[1-\mu(x_j+\Delta)]
}{
\mu(x_j)/[1-\mu(x_j)]
}
=
\exp(\beta_j\Delta),
$$

holding the other included regressors fixed. A one-unit change therefore multiplies the conditional-mean odds by $\exp(\beta_j)$.

::: {.Heads-up}
:::: {.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up: this is not an event odds ratio!
::::
:::: {.Heads-up-container}
The algebra in @eq-beta-conditional-mean-odds resembles Binary Logistic regression, but the object being transformed is different. In Binary Logistic regression, $\pi_i$ is the probability of an event, so $\pi_i/(1-\pi_i)$ represents **event odds**. In this Beta regression,

$$
\mu_i
=
\mathbb{E}(Y_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i)
$$

is the conditional mean of a continuous grade proportion. Hence,

$$
\frac{\mu_i}{1-\mu_i}
$$

is a transformation of that **conditional mean**, not the odds of an event.

Consequently, $\exp(\beta_j)$ should not be described as "*the odds ratio of receiving a higher grade*", "*the odds of success*", or any similar event-based statement. It is a multiplicative change in $\mu/(1-\mu)$. For substantive communication, the fitted conditional mean on the original grade-percentage scale will usually be more intuitive.
::::
:::

### Study Time Category Contrasts {#sec-beta-categorical-interpretation}

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-college-3702064/).](img/plug.png){width="500"}

We can now apply these rules to the frozen training fit. The first four elements of `beta_variable_parameters` are the mean-submodel coefficients; the remaining four belong to the precision submodel.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-mean-coefficient-interpretation-r
#| tbl-cap: "Training-fit mean-submodel coefficients and their exponentiated values for the frozen Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_mean_parameters <- beta_variable_parameters[1:4]
beta_mean_exponentiated <- exp(beta_mean_parameters)
stopifnot(length(beta_mean_parameters) == 4L)

beta_mean_interpretation <- tibble(
  Term = c("Intercept (<1 hour)", "1–3 hours vs <1 hour",
    "3–5 hours vs <1 hour", "5+ hours vs <1 hour"),
  Estimate = beta_mean_parameters,
  `Exponentiated coefficient` = beta_mean_exponentiated)

beta_mean_interpretation |>
  kable(digits = 3, align = c("c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_mean_parameters = beta_variable_parameters[:4]
beta_mean_exponentiated = np.exp(beta_mean_parameters)
assert beta_mean_parameters.size == 4

beta_mean_interpretation = pd.DataFrame({
    "Term": [
        "Intercept (<1 hour)", "1–3 hours vs <1 hour",
        "3–5 hours vs <1 hour", "5+ hours vs <1 hour"],
    "Estimate": beta_mean_parameters,
    "Exponentiated coefficient": beta_mean_exponentiated,
})
beta_mean_interpretation_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_mean_interpretation, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.3f}")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-mean-coefficient-interpretation-py
#| tbl-cap: "Training-fit mean-submodel coefficients and their exponentiated values for the frozen Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_mean_interpretation_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

The intercept in @tbl-beta-mean-coefficient-interpretation-r is the fitted logit of the conditional mean grade proportion for students in the `<1 hour` reference category. Its exponentiated value is the fitted conditional-mean odds for that category; it is not a comparison with another study-time category. The remaining rows are contrasts with `<1 hour`. For `1–3 hours`, $\widehat{\beta}_1=\text{`r formatC(beta_mean_parameters[2], format = "f", digits = 3)`}$, so the fitted conditional-mean odds are multiplied by `r formatC(beta_mean_exponentiated[2], format = "f", digits = 3)` relative to `<1 hour`. For `3–5 hours`, the corresponding multiplier is `r formatC(beta_mean_exponentiated[3], format = "f", digits = 3)`, and for `5+ hours` it is `r formatC(beta_mean_exponentiated[4], format = "f", digits = 3)`.

These comparisons require no "*holding the other regressors fixed*" clause because the frozen mean model contains no other regressor. They are also **reference-category comparisons**, not statements that moving an individual student from one study-time category to another would cause the stated change in grade. The coefficients describe fitted conditional-mean differences across the categories represented in the model. Changing the treatment-coding reference category would change the individual coefficient values and reverse some comparison directions, but it would not change the fitted conditional means themselves. For example, the contrast from `<1 hour` to `5+ hours` is $\beta_3$, whereas the reverse contrast is $-\beta_3$; the corresponding exponentiated values are reciprocals.

### Meaningful Conditional-mean Contrasts {#sec-beta-mean-contrasts}

The coefficient and exponentiated-coefficient scales (as in @tbl-beta-mean-coefficient-interpretation-r) are mathematically useful, but neither is the most natural scale for communicating final-grade differences. Because the logit link is nonlinear, a fixed change in the logit of $\mu$ does not correspond to a fixed percentage-point change in the conditional mean.

For the `<1 hour` reference category,

$$
\mu_{<1}
=
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0),
$$

while, for a non-reference study-time category $g$,

$$
\mu_g
=
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\beta_0+\beta_g).
$${#eq-beta-study-time-fitted-means}

The frozen boundary transformation must then be reversed to express the fitted conditional mean in the original grade-percentage units. Using the full-sample value of $n$ fixed in @sec-beta-boundary-strategy,

$$
\widehat{g}_g
=
100 \times
\left(
\frac{n\widehat{\mu}_g-0.5}{n-1}
\right).
$${#eq-beta-interpretation-grade-scale}

::: {.Heads-up}
:::: {.Heads-up-header}
Heads-up on returning to the original grade scale!
::::
:::: {.Heads-up-container}
The expression in @eq-beta-interpretation-grade-scale comes directly from **reversing the boundary transformation** introduced in @sec-beta-boundary-strategy. Recall from @eq-beta-smithson-verkuilen that the original rescaled grade proportion $y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}$ was transformed to the Beta-regression modelling scale as

$$
y_i
=
\frac{
y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}(n-1)+0.5
}{
n
}.
$$

To recover the original proportion, solve this equation for $y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}$. Multiplying by $n$ gives

$$
ny_i
=
y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}(n-1)+0.5,
$$

so

$$
ny_i-0.5
=
y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}(n-1),
$$

and therefore

$$
y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}
=
\frac{ny_i-0.5}{n-1}.
$$

The fitted quantity $\widehat{\mu}_g$ is the conditional mean of the **transformed Beta-regression response** for study-time category $g$. Because the Smithson--Verkuilen transformation is **affine** (i.e., a linear rescaling plus a constant shift), the same inverse transformation applies exactly to the conditional mean:

$$
\widehat{\mu}_g^{\mathrm{raw}}
=
\frac{
n\widehat{\mu}_g-0.5
}{
n-1
}.
$$

Finally, $y_i^{\mathrm{raw}}$ is a proportion, whereas the original final grade is expressed as a percentage. Multiplying by $100$ gives

$$
\widehat{g}_g
=
100 \times
\left(
\frac{
n\widehat{\mu}_g-0.5
}{
n-1
}
\right),
$$

which is precisely @eq-beta-interpretation-grade-scale.

The same **full-sample value of $n$** fixed before the training/testing split is used here. We do not estimate or recompute a new value of $n$ when interpreting fitted means or making held-out predictions.
::::
:::

A percentage-point contrast between any two study-time categories $g$ and $h$ is therefore

$$
\widehat{\Delta}_{g,h}
=
\widehat{g}_g-\widehat{g}_h.
$${#eq-beta-mean-percentage-point-contrast}

This formulation is not restricted to the treatment-coding reference category. Once the fitted means have been obtained, any scientifically useful pairwise contrast can be formed directly on the original grade scale.

The training-stage fitted means already computed in @sec-beta-extended-observed-fitted provide the following interpretation of the frozen model.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-mean-contrasts-r
#| tbl-cap: "Training-fit conditional mean grades and percentage-point contrasts with the <1 hour reference category."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_mean_fitted <- beta_variable_mean_calibration |>
  transmute(`Study Time`,
    `Fitted conditional mean grade (%)` = `Fitted mean grade (%)`)
beta_mean_reference_grade <- beta_mean_fitted[["Fitted conditional mean grade (%)"]][1]
beta_mean_fitted <- beta_mean_fitted |>
  mutate(`Difference vs <1 hour (percentage points)` =
    `Fitted conditional mean grade (%)` - beta_mean_reference_grade)

beta_mean_fitted |>
  kable(digits = 2, align = c("c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_mean_fitted = beta_variable_mean_calibration.loc[
    :, ["Study Time", "Fitted mean grade (%)"]].copy()
beta_mean_fitted = beta_mean_fitted.rename(columns={
    "Fitted mean grade (%)": "Fitted conditional mean grade (%)"})
beta_mean_reference_grade = beta_mean_fitted.loc[
    0, "Fitted conditional mean grade (%)"]
beta_mean_fitted["Difference vs <1 hour (percentage points)"] = (
    beta_mean_fitted["Fitted conditional mean grade (%)"]
    - beta_mean_reference_grade)
beta_mean_fitted_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_mean_fitted, float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.2f}")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-mean-contrasts-py
#| tbl-cap: "Training-fit conditional mean grades and percentage-point contrasts with the <1 hour reference category."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_mean_fitted_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

According to @tbl-beta-mean-contrasts-r, on the original grade scale, the frozen training model estimates **conditional mean grades** of `r formatC(beta_mean_fitted[["Fitted conditional mean grade (%)"]][1], format = "f", digits = 2)`% for `<1 hour`, `r formatC(beta_mean_fitted[["Fitted conditional mean grade (%)"]][2], format = "f", digits = 2)`% for `1–3 hours`, `r formatC(beta_mean_fitted[["Fitted conditional mean grade (%)"]][3], format = "f", digits = 2)`% for `3–5 hours`, and `r formatC(beta_mean_fitted[["Fitted conditional mean grade (%)"]][4], format = "f", digits = 2)`% for `5+ hours`. Then, relative to `<1 hour`, these correspond to **fitted differences** of `r formatC(beta_mean_fitted[["Difference vs <1 hour (percentage points)"]][2], format = "f", digits = 2)`, `r formatC(beta_mean_fitted[["Difference vs <1 hour (percentage points)"]][3], format = "f", digits = 2)`, and `r formatC(beta_mean_fitted[["Difference vs <1 hour (percentage points)"]][4], format = "f", digits = 2)` percentage points for `1–3 hours`, `3–5 hours`, and `5+ hours`, respectively. These original-scale contrasts are the most direct substantive description of how the **fitted conditional mean grade** differs across the four study-time categories.

The conditional-mean contrasts should not be mistaken for complete descriptions of the fitted conditional distributions. In the frozen model, `Study Time` also enters the precision submodel, so categories can differ in both **centre** and **spread**. The quantities in @tbl-beta-mean-contrasts-r isolate the mean component; predictive-distribution comparisons later in the chapter will use both $\widehat{\mu}$ and $\widehat{\phi}$.

For the final inferential analysis, these same original-scale fitted means and percentage-point contrasts will be recomputed from the **testing-set refit of the frozen specification** and accompanied by model-based CIs where appropriate. Those intervals must propagate the joint uncertainty in the relevant mean-submodel coefficients through the nonlinear inverse-logit transformation. In particular, a CI for an exponentiated coefficient is not a CI for a percentage-point difference. Hence, we reserve the final CIs and inferential claims for the protected testing-stage analysis rather than treating the training-fit values above as final evidence.

## Prediction with Beta Regression {#sec-beta-prediction}

The model-development stage is complete and the specification has been frozen. We can therefore turn to the chapter's predictive inquiry without reopening any modelling decisions. As established in @sec-beta-testing-roles, prediction uses the **variable-precision model already fitted to the training data**. The testing regressors determine which fitted conditional distribution applies to each held-out student, but the testing responses do not enter the prediction calculations themselves.

Throughout this section, a **hat** denotes a quantity obtained from that frozen training fit. Thus, $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ and $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}$ are the maximum-likelihood parameter estimates obtained from the training data, following the estimation framework in @sec-beta-estimation. Quantities such as $\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}$ and $\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}}$ are then computed from those same fitted coefficients for a new student's regressor values. We therefore retain the notation established earlier rather than introducing an additional `train` superscript.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-winner-3702063/).](img/trophy.png){width="550"}

Because the frozen model contains `Study Time` in both the mean and precision submodels, a prediction consists of more than one number. For a new or held-out student, the model supplies a fitted conditional mean, a fitted precision, and therefore an entire conditional Beta distribution from which predictive quantiles and intervals can be obtained.

### What Does Beta Regression Predict? {#sec-beta-prediction-target}

Let $\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}}$ denote the **intercept-augmented mean-submodel design vector** for a new student. Under the frozen treatment coding,

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
x_{\mathrm{new},1}\\
x_{\mathrm{new},2}\\
x_{\mathrm{new},3}
\end{pmatrix},
$$

where the leading $1$ represents the intercept and $x_{\mathrm{new},1}$, $x_{\mathrm{new},2}$, and $x_{\mathrm{new},3}$ are the indicators for `1–3 hours`, `3–5 hours`, and `5+ hours`, respectively. Thus,

$$
\begin{aligned}
<1\text{ hour:}&\quad
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
(1,0,0,0)^\mathsf{T},\\
1\text{–}3\text{ hours:}&\quad
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
(1,1,0,0)^\mathsf{T},\\
3\text{–}5\text{ hours:}&\quad
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
(1,0,1,0)^\mathsf{T},\\
5+\text{ hours:}&\quad
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
(1,0,0,1)^\mathsf{T}.
\end{aligned}
$$

With

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat{\beta}_0\\
\widehat{\beta}_1\\
\widehat{\beta}_2\\
\widehat{\beta}_3
\end{pmatrix},
$$

the fitted mean linear predictor is

$$
\widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}}^\mathsf{T}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
$$

and therefore

$$
\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
g^{-1}
\left(
\widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{new}}
\right)
=
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}
\left(
\widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{new}}
\right).
$${#eq-beta-new-mean-prediction}

Following the intercept-augmented notation introduced in @eq-beta-augmented-regressor-vectors, let $\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathrm{new}}$ denote the **precision-submodel design vector** for the same new student:

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
1\\
z_{\mathrm{new},1}\\
z_{\mathrm{new},2}\\
z_{\mathrm{new},3}
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

In the frozen model, the same three `Study Time` indicators enter both submodels. Hence,

$$
z_{\mathrm{new},j}
=
x_{\mathrm{new},j},
\qquad
j=1,2,3,
$$

so $\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathrm{new}}$ and $\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}}$ have the same numerical entries for a given student. We retain separate symbols because they represent design vectors for **different submodels**.

With

$$
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
\widehat{\gamma}_0\\
\widehat{\gamma}_1\\
\widehat{\gamma}_2\\
\widehat{\gamma}_3
\end{pmatrix},
$$

the fitted precision linear predictor is

$$
\widehat{\zeta}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathrm{new}}^\mathsf{T}
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}},
$$

and therefore

$$
\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
h^{-1}
\left(
\widehat{\zeta}_{\mathrm{new}}
\right)
=
\exp
\left(
\widehat{\zeta}_{\mathrm{new}}
\right).
$${#eq-beta-new-precision-prediction}

Together, $\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}$ and $\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}}$ determine the fitted conditional Beta distribution. Thus, Beta regression can provide several related predictive quantities as shown in @tbl-beta-predictive-quantities.

| **Predictive quantity** | **Meaning** |
|:---:|:---:|
| $\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}$ | Predicted conditional mean on the transformed Beta-regression scale |
| $\widehat{g}_{\mathrm{new}}$ | Predicted conditional mean translated back to the original grade-percentage scale |
| $\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}}$ | Fitted conditional precision governing concentration around the mean |
| Fitted Beta distribution | Full plug-in distribution for the new transformed response |
| Predictive quantile | A specified quantile of that fitted Beta distribution |
| Predictive interval | A range containing a specified proportion of the fitted predictive distribution |

: Predictive quantities available from the frozen Beta regression. {#tbl-beta-predictive-quantities .striped .hover}

The distinction between the point prediction and the realized response is central. The conditional mean answers:

> **Where is the fitted distribution centred?** 

On the other hand, the precision and full Beta distribution answer:

> **How much conditional variation does the fitted model allow around that centre?** 

Then, predictive quantiles and intervals summarize particular features of that distribution.

### Manual Prediction for a New Observation {#sec-beta-manual-prediction}

Consider a new student whose `Study Time` category is `3–5 hours`. Under the treatment coding fixed in @sec-beta-extended-specification, this student has

$$
x_{1}=0,\qquad x_{2}=1,\qquad x_{3}=0.
$$

Because the same indicators enter the precision submodel, the corresponding precision indicators are also $(0,1,0)$. The fitted mean and precision linear predictors are therefore

$$
\widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_2
$$

and

$$
\widehat{\zeta}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\widehat{\gamma}_0+\widehat{\gamma}_2.
$$

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-school-enrollment-3702056/).](img/team.png){width="500"}

The following calculations use only the coefficients already estimated from the training data.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_precision_parameters <- beta_variable_parameters[5:8]
beta_manual_eta <- beta_mean_parameters[1] + beta_mean_parameters[3]
beta_manual_mu <- plogis(beta_manual_eta)
beta_manual_zeta <- beta_precision_parameters[1] + beta_precision_parameters[3]
beta_manual_phi <- exp(beta_manual_zeta)
beta_manual_alpha <- beta_manual_mu * beta_manual_phi
beta_manual_beta_shape <- (1 - beta_manual_mu) * beta_manual_phi
beta_manual_grade <- beta_grade_scale_factor * beta_manual_mu + beta_grade_scale_offset

stopifnot(length(beta_precision_parameters) == 4L, beta_manual_mu > 0,
  beta_manual_mu < 1, beta_manual_phi > 0)
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

from scipy.special import expit

beta_precision_parameters = beta_variable_parameters[4:8]
beta_manual_eta = beta_mean_parameters[0] + beta_mean_parameters[2]
beta_manual_mu = expit(beta_manual_eta)
beta_manual_zeta = beta_precision_parameters[0] + beta_precision_parameters[2]
beta_manual_phi = np.exp(beta_manual_zeta)
beta_manual_alpha = beta_manual_mu * beta_manual_phi
beta_manual_beta_shape = (1 - beta_manual_mu) * beta_manual_phi
beta_manual_grade = (
    beta_grade_scale_factor * beta_manual_mu + beta_grade_scale_offset)

assert beta_precision_parameters.size == 4
assert 0 < beta_manual_mu < 1 and beta_manual_phi > 0
```

:::

For this student, the training-fitted mean linear predictor is

$$
\widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\widehat{\beta}_0+\widehat{\beta}_2
=
\text{`r formatC(beta_manual_eta, format = "f", digits = 3)`},
$$

so the inverse-logit transformation gives

$$
\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}
\left(
\widehat{\eta}_{\mathrm{new}}
\right)
=
\text{`r formatC(beta_manual_mu, format = "f", digits = 4)`}.
$$

For precision,

$$
\widehat{\zeta}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\widehat{\gamma}_0+\widehat{\gamma}_2
=
\text{`r formatC(beta_manual_zeta, format = "f", digits = 3)`},
$$

and the inverse log link gives

$$
\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\exp\left(
\widehat{\zeta}_{\mathrm{new}}
\right)
=
\text{`r formatC(beta_manual_phi, format = "f", digits = 2)`}.
$$

The implied Beta shape parameters are therefore

$$
\widehat{\alpha}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}
\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\text{`r formatC(beta_manual_alpha, format = "f", digits = 2)`}
$$

and

$$
\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\left(
1-\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}
\right)
\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\text{`r formatC(beta_manual_beta_shape, format = "f", digits = 2)`}.
$$

Finally, applying the inverse boundary transformation already derived in @sec-beta-mean-contrasts gives the predicted conditional mean on the original grade scale:

$$
\widehat{g}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\text{`r formatC(beta_manual_grade, format = "f", digits = 2)`}\%.
$$

This final percentage is the **conditional-mean point prediction**. It summarizes the centre of the fitted distribution, but it does not describe the range of individual grades that the model regards as plausible.

### Predictive Distribution {#sec-beta-predictive-distribution}

The full plug-in predictive distribution combines the fitted mean and precision from the **training-fitted frozen model**. Using the augmented-vector notation introduced in @eq-beta-augmented-regressor-vectors,

$$
Y_{\mathrm{new}}
\mid
\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}_{\mathrm{new}},
\widetilde{\mathbf{z}}_{\mathrm{new}};
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}},
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}
\left(
\widehat{\alpha}_{\mathrm{new}},
\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{new}}
\right),
$$

where

$$
\widehat{\alpha}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}
\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}},
\qquad
\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{new}}
=
\left(
1-\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}
\right)
\widehat{\phi}_{\mathrm{new}}.
$${#eq-beta-new-predictive-distribution}

For the `3–5 hours` example,

$$
Y_{\mathrm{new}}
\mid
\texttt{Study Time}=\texttt{3–5 hours}
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}
\left(
\text{`r formatC(beta_manual_alpha, format = "f", digits = 2)`},
\text{`r formatC(beta_manual_beta_shape, format = "f", digits = 2)`}
\right).
$$

To visualize this distribution on the original grade-percentage scale, we evaluate the fitted density over a fine grid of grades. Because this is a density for the **reported grade scale**, the Beta density on the modelling scale is transformed through the same affine map discussed in @sec-beta-mean-contrasts.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-beta-manual-predictive-distribution-r
#| fig-cap: "Plug-in predictive Beta density on the original grade-percentage scale for a new student in the `3–5 hours` study-time category. The orange vertical line marks the predicted conditional mean grade."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.width: 14
#| fig.height: 8

beta_manual_grade_grid <- seq(0, 100, length.out = 1000)
beta_manual_beta_grid <- (
  beta_manual_grade_grid - beta_grade_scale_offset
) / beta_grade_scale_factor
beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data <- tibble(
  grade = beta_manual_grade_grid,
  density = dbeta(
    beta_manual_beta_grid,
    shape1 = beta_manual_alpha,
    shape2 = beta_manual_beta_shape
  ) / beta_grade_scale_factor
)
beta_manual_density_ymax <- 1.05 * max(
  beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data$density
)

beta_manual_predictive_distribution_plot <- ggplot(
  beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data,
  aes(x = grade, y = density)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = beta_manual_grade,
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(0, 100),
    ylim = c(0, beta_manual_density_ymax)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 10)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 15.5),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 20),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 20,
      vjust = 0.5, margin = margin(r = 12)),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "\n Final grade (%)",
    y = "Predictive density"
  )

beta_manual_predictive_distribution_plot
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-beta-manual-predictive-distribution-py
#| fig-cap: "Plug-in predictive Beta density on the original grade-percentage scale for a new student in the `3–5 hours` study-time category. The orange vertical line marks the predicted conditional mean grade."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.width: 14
#| fig.height: 8

beta_manual_grade_grid = np.linspace(0, 100, 1000)
beta_manual_beta_grid = (
    beta_manual_grade_grid - beta_grade_scale_offset
) / beta_grade_scale_factor
beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "grade": beta_manual_grade_grid,
    "density": stats.beta.pdf(
        beta_manual_beta_grid,
        beta_manual_alpha,
        beta_manual_beta_shape,
    ) / beta_grade_scale_factor,
})
beta_manual_density_ymax = 1.05 * (
    beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data["density"].max()
)

beta_manual_predictive_distribution_plot, beta_manual_predictive_distribution_axis = (
    plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 8))
)

_ = beta_manual_predictive_distribution_axis.plot(
    beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data["grade"],
    beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data["density"],
    linewidth=1.2,
    color="#0072B2",
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_distribution_axis.axvline(
    beta_manual_grade,
    color="#D55E00",
    linewidth=1.1,
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_distribution_axis.set_xlim(0, 100)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_distribution_axis.set_ylim(
    0, beta_manual_density_ymax
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_distribution_axis.set_xticks(
    np.arange(0, 101, 10)
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_distribution_axis.set_xlabel(
    "\n Final grade (%)",
    fontsize=20,
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_distribution_axis.set_ylabel(
    "Predictive density",
    fontsize=20,
    labelpad=12,
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_distribution_axis.tick_params(
    axis="both",
    labelsize=15.5,
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_distribution_axis.grid(
    True,
    which="major",
    axis="both",
    alpha=0.3,
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_distribution_axis.grid(
    False,
    which="minor",
)

_ = beta_manual_predictive_distribution_plot.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

@fig-beta-manual-predictive-distribution-r (or @fig-beta-manual-predictive-distribution-py) shows the entire **plug-in predictive distribution**, not just its centre. The orange line marks the **predicted conditional mean grade** of `r formatC(beta_manual_grade, format = "f", digits = 2)`%, while the curve height indicates how strongly the fitted model concentrates probability density around different grade values. A taller, narrower curve would correspond to a larger fitted precision, and a flatter, broader curve would correspond to a smaller one.

The point prediction $\widehat{\mu}_{\mathrm{new}}$ tells us only the conditional centre. The fitted Beta distribution adds information about **conditional dispersion, asymmetry, and tail behaviour**. Two predictions can have similar conditional means but very different predictive distributions if their fitted precisions differ. This is precisely why the chapter froze both a mean submodel and a precision submodel, and why the later held-out evaluation includes NLPD, predictive-interval coverage and width, and PIT rather than relying only on MAE or RMSE.

[As previously defined](#Definition-plugin-predictive-distribution), this is a **plug-in predictive distribution**. The training-estimated coefficients are treated as fixed when the new response is predicted. Hence, the distribution represents conditional response variability under the frozen fitted model; it does not integrate over uncertainty in the estimated coefficients.

### Prediction Intervals / Predictive Quantiles {#sec-beta-prediction-intervals}

A predictive quantile is obtained directly from the fitted conditional Beta CDF. For probability level $p$,

$$
\widehat{q}_{p,\mathrm{new}}
=
F_{\operatorname{Beta}}^{-1}
\left(
p;
\widehat{\alpha}_{\mathrm{new}},
\widehat{\beta}_{\mathrm{new}}
\right).
$${#eq-beta-new-predictive-quantile}

The frozen evaluation plan uses an **equal-tailed 90% plug-in predictive interval**, so the modelling-scale endpoints are

$$
\left[
\widehat{q}_{0.05,\mathrm{new}},
\widehat{q}_{0.95,\mathrm{new}}
\right].
$$

For the manual `3–5 hours` example, we now compute those quantiles and display them on the predictive-density plot.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-beta-manual-predictive-interval-r
#| fig-cap: "Plug-in predictive Beta density for a new student in the `3–5 hours` study-time category, with the equal-tailed 90% predictive interval shaded. The dashed green lines mark the 5th and 95th predictive quantiles, and the orange vertical line marks the predicted conditional mean grade."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.width: 14
#| fig.height: 8

beta_manual_interval_beta <- qbeta(
  c(0.05, 0.95),
  beta_manual_alpha,
  beta_manual_beta_shape
)
beta_manual_interval_grade <- beta_grade_scale_factor *
  beta_manual_interval_beta + beta_grade_scale_offset
beta_manual_predictive_interval_data <- beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data |>
  mutate(in_interval = dplyr::between(
    grade,
    beta_manual_interval_grade[1],
    beta_manual_interval_grade[2]
  ))

beta_manual_predictive_interval_plot <- ggplot(
  beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data,
  aes(x = grade, y = density)
) +
  geom_area(
    data = beta_manual_predictive_interval_data |>
      filter(in_interval),
    fill = "#56B4E9",
    alpha = 0.45
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2, colour = "#0072B2") +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = beta_manual_grade,
    colour = "#D55E00",
    linewidth = 1.1
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = beta_manual_interval_grade,
    colour = "#009E73",
    linewidth = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  coord_cartesian(
    xlim = c(0, 100),
    ylim = c(0, beta_manual_density_ymax)
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 100, by = 10)) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 15.5),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 20),
    axis.title.y = element_text(size = 20,
      vjust = 0.5, margin = margin(r = 12)),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "\n Final grade (%)",
    y = "Predictive density"
  )

beta_manual_predictive_interval_plot
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| label: fig-beta-manual-predictive-interval-py
#| fig-cap: "Plug-in predictive Beta density for a new student in the `3–5 hours` study-time category, with the equal-tailed 90% predictive interval shaded. The dashed green lines mark the 5th and 95th predictive quantiles, and the orange vertical line marks the predicted conditional mean grade."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig.width: 14
#| fig.height: 8

beta_manual_interval_beta = stats.beta.ppf(
    [0.05, 0.95],
    beta_manual_alpha,
    beta_manual_beta_shape,
)
beta_manual_interval_grade = (
    beta_grade_scale_factor * beta_manual_interval_beta
    + beta_grade_scale_offset
)
beta_manual_predictive_interval_data = (
    beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data.copy()
)
beta_manual_predictive_interval_data["in_interval"] = (
    (beta_manual_predictive_interval_data["grade"]
     >= beta_manual_interval_grade[0])
    & (beta_manual_predictive_interval_data["grade"]
       <= beta_manual_interval_grade[1])
)

beta_manual_predictive_interval_plot, beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis = (
    plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 8))
)

_ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis.fill_between(
    beta_manual_predictive_interval_data["grade"],
    0,
    beta_manual_predictive_interval_data["density"],
    where=beta_manual_predictive_interval_data["in_interval"],
    interpolate=True,
    alpha=0.45,
    color="#56B4E9",
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis.plot(
    beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data["grade"],
    beta_manual_predictive_distribution_data["density"],
    linewidth=1.2,
    color="#0072B2",
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis.axvline(
    beta_manual_grade,
    color="#D55E00",
    linewidth=1.1,
)

for quantile in beta_manual_interval_grade:
    _ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis.axvline(
        quantile,
        color="#009E73",
        linewidth=1,
        linestyle="dashed",
    )

_ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis.set_xlim(0, 100)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis.set_ylim(
    0, beta_manual_density_ymax
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis.set_xticks(
    np.arange(0, 101, 10)
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis.set_xlabel(
    "\n Final grade (%)",
    fontsize=20,
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis.set_ylabel(
    "Predictive density",
    fontsize=20,
    labelpad=12,
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis.tick_params(
    axis="both",
    labelsize=15.5,
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis.grid(
    True,
    which="major",
    axis="both",
    alpha=0.3,
)
_ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_axis.grid(
    False,
    which="minor",
)

_ = beta_manual_predictive_interval_plot.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

The resulting **90% plug-in predictive interval** is `r formatC(beta_manual_interval_grade[1], format = "f", digits = 2)`% to `r formatC(beta_manual_interval_grade[2], format = "f", digits = 2)`% on the **original grade scale**. In @fig-beta-manual-predictive-interval-r (or @fig-beta-manual-predictive-interval-py), the dashed green lines mark the 5th and 95th predictive quantiles, and the shaded region between them contains 90% of the fitted predictive probability. The orange line remains the predicted conditional mean, making it easy to distinguish the distribution's centre from its predictive spread. Under the fitted plug-in Beta distribution, 90% of the predictive probability lies between those two conditional quantiles. This is the **nominal interval probability** under the fitted distribution; empirical coverage will be evaluated later using the frozen testing set. Note that the Beta distribution also respects the bounded $(0,1)$ support of the modelling-scale response, so its predictive quantiles cannot extend outside that interval. We then apply the same fixed inverse boundary transformation to report the quantiles in grade-percentage units.

A predictive interval should not be confused with a CI for the conditional mean as indicated in @tbl-beta-predictive-vs-confidence-interval.

| **Interval** | **Target** | **Main source of uncertainty represented here** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| Predictive interval | A new realized response $Y_{\mathrm{new}}$ | Conditional response variability under the fitted Beta distribution |
| CI for $\mu_{\mathrm{new}}$ | The conditional mean $\mu_{\mathrm{new}}$ | Estimation uncertainty in the fitted mean function |

: Predictive intervals and conditional-mean CIs answer different questions. {#tbl-beta-predictive-vs-confidence-interval .striped .hover}

Because the interval used here is **plug-in**, it treats the fitted coefficients as fixed and therefore does not add parameter-estimation uncertainty to the predictive distribution. The CIs used later for inferential contrasts address a different target and should not be substituted for predictive intervals.

Interval **width** is also meaningful only together with coverage. A very broad interval may cover many observations simply because it is uninformative, whereas a narrow interval is useful only if its empirical coverage remains compatible with the nominal level. The later predictive evaluation will therefore report both empirical 90% coverage and average 90% interval width, exactly as frozen in @sec-beta-freeze.

### Held-out Predictions {#sec-beta-held-out-predictions}

<br>

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/?utm_source=link-attribution&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=image&utm_content=3699345) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-pixel-social-network-3704049/).](img/paint.png){width="525"}

Now, we generate predictions for the canonical testing observations. No testing response is used to estimate or modify the model. For each study-time category $g$, let $\widehat{\mu}_g$ and $\widehat{\phi}_g$ denote the conditional mean and precision obtained from the frozen training fit. Because both frozen submodels contain only `Study Time`, every testing student in category $g$ receives the same $\widehat{\mu}_g$, $\widehat{\phi}_g$, Beta shape parameters, and predictive quantiles. Hence, we can compute the four category-specific predictive distributions once and then match them to the testing regressors.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-held-out-predictions-r
#| tbl-cap: "First eight held-out predictions from the frozen training-fitted Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_prediction_reference <- tibble(
  `Study Time` = factor(study_time_levels, levels = study_time_levels),
  mean_eta = beta_mean_parameters[1] + c(0, beta_mean_parameters[2:4]),
  precision_eta = beta_precision_parameters[1] +
    c(0, beta_precision_parameters[2:4])) |>
  mutate(predicted_mean_beta = plogis(mean_eta),
    predicted_precision = exp(precision_eta),
    alpha = predicted_mean_beta * predicted_precision,
    beta_shape = (1 - predicted_mean_beta) * predicted_precision,
    lower_90_beta = qbeta(0.05, alpha, beta_shape),
    upper_90_beta = qbeta(0.95, alpha, beta_shape),
    predicted_mean_grade = beta_grade_scale_factor * predicted_mean_beta +
      beta_grade_scale_offset,
    lower_90_grade = beta_grade_scale_factor * lower_90_beta +
      beta_grade_scale_offset,
    upper_90_grade = beta_grade_scale_factor * upper_90_beta +
      beta_grade_scale_offset)

beta_testing_predictions <- testing_data |>
  transmute(`Study Time`) |>
  left_join(beta_prediction_reference, by = "Study Time")

stopifnot(nrow(beta_testing_predictions) == nrow(testing_data),
  all(is.finite(beta_testing_predictions$predicted_mean_grade)))

beta_testing_predictions |>
  transmute(`Study Time`,
    `Predicted conditional mean (%)` = predicted_mean_grade,
    `Lower 90% predictive bound (%)` = lower_90_grade,
    `Upper 90% predictive bound (%)` = upper_90_grade) |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  kable(digits = 2, align = c("c", "c", "c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_prediction_reference = pd.DataFrame({
    "Study Time": pd.Categorical(
        study_time_levels, categories=study_time_levels, ordered=False),
    "mean_eta": beta_mean_parameters[0]
        + np.r_[0, beta_mean_parameters[1:4]],
    "precision_eta": beta_precision_parameters[0]
        + np.r_[0, beta_precision_parameters[1:4]],
})
beta_prediction_reference["predicted_mean_beta"] = expit(
    beta_prediction_reference["mean_eta"])
beta_prediction_reference["predicted_precision"] = np.exp(
    beta_prediction_reference["precision_eta"])
beta_prediction_reference["alpha"] = (
    beta_prediction_reference["predicted_mean_beta"]
    * beta_prediction_reference["predicted_precision"])
beta_prediction_reference["beta_shape"] = (
    (1 - beta_prediction_reference["predicted_mean_beta"])
    * beta_prediction_reference["predicted_precision"])
beta_prediction_reference["lower_90_beta"] = stats.beta.ppf(
    0.05, beta_prediction_reference["alpha"],
    beta_prediction_reference["beta_shape"])
beta_prediction_reference["upper_90_beta"] = stats.beta.ppf(
    0.95, beta_prediction_reference["alpha"],
    beta_prediction_reference["beta_shape"])
for target, source in [
    ("predicted_mean_grade", "predicted_mean_beta"),
    ("lower_90_grade", "lower_90_beta"),
    ("upper_90_grade", "upper_90_beta"),
]:
    beta_prediction_reference[target] = (
        beta_grade_scale_factor * beta_prediction_reference[source]
        + beta_grade_scale_offset)

beta_testing_predictions = (
    testing_data[["Study Time"]].reset_index(drop=True)
    .merge(beta_prediction_reference, on="Study Time", how="left", sort=False))

assert len(beta_testing_predictions) == len(testing_data)
assert np.isfinite(beta_testing_predictions["predicted_mean_grade"]).all()

beta_testing_predictions_display = beta_testing_predictions[[
    "Study Time", "predicted_mean_grade",
    "lower_90_grade", "upper_90_grade"]].copy()
beta_testing_predictions_display.columns = [
    "Study Time", "Predicted conditional mean (%)",
    "Lower 90% predictive bound (%)", "Upper 90% predictive bound (%)"]
beta_testing_predictions_html = scrollable_table_html(
    beta_testing_predictions_display.head(8),
    float_format=lambda value: f"{value:.2f}")
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-held-out-predictions-py
#| tbl-cap: "First eight held-out predictions from the frozen training-fitted Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_testing_predictions_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

@tbl-beta-held-out-predictions-r contains only quantities determined by the **training-fitted frozen model and the testing `Study Time` values**. The testing grade responses remain uninspected at this stage. Therefore, we do not yet compute ME, MAE, RMSE, NLPD, empirical interval coverage, average interval width, or PIT summaries. The object `beta_testing_predictions` stores only the frozen held-out predictive quantities needed for the pre-specified evaluation that follows. Because the model contains only `Study Time`, repeated predicted means and interval endpoints within a category are expected rather than evidence of a coding error.

## Results and Statistical Interpretation {#sec-beta-results}

The model-development stage is complete, the final specification has been frozen, and the held-out predictive quantities have already been generated. We can now use the protected testing data for the two roles fixed in advance: **final inference from a testing-set refit of the frozen specification** and **held-out predictive evaluation of the frozen training-fitted model**.

![Image by [*Manfred Steger*](https://pixabay.com/users/manfredsteger-1848497/) via [*Pixabay*](https://pixabay.com/vectors/pixel-cells-emotion-confused-6230199/).](img/aha.png){width="300"}

### Returning to the Two Guiding Inquiries {#sec-beta-results-inquiries}

Recall the two guiding inquiries introduced in @sec-beta-study-design. The **inferential inquiry** is:

> **How does the conditional mean final-grade proportion differ across weekly study time categories?**

To answer this question, we refit the already frozen Beta regression specification on the testing data, exactly as established in @sec-beta-testing-roles. The mean submodel remains `Study Time`, the precision submodel remains `Study Time`, the logit and log links remain fixed, and `<1 hour` remains the treatment-coding reference category. This testing-set refit is used **for inference only**; its results cannot be used to change the model.

On the other hand, the **predictive inquiry** is:

> **How accurately can the developed Beta regression model predict held-out final-grade proportions, and how well does its fitted conditional Beta distribution represent predictive uncertainty?**

This inquiry keeps the variable-precision model already fitted on the **training data** fixed. The testing responses are used only after the predictions have been generated, so they evaluate rather than estimate the predictive model. The final study-time model is compared with the pre-specified intercept-only Beta baseline, also fitted using the training data only.

@tbl-beta-results-inquiry-map summarizes the distinction. Also, note that neither branch reopens model development. In particular, no testing result may be used to add or remove regressors, revise the mean or precision structure, change the links, alter the boundary transformation, or redefine the pre-specified predictive assessment.

| **Inquiry** | **Final model used** | **Role of testing responses** | **Final evidence** |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Inference** | Frozen `Study Time` mean + `Study Time` precision specification refitted on the testing data | Used to estimate the fixed specification and obtain protected inferential quantities | Joint mean-submodel `Study Time` test; coefficient-level inference; original-scale fitted means and percentage-point contrasts |
| **Prediction** | Frozen variable-precision study-time model fitted on the training data, compared with the training-fitted intercept-only Beta baseline | Used only after predictions have been generated to evaluate held-out performance | ME, MAE, RMSE; mean NLPD; 90% predictive-interval coverage and width; PIT histogram; model-versus-baseline comparison |

: Mapping the two guiding inquiries to their pre-specified final analyses and evidence. {#tbl-beta-results-inquiry-map .striped .hover}

### Final Inferential Analysis {#sec-beta-final-inference}

The inferential branch now uses the testing observations to estimate the **fixed model specification** selected from the training analysis. This is deliberately different from the predictive branch later in the section: the testing-set fit constructed here will not be used to generate the held-out predictions or predictive scores.

#### Fixed-specification Testing-set Refit

We refit exactly the frozen specification,

$$
\text{mean}\sim\texttt{Study Time},
\qquad
\text{precision}\sim\texttt{Study Time},
$$

using the testing observations. No formula, coding, link, or response transformation is reconsidered.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-testing-refit-r
#| lst-cap: "Refitting the frozen variable-precision Beta regression on the testing data for inference."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_testing_refit <- betareg(
  grade_beta ~ `Study Time` | `Study Time`, data = testing_data,
  link = "logit", link.phi = "log", type = "ML", dist = "beta",
  control = betareg.control(method = "BFGS")
)
beta_testing_refit_parameters <- coef(beta_testing_refit)
beta_testing_refit_standard_errors <- sqrt(diag(vcov(beta_testing_refit)))
beta_testing_refit_converged <- isTRUE(beta_testing_refit$converged)
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| lst-label: lst-beta-testing-refit-py
#| lst-cap: "Refitting the frozen variable-precision Beta regression on the testing data for inference."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_testing_refit = BetaModel.from_formula(
    'grade_beta ~ C(Q("Study Time"), Treatment(reference="<1 hour"))',
    data=testing_data,
    exog_precision_formula='C(Q("Study Time"), Treatment(reference="<1 hour"))',
    link=sm.families.links.Logit(), link_precision=sm.families.links.Log(),
).fit(method="bfgs", maxiter=1000, disp=False)
beta_testing_refit_parameters = np.asarray(beta_testing_refit.params)
beta_testing_refit_standard_errors = np.asarray(beta_testing_refit.bse)
beta_testing_refit_converged = bool(beta_testing_refit.mle_retvals["converged"])
```

:::

Before using this refit for the pre-specified inferential analysis, we repeat the numerical-stability checks from @sec-beta-extended-stability: optimizer convergence, finite coefficient estimates and model-based SEs, fitted conditional means strictly inside $(0,1)$, and positive fitted precisions.

::: {.panel-tabset}

## **`R`**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| label: tbl-beta-testing-refit-stability-r
#| tbl-cap: "Numerical-stability checks for the testing-set refit of the frozen variable-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean <- predict(beta_testing_refit, type = "response")
beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision <- predict(beta_testing_refit, type = "precision")
beta_testing_refit_fitted_grade <- beta_grade_scale_factor *
  beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean + beta_grade_scale_offset

stopifnot(beta_testing_refit_converged,
  all(is.finite(beta_testing_refit_parameters)),
  all(is.finite(beta_testing_refit_standard_errors)),
  all(beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean > 0 & beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean < 1),
  all(beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision > 0))

beta_testing_refit_stability <- tibble(
  Check = c("Optimizer converged", "All coefficient estimates finite",
    "All model-based SEs finite", "Minimum fitted conditional mean (%)",
    "Maximum fitted conditional mean (%)", "Minimum fitted precision",
    "Maximum fitted precision"),
  Result = c(rep("Yes", 3),
    formatC(min(beta_testing_refit_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2),
    formatC(max(beta_testing_refit_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2),
    formatC(min(beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision), format = "f", digits = 3),
    formatC(max(beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision), format = "f", digits = 3)))

beta_testing_refit_stability |> kable(align = c("c", "c"))
```

## **`Python`**

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false

beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean = beta_testing_refit.model.predict(
    beta_testing_refit.params, which="mean")
beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision = beta_testing_refit.model.predict(
    beta_testing_refit.params, which="precision")
beta_testing_refit_fitted_grade = (
    beta_grade_scale_factor * beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean
    + beta_grade_scale_offset)

assert beta_testing_refit_converged
assert np.isfinite(beta_testing_refit_parameters).all()
assert np.isfinite(beta_testing_refit_standard_errors).all()
assert ((beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean > 0) &
        (beta_testing_refit_fitted_mean < 1)).all()
assert (beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision > 0).all()

beta_testing_refit_stability = pd.DataFrame({
    "Check": ["Optimizer converged", "All coefficient estimates finite",
        "All model-based SEs finite", "Minimum fitted conditional mean (%)",
        "Maximum fitted conditional mean (%)", "Minimum fitted precision",
        "Maximum fitted precision"],
    "Result": ["Yes", "Yes", "Yes",
        f"{beta_testing_refit_fitted_grade.min():.2f}",
        f"{beta_testing_refit_fitted_grade.max():.2f}",
        f"{beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision.min():.3f}",
        f"{beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision.max():.3f}"]})
beta_testing_refit_stability_html = scrollable_table_html(beta_testing_refit_stability)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| label: tbl-beta-testing-refit-stability-py
#| tbl-cap: "Numerical-stability checks for the testing-set refit of the frozen variable-precision Beta regression."
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| results: asis

cat("\n", py$beta_testing_refit_stability_html, "\n", sep = "")
```

:::

The testing-set refit passes the numerical-stability checks in both implementations. Its **fitted conditional mean grades** range from `r formatC(min(beta_testing_refit_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2)`% to `r formatC(max(beta_testing_refit_fitted_grade), format = "f", digits = 2)`%, while its **fitted precisions** range from `r formatC(min(beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision), format = "f", digits = 3)` to `r formatC(max(beta_testing_refit_fitted_precision), format = "f", digits = 3)` and remain positive throughout. These checks establish that the fixed-specification testing refit is numerically usable for the pre-specified inferential analysis. Note that they are not a new model-selection or model-development stage, so the testing results cannot revise the frozen mean or precision submodels, links, coding, or response transformation.

#### Joint Study Time Test

The first inferential question is joint rather than coefficient-by-coefficient. We test whether `Study Time` contributes to the **conditional mean** after preserving the study-time-dependent precision structure that was frozen during model development. Hence, on the testing data, the competing models are:

- **Reduced model:** intercept-only mean and `Study Time` precision;
- **Full model:** `Study Time` mean and `Study Time` precision.

Using the same treatment-coded indicators defined in @eq-beta-variable-mean and @eq-beta-variable-precision, the **reduced model** is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{logit}(\mu_i)
&=
\beta_0,\\
\log(\phi_i)
&=
\gamma_0
+
\gamma_1x_{i,1}
+
\gamma_2x_{i,2}
+
\gamma_3x_{i,3},
\end{aligned}
$${#eq-beta-joint-test-reduced}
